#6334. CT Scans Reveal the Secret of a Mysterious 400-Year-Old Lock

X-ray scans cracked an Elizabethan padlock’s code, revealing how a centuries-old security mechanism worked without damaging an unusually well-preserved piece of maritime history.

For more than 400 years, a brass combination lock recovered from a shipwreck off the Welsh coast kept its secret. Lost when a violent storm wrecked the Ann Francis, the remarkably well-preserved Elizabethan lock still had working letter dials, but no one knew the four-letter combination needed to open it.

Opening it more than 400 years later meant working out its four-letter code without damaging an exceptionally well-preserved Elizabethan artifact, a challenge that brought museum specialists together with researchers more accustomed to studying bones.

The lock came from the Ann Francis, which was returning from Spain when a ferocious storm blew it off course on the evening of December 28, 1583. The ship wrecked on Margam Beach, near Port Talbot, leaving its extraordinary cargo buried beneath the sand for centuries.

Dredging and storms eventually stripped away layers of sand, exposing traces of the sixteenth-century hoard. Metal detectorist Peter Hughes discovered most of it over 21 years, between 1996 and 2017. The finds, recovered by Hughes and other metal detectorists, were subsequently acquired by Amgueddfa Cymru (Museum Wales).

“When I found the lock, I was immediately astonished by the incredible workmanship and its astonishing condition. When I moved the ring dials of the combination, they turned with ease after over 400 years beneath the sands, and I was left in disbelief. I also remember being left excited at the prospect of finding wonderful things from the treasure chest it once locked,” said Hughes, finder of the hoard.

What the lock once protected remains uncertain. Researchers believe it secured a small chest containing valuable items, and its position near a collection of Spanish silver coins and two coin weights recovered from the wreck offers some clues. It may have guarded those objects or a chest holding valuables that did not survive, such as documents or textiles.

To investigate the mechanism, museum experts worked with specialists at Cardiff University using micro-CT, a form of X-ray imaging that can reveal fine details inside an object. Dr. David Williams, a postdoctoral research associate based at the Musculoskeletal Biomechanics Research Facility in the university’s School of Engineering, explained the advantage of examining the lock this way.

“Micro-CT scanning allowed us to look inside the lock without damaging it.”

The task was to connect the letters visible on the outside with the concealed parts that determined whether the lock would open. Williams could examine those relationships in the scan, then pass the combination to the museum team for the physical test.

“By creating a detailed 3D image of the internal mechanism, I could see how the notches lined up with the letters and identify the exact combination. We normally use this technology to study bones and other biological structures, so investigating a 400-year-old padlock was certainly a first for us. I had to wait until later that evening for the museum team to test the combination, so getting the message that we’d cracked it was incredibly satisfying,” said Williams.

The four letters were ANCE, and when the museum team tested the combination, the centuries-old lock opened.

“It’s not every day you get to solve a 400-year-old mystery!” Williams said.

Its remarkable condition and connection to a shipwreck with a known date make the lock especially valuable as a historical find. Deciphering the combination also leaves a more personal question about whoever chose those letters.

“Elizabethan combination locks are known in Britain, but this one is in exceptionally good condition and is associated with a dated wreck, making it a unique find and the code a tantalizing mystery to solve. Of course, now we’ve solved it, we are left wondering if the code meant something to its owner,” said Alastair Willis, senior curator for numismatics and the Welsh economy at Amgueddfa Cymru.

The lock is currently on display at the National Waterfront Museum in Swansea alongside other artifacts from the Ann Francis hoard. They include rare gold coins dating from the reign of Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain and a boatswain’s whistle recovered from the wreck.

#6333. Earwax’s surprisingly slippery but sticky properties deters insects

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Earwax is anything but waxy and may help protect the ear against insect intrusions

This fire ant is struggling to walk on a clump of earwax, a substance that experts think may exist in part to help keep our ears free of insects.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

There are few things more annoying than having a bug fly into your ear. But the body is prepared to fend off these insect invasions, says David Hu, a bioengineer at Georgia Tech.

The goop inside our ears may act as a natural insect repellent, Hu’s team reports 28 October in Soft Matter. What we call earwax is not really waxy at all. Instead, the brownish substance absorbs water, a property that might help it regulate moisture in the ear and keep bugs out, the new analysis shows. “[This] familiar biological material may represent a sophisticated physical defense against small arthropods,” says Stanislav Gorb, a functional morphologist at the University of Kiel in Germany, who was not involved with the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have not studied earwax as much as other body fluids, such as snot, spit or even pee. “It’s a big mystery why we even have [it] in our ears,” Hu says. It can frankly seem like a nuisance. Earwax can build up, clogging earbuds and hearing aids and interfering with hearing, so understanding this substance better may help resolve those problems.

Hu and colleagues analyzed the mechanical and chemical properties of 36 earwax samples from pigs, sheep, dogs, cows, rabbits and humans. They also observed how fire ants (Solenopsis invicta) reacted to both natural and synthetic earwax.

Even though ants seem able to scale kitchen cabinets with ease to invade countertops, they flounder when they attempt to climb earwax. Hu thinks the earwax sucks moisture from the ants’ feet that helps them grip. But earwax also sticks to ants’ bodies, causing the insects to start grooming incessantly trying to get rid of it. “It’s both sticky and slippery,” Hu says.

The chemical analyses provide some clues about the origins of these properties. Dead skin cells make up 60 percent of earwax, along with a smattering of oils and moisture. The earwax contains pores that Hu believes may be shaped like ink bottles to help it absorb twice its weight in water and prevent water from sloshing around in the ear canal. Like snot, earwax has a huge range of consistencies.

Under normal conditions, earwax becomes dry and crumbly in about 10 weeks. As it dries, it’s moved outward by a layer of cells lining the ear canal that act as a cleaning conveyor belt. In this way, the ear maintains just the right thickness of earwax to keep insects at bay, Hu says. “It’s most potent when it’s thin,” he explains. “Too much, and the ants can use their tiny claws to grab hold and climb in.”

Hu admits there’s no practical way to turn earwax into a commercial insect repellent. Each person has a volume of earwax about equivalent to that of a grain of rice in each ear at any given time, says Hu, so even if you add up all the earwax on Earth, “it’s a pretty rare substance.” But, he adds, companies “are trying to come up with biodegradable and biofriendly ways to deal with insects.” And, says Gorb, perhaps earwax “could inspire a new generation of physical, nontoxic pest control surfaces,” that could provide coatings for protecting stored food, agricultural products and technology.

#6332. After Testing Bose and Denon, I’m Convinced the Sonos Beam Ultra Is the Best Small Soundbar

Between its Beam and Arc Ultra soundbars, Sonos finds a new, more compact sweet spot.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

The Sonos Beam Ultra soundbar is the whole-home audio brand’s attempt to find a middle ground in the home theater space. Wedged between its compact Sonos Beam and flagship Arc Ultra soundbar, the Beam Ultra sits in the middle in terms of size, power, and price.

That’s an intriguing proposition: The Beam Ultra has many of the advanced features I loved in the Arc Ultra, including Dolby Atmos with up-firing speakers and A.I.-powered speech enhancement to boost dialogue in the mix. But the Arc Ultra is made for big TVs and carries a $1,099 price tag: It’s an upgrade for serious home theater fans with a big budget. At $699, the Beam Ultra is still a serious investment, but seems far more attainable than the tubular Arc.

And, after a few weeks of testing, I feel comfortable saying that Beam Ultra sounds more like the Arc Ultra’s little brother than a slightly bigger Beam. Its stellar audio performance, which I’ll break down shortly, deserves the Ultra name. And the Beam Ultra delivers it in a much smaller footprint than the Arc Ultra—at about 30 inches wide, it’s only 4 inches wider than the second-generation Beam, but more than a foot narrower than the Arc Ultra.

If you are a serious cinephile with the budget to upgrade, but don’t have a stand or space to accommodate a full-size soundbar, the Sonos Beam Ultra almost certainly sets a new gold standard for compact soundbars, delivering top-tier audio with minimal compromises.

Compared to other small soundbars, the Sonos Beam Ultra has tremendous firepower behind it, which may explain why it sounds bigger than it is. It’s a 7.1.2 system, which means it has seven forward-facing speakers, a single down-firing unit, and two up-firing speakers for Dolby Atmos virtual surround sound. That’s more than the Bose Smart Soundbar (five audio drivers in a 3.0.2-channel layout) and the Denon Home 550, which I previously would’ve called the top compact options in the space.

More audio drivers don't automatically mean better sound. Still, they do let the Beam Ultra project a wider soundstage and reduce the number of audio channels that need to be combined and condensed. The results are, in a word, powerful. It generates an impressive soundstage, simultaneously expansive and precise. It is certainly more immersive and capable than any soundbar I’ve ever considered describing as “compact.”

At the same time, it can convey incredible nuance. The eclectic selection of music I played—from bass-heavy downtempo tracks to classical jazz albums—came through with clear separation across bass, treble, and midrange, unlike lesser-equipped alternatives from other makers. For folks who plan to stream music from their phone, the Beam Ultra supports lossless audio files and can play them over WiFi without compression. (If you connect your soundbar to your phone via Bluetooth, you'll get some audio degradation, whether the soundbar supports lossless or not.)

The more varied your audio diet, the more important it is to fine-tune the soundbar with EQ settings that match the music, movies, sports, or video games you’re listening to. The Sonos companion app makes it easy to swap modes or tweak settings on-the-fly, including the height of the sound from the up-firing speakers. This trick can further enhance scenes in Dolby Atmos content, especially action sequences (e.g., explosions, flying aircraft, etc.).

You can also adjust advanced features like Sonos’s signature AI-powered voice enhancement. The voice-enhancement feature, which was introduced in the Arc Ultra, works wonders when you’re watching movies or sports, cranking up the volume and clarity of dialogue amid other sounds so you can hear clearly. The feature comes with some drawbacks: Cranking up voice enhancement to “high” takes a toll on overall sound quality. I would avoid going above “medium.” This was not specific to Beam Ultra, though; I experienced similar issues with the Arc Ultra as well.

Beyond audio playback via the Sonos platform, the Beam Ultra soundbar supports Apple AirPlay 2 for streaming audio from an iPhone, a MacBook, or an iPad. Basic Bluetooth is built in, just in case, and, to my surprise, you can also connect a device directly to the soundbar via a USB-C cable.

Like the Arc Ultra soundbar, the Beam Ultra can deliver a truly private Dolby Atmos audio experience by connecting to the excellent Sonos Ace and Ace Ultra wireless headphones. The feature, known as “TV Audio Swap,” is easy to set up and works seamlessly. It allowed me to watch late-night movies and live NBA games without disturbing those around me.

The revamped Sonos app is much better and easier to navigate than the previous edition. Its learning curve is minimal compared to before, and it brings a host of thoughtful extra touches. My favorite is the addition of Live Activities to the iOS app, which lets me access playback and volume controls directly from my iPhone’s lock screen or by long-pressing the Dynamic Island.

And, as ever, one of the biggest advantages of Sonos is its modular wireless connectivity, which allows you to build out a whole-home audio system over time. A soundbar can turn into a proper surround-sound system by adding a Sonos Sub Mini and a pair of Era 100 rear surround speakers for a full private-theater sound experience. And a home theater system can turn into audio for the whole house if you add more speakers in other rooms.

There is an obvious customer for the Sonos Beam Ultra: a discerning audiophile/home theater devotee with limited space who wants to compromise on quality as little as possible. This is a noticeable upgrade over just about any compact soundbar, and it may sound better than many full-size models, too. It’s very powerful, just as acoustically proficient, and offers processing features that I generally associate with larger bars.

As impressive as this is, the Arc Ultra remains the best Sonos soundbar, though. With 14 onboard audio drivers, it's simply more capable than the Beam Ultra: You’re getting similar sound, but it’s bigger, punchier, and more expressive. If you have the room, it’s the option to beat. (And Sonos specifically recommends the Beam Ultra for 65-inch TVs and smaller. If you have a 75-inch TV or larger, Beam Ultra may not meet the spec.) Ultimately, the Beam Ultra is incredibly impressive, though, and should open the door for many upgraders who want something that sounds special but can’t or don’t want to break that four-figure price barrier.

Stefan is an award-winning consumer technology editor with over a decade of experience in reviewing gadgets, particularly smartphones, tablets, smartwatches, desktop and laptop computers across multiple form factors and platforms, as well as accessories for them. #6331. A 6-Million-Year-Old Whale Had a Face So Strange Scientists Thought It Was Crushed

A newly identified prehistoric whale had unusual adaptations that may have allowed it to hunt along the seafloor millions of years ago.

An ancient whale that lived millions of years ago had a skull so dramatically distorted that its face appeared pushed to one side. Its bony nostrils were displaced entirely to the left, and its oversized snout curved sharply downward. Scientists have identified the animal as Scaphokogia huachafo, an extinct pygmy sperm whale with the most extreme facial asymmetry ever documented in a cetacean.

The fossil dates to the Late Miocene, approximately 6.3 to 5.6 million years ago, and belonged to a whale measuring about 2.7 meters (8.9 feet) long. Researchers believe its skull may also represent the greatest facial asymmetry known in any mammal.

Most vertebrates have skulls that are approximately symmetrical, with corresponding structures on either side of the head. Toothed whales are an exception. Their skulls have evolved asymmetrical shapes to accommodate specialized organs involved in producing sound and echolocation, allowing them to navigate and detect prey underwater.

“Cranial asymmetry in toothed whales is directly linked to the development of fatty structures in the forehead that are involved in sound production. But in Scaphokogia huachafo, this asymmetry went far beyond the area around the blowhole. Both bony nostrils are shifted entirely to the left side of the skull, while the facial bones differ dramatically in size and position. The skull looks completely crooked,” explains Aldo Benites-Palomino, lead author of the study. He investigated the fossil during his doctoral research at the University of Zurich and is now an assistant professor at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU).

The whale’s unusual anatomy suggests a feeding strategy very different from that of modern sperm whales, which pursue squid in deep ocean waters. Scaphokogia huachafo appears to have been adapted for searching for food along the bottom of shallow coastal seas. Its thick, tubular snout contained dense bone and hardened cartilage that added weight toward the front of its body. The snout angled downward by 31 degrees, while reconstructions of the joint between the skull and first neck vertebra suggest the animal could lower its head by as much as 55 degrees.

“The entire cranio-cervical complex is modified to point the snout directly toward the bottom,” explains Gabriel Aguirre-Fernández, study co-author and doctoral advisor at the University of Zurich. “The combination of dense bone, the downward-curving snout and the flexible neck articulation allowed the animal to move directly above the seabed and feed close to the sediment.”

Unlike some modern marine mammals that forage along the bottom, Scaphokogia lacked specialized facial whiskers and visual adaptations associated with locating prey in sediment. Researchers therefore suspect it relied on its unusually developed biosonar system to detect food hidden in soft seabed deposits. This remains a hypothesis based on its anatomy rather than direct evidence of its hunting behavior. Its specialized ecological niche apparently disappeared as ocean conditions changed near the end of the Miocene.

The skull was recovered in the mid-1990s from the Pisco Formation in southern Peru, a desert region famous for exceptionally preserved marine fossils. Benites-Palomino encountered the specimen in 2015 while working on his bachelor’s thesis at the Museo de Historia Natural in Lima. Its extreme shape initially raised the possibility that geological forces had distorted the skull after the animal died.

“The initial suspicion with skulls this distorted is always taphonomy – that the specimen may have been flattened or twisted by sediment pressure over millions of years,” says Benites-Palomino. “But the sutures are fully closed, and there are no fractures, pathologies or deformations elsewhere on the skull. This was genuine biology, not a result of poor preservation.”

The researchers chose a species name that reflects the animal’s unconventional appearance. Huachafo comes from Peruvian Spanish and describes something extravagant, flashy, bizarre, or aesthetically excessive.

“In Peru, huachafo is an everyday word for anything that is flashy, over-the-top, bizarre, extravagant, or difficult to categorize aesthetically,” says Benites-Palomino.

“When we looked at the proportions of this whale – with its face strongly shifted to the left and its oversized, downward-curving snout – it broke every rule of symmetry and elegance seen in living cetaceans. Its anatomy is so extravagant and odd that huachafo seemed the perfect name for it.”

Reference: “Extreme cranial asymmetry in extinct benthic feeding sperm whales” by Aldo Benites-Palomino, Marcelo R. Sánchez-Villagra, Florencia Paolucci, Jorge Vélez-Juarbe, Alberto Collareta, Apolline Alfsen, Alton Dooley, Dan Omura, Mario Urbina, Rodolfo Salas-Gismondi and Gabriel Aguirre-Fernández, 9 November 2026, Communications Biology. DOI: 10.1038/s42003-026-11074-2

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope could capture images 30% sharper than — and remain operational for twice as long as — initially expected. Researchers say these "remarkable" developments could greatly enhance the volume and quality of the data they will analyze.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is nearing its final destination more than 1 million miles (1.6 million kilometers) from Earth, where it will soon scour the universe for a host of cosmological treasures, including an estimated 100,000 new alien worlds.

But even before its mission truly begins, recent developments suggest the state-of-the-art spacecraft could take better images than — and remain operational for more than twice as long as — initially expected, further delighting already-excited astronomers.

"It is fantastic to learn that Roman is not just reaching its design goals but exceeding them," Eamonn Kerins, an astronomer at the University of Manchester in the U.K. who will help lead one of Roman's major surveys, told Live Science.

Roman is NASA's latest flagship space telescope, following in the footsteps of iconic observatories like the Hubble Space Telescope and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The $4 billion machine ‪—‬ which is over 42 feet (12.7 meters) long and weighs around the same as a fully grown Tyrannosaurus rex ‪—‬ successfully launched into space on Aug. 30, more than a decade after scientists started building it.

The telescope is now en route to Lagrange point 2 (L2), a fixed point relative to our planet where Earth's gravity and the sun's gravity cancel each other out. There, Roman will join several other important spacecraft, including JWST and the European Space Agency's Euclid telescope.

Roman was launched into space on board one of SpaceX's Falcon heavy rockets. It lifted off Aug. 30 from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

During Roman's journey to L2, which is currently around 85% complete, mission scientists have remotely switched on the telescope's various instruments to test whether they function as expected. So far, this "commissioning process" has gone off without a hitch, and by the time Roman arrives in less than two weeks, it should be ready to snap its first in-depth images of the cosmos.

Researchers were already pumped to see what Roman will be able to do once it is in place and fully switched on. However, that excitement has further intensified in recent weeks, thanks to two postlaunch developments.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

First, a series of near-perfect rocket burns, executed during and shortly after launch, saved more than a decade's worth of fuel that can now be used to extend Roman's mission. Second, after remotely adjusting the telescope's mirror, researchers discovered it should be capable of snapping images with around 30% greater detail than engineers predicted.

The team that designed, launched and remotely commissioned the orbital observatory has "done an amazing job" and "their work has ensured that Roman is more than up to the task," Kerins said.

Shortly after Roman arrived in space on board a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket that lifted off from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, mission scientists conducted two major burns, or engine firings, which gave the spacecraft enough momentum to escape Earth's orbit and make the journey to L2.

Roman is around the same size as a small truck and was packed into the nose cone of the Falcon Heavy rocket prior to launch.

Thanks to a combination of "exquisite planning by our orbital dynamics team" and "brilliant execution by the operations team," these burns were so precise that each one saved up to four years' worth of fuel, Jamie Dunn, director of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, said in a Sept. 14 statement.

On top of this, Roman ended up being much lighter than initially planned, which allowed engineers to pack another four years' worth of fuel into the spacecraft before launch. "Since Roman's [weight] was lower than we budgeted for, we were able to fill the propellant tanks to their capacity rather than only filling them as much as we needed," Alison Rao, the Roman propulsion lead at NASA Goddard, said in the statement.

In total, these savings could give Roman an additional 12 years of fuel, which could more than double the mission's planned 10-year lifespan. That means Roman could still be capturing images of the cosmos in 2048.

Given that Roman can collect data up to 1,000 times faster than Hubble, this extended lifespan will greatly enhance the amount of data the new space telescope will be able to capture. "With a 20-year Roman lifetime, we could, in theory, do over 20,000 years of Hubble survey work," Kerins said. "That's a lot of science!"

Roman is now on its way to L2, where the gravity of Earth and the sun cancel out, allowing it to remain in one place without expending much fuel.

This prolonged lifespan will let astronomers compare images of specific objects decades apart — such as expanding nebulas or colliding galaxies — allowing them to detect changes they otherwise might have missed.

It may also let them study objects or phenomena that we haven't even discovered yet, which is particularly exciting, Kerins noted. "The real show-stopper results will be new things we just aren't even thinking about right now," he said. "The possibilities are truly breathtaking."

There is also the chance that Roman's mission could be extended even further, because engineers often find clever ways of making active spacecraft last longer. For example, Hubble is more than two decades past its initial mission parameters, and the recently deceased Swift Observatory lasted 10 times longer than initially predicted before falling back to Earth last week.

Roman's secret weapon is arguably its Wide Field Instrument (WFI), made up of a 288-megapixel camera attached to a 7.9-foot (2.4 m) mirror, which will capture ultra-detailed images with a field of view roughly 100 times larger than Hubble's.

Roman's WFI consists of a 288-megapixel camera attached to a 7.9-foot (2.4 m) mirror. It will be capable of capturing images with a field of view 100 times greater than Hubble.

We have already seen the first WFI images — a series of blurry, green dots captured during a test of the instrument's 18 different light detectors ( see below). However, those photos were nothing like what WFI will capture in the future; those images will be so detailed that you would need dozens of high-definition TVs to properly display a single snap in full resolution, Kerins said.

After Roman completes the initial WFI commissioning phase, those images will be around 30% sharper than designers predicted. "All of the images from Roman's cosmic surveys will be even sharper than we expected," Alden Jurling, a senior optical engineer who works on Roman at NASA Goddard, said in an Oct. 14 statement. "It's a great outcome."

The improvements were first noticed after the WFI's car-sized mirror was realigned by just one-sixteenth the diameter of a human hair, demonstrating just how intricate the commissioning process has been. "Calibrating an instrument is like tuning a piano or guitar before a concert," Maxime Rizzo, a WFI systems engineer at NASA Goddard, said in the statement. "You adjust everything until it's just how you want it and then leave the settings alone so it performs consistently while you use it."

NASA released Roman's first photos on Sept. 15. Each small square represents one of the telescope's light detectors, and each blurry green spot is a distant star. (This is just a test image and does not represent how the telescope's proper photos will look.)

The improved image quality could really come to the fore during Roman's hunt for potentially habitable exoplanets, which is what Live Science's readers are most excited about for this mission.

Kerins, who is leading the Exoplanet Demographics Working Group for the Transits in the Roman Exoplanets Survey, is particularly excited about this development, but he said it does not necessarily guarantee that Roman will find more exoplanets than initially predicted.

The rest of Roman's commissioning phase is also proceeding as planned.

Roman's coronagraph instrument, which will block out the light from distant stars to allow WFI to spot alien worlds, has passed its main commissioning phase and is working as intended, according to a NASA blog post.

Roman has completed around 85% of its journey to L2 and should arrive at its final destination in the next few weeks. (The timeline in this image is a screenshot from Roman's commissioning process website, captured on Nov. 11.)

Meanwhile, a global network of ground stations, which will receive up to 1.4 terabytes of data from Roman every day, has established contact with the spacecraft and is receiving signals as expected, another blog post revealed.

All of these early wins raise hopes that Roman can have a long and successful career, and are a testament to the years of work that went into designing the spacecraft and planning the mission.

"What we're seeing now with the actual optical performance and estimated lifetime of Roman is just how good that design process has been," Kerins said. "It's a remarkable achievement. I can't wait to see what Roman is going to give us."

Harry is a U.K.-based senior staff writer at Live Science. He studied marine biology at the University of Exeter before training to become a journalist. #6329. These 1,500-Year-Old Warriors Were Buried With Riches. Their Wounds Paint a Darker Picture.

The rare cemetery could finally shed light on a shadowy era after Rome’s collapse in what is now France.

Archaeologists with the French National Institute for Preventive Archaeological Research (Inrap) were excavating ahead of a residential construction project near Colmar, on the banks of the Ill River in eastern France. According to a translated statement, they found both a Gallo-Roman village occupied from the first to the third century C.E., and a fifth-century funerary complex containing 14 human burials and two horse burials.

The human burials included 11 adults or older adolescents and three children. Human bone fragments found west of the necropolis suggest that more burials may lie beyond the site’s boundaries. The burial pits were typically quadrangular or trapezoidal in shape and sized to fit the person buried inside. Some of the pits were also filled with artifacts.

Those artifacts caught the archaeologists’ attention. Two graves contained high-quality goods associated with warriors, including a sword partially preserved in a wooden scabbard, a single-edged knife, a shield, and a barbed javelin. The Inrap experts said the grave goods match those of Germanic chieftains, whose peoples allied with and joined the Roman army in the region near the Empire’s Rhine frontier during the fifth century.

The weapons and the clothing both featured decorative elements made of gold and silver and inlaid with garnets, further evidence of the high status of those buried.

Two graves associated with women also produced impressive finds, including silver-gilt bow brooches, silver bird-shaped brooches, glass-bead necklaces, belt buckles, and a bone comb. Even the horses received grave goods: harness equipment was buried with both animals.

The skeletons, however, told a grimmer story, with signs of injury and poor health found throughout the 14 burials. At least two of the deceased had fractures that were never set, and one of these likely left a man’s lower leg useless. Two other individuals had bone injuries likely caused by edged weapons. “The complete absence of perilesional bone remodeling suggests that death followed these violent acts rapidly,” the experts wrote.

The team was surprised to find so many injuries linked to violence in such a small sample of burials.

The fifth-century funerary complex was the excavation’s most striking discovery, but it wasn’t the only one. The team also uncovered part of the Gallo-Roman village’s core, including a residential district and a network of streets, showing that people lived there continuously from the first to the third century C.E.

Human activity at the site began in the middle of the first century C.E., and the site was most densely occupied from the second into the third century. Houses built of perishable materials stood on stone footings and were arranged along a street network that changed over time. Archaeologists also found hearths and wells, along with other structures that they said may have been used for industrial work.

After the village declined, a layer of silt covered the area. The silt shows only occasional use and little human activity through the fourth century, until the burials appeared in the fifth century.

Because evidence from this era is so rare, the funerary complex helps shed light on the poorly understood transition between the end of the Western Roman Empire and the Merovingian era in the Alsace region. “The exceptional nature of this find stems, in particular, from the scarcity of sites that document Germanic settlements during the specific chronological period in the region,” the statement reads. “These new findings will undoubtedly provide a fresh impetus for examining the region’s settlement dynamics, as well as the profound upheavals that shaped this territory during the second half of the fifth century.”

#6328. Scientists Discover Mysterious New Fish in the Red Sea – and Have Never Seen It Again

Scientists discovered a tiny new fish species in the Red Sea but have never found it again, suggesting it may live mostly on deeper reefs that remain largely unexplored.

In Greek mythology, Charon ferried the dead across a river into the underworld. People were traditionally buried with a coin to pay for the crossing. That tradition helped inspire the name of a newly described fish species from the northern Red Sea, Charon’s pygmygoby (Trimma charon).

“One of the most striking features of the new species is the golden spots scattered across its tail fin,” said study leader Viktor Nunes Peinemann of King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST) in Saudi Arabia. “They cover most of the fin and resemble small gold coins.”

The tiny fish is translucent, with a broad orange-red stripe and an unusual four-part eye. The two known specimens measure just 12 and 17 millimeters long, roughly half an inch and two-thirds of an inch.

The new species resembles the pallid pygmygoby (Trimma anaima), a fish found from East Africa to the Pacific but never recorded in the Red Sea. Genetic data suggest the two are close relatives, although further work is needed to confirm that relationship.

“While one species seems to have spread across much of the Indian and Pacific Oceans, its closest relative appears to have stayed in the Red Sea and evolved separately for millions of years,” said Peinemann.

Researchers collected the two specimens in May 2023 at Walih Island, at the entrance to a cave on a steep reef slope. They were found 30 meters, about 98 feet, below the surface, the maximum depth of the team’s scientific diving. Extensive searches of similar habitats since then have produced no further sightings. “So far, the entire species is known from only a single encounter and two specimens,” said Peinemann.

The team suspects that the encounter took place at the shallow edge of the species’ range. The fish may be more common on largely unexplored mesophotic reefs below 30 meters, where sunlight is faint. That possible habitat provides another connection to its mythological namesake.

“These dark, deeper, unexplored reefs could be viewed as a kind of ‘underworld’ beneath the shallow, well-lit, and better studied reefs most of us are more familiar with,” he said.

“Red Sea reefs below that depth almost certainly hold more undiscovered gobies.”

The discovery brings the number of known Trimma species in the Red Sea to 11, making it the region’s most species-rich goby genus. At least nine appear to live nowhere else in the world. To help researchers distinguish them, the paper provides an illustrated identification key to all 11 species, along with photographs and field notes describing where each lives.

The study is published in the open-access journal ZooKeys. Peinemann is based in the Marine Science Program within KAUST’s Division of Biological and Environmental Science and Engineering. His co-authors are Matthew D. Tietbohl Talas and Michael L. Berumen of KAUST, and Sergey V. Bogorodsky of the Senckenberg Research Institute and Natural History Museum Frankfurt, Germany.

“Knowing which species are present, how to accurately identify them, and where they live, is the most foundational step to building a stronger understanding of these species and ecosystems,” said Peinemann. “They still have many secrets and deserve much more attention.”

Reference: “Trimma charon, a new species of pygmygoby (Teleostei, Gobiidae) from the Red Sea with a key to the Red Sea species of the genus” by Viktor N. Peinemann, Sergey V. Bogorodsky, Matthew D. Tietbohl Talas and Michael L. Berumen, 24 September 2026, ZooKeys. DOI: 10.3897/zookeys.1293.204097

#6327. Little Ice Age cooling in Europe may have raised the risk of rickets

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Skeletal remains with signs of vitamin D deficiencies hint at how climate change impacted health

A volcano-fueled chilly climate during the 18th and 19th centuries may have made winter in England so bad, as depicted in this 19th century painting of a man collecting wood, that it raised the risk of kids getting rickets, a condition caused by vitamin D deficiency.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

England isn’t renowned for its weather. But just a few centuries ago, climate change–fueled conditions may have been so bad that they put children’s health at risk.

Calcium mineralization in the teeth and skeletons of people who lived in rural northern England suggests that children growing up during the height of the Little Ice Age routinely developed vitamin D deficiencies, researchers report November 5 in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. In the worst cases, these deficiencies developed into rickets, a bone disorder that can occur when people don’t get enough ultraviolet light.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Previous skeletal studies suggest that rickets became more common among Europeans during the 18th and 19th centuries. One culprit may have been the Industrial Revolution, when many Europeans lived in UV-poor polluted cities and often worked indoors. The unusually cold climate may have added “an extra layer of difficulty” to getting enough sunlight, says Ellen Kendall, a bioarcheologist at Durham University in England

The Little Ice Age was a period of global cooling from the 13th to 19th centuries caused by extreme solar cycles and a series of volcanic eruptions, which can cool the planet by ejecting aerosols into the atmosphere that block sunlight. In the last 200 years of the era, 18 major eruptions helped spur a temperature drop of 2 to 3 degrees Celsius over northern Europe.

Kendall and colleagues wondered how this cold climate affected health. They examined calcium deposition — how the essential mineral is incorporated into bones — in the remains of 21 people buried from 1711 to 1829 in the town of North Shields. Calcium often doesn’t fully mineralize in people with vitamin D delicacies, leaving voids in teeth as they grow.

The team found bands of failed calcium mineralization in the teeth, suggesting seasonal spates of vitamin D deficiencies. Some skeletons also showed signs of rickets. North Shields was a small rural town that hadn’t yet undergone industrialization, so these deficiencies probably weren’t due to bad air conditions.

The unusually cold weather may have changed people’s behavior during the winter, Kendall says. Residents may have kept their kids indoors or bundled them up so that little skin was exposed when they did go outside, preventing them from getting enough UV light, she says.

However, climate was still just one factor among many — including gender roles, diet and pollution — that shaped vitamin D deficiencies at the time, says Kendall. “Humans are very messy to study,” she says. “That’s one of the things that makes them so very fascinating.”

#6326. Scientists Crack a Decades-Old Mystery That Could Unlock Faster Internet

By untangling how the crystal barium titanate interacts with light, researchers have supplied data that could reduce costly trial and error in designing faster optical communication devices.

When light carries data through a communication device, absorption by the materials inside can weaken the signal. Engineers trying to build faster, more efficient devices need to predict how light will travel through those materials and how much will be lost before they commit to a design.

For a promising material called barium titanate, or BTO, those measurements have varied widely for decades. A KAIST-led research team has now clarified how it interacts with light, providing data that could help engineers design devices more reliably and reduce costly rounds of fabrication and redesign.

BTO offers a useful way to control light because applying an electric field changes its refractive index, a measure of how much light slows as it passes through a material. Its strong response to an electric field, known as the Pockels effect, makes it promising for optical modulators. These devices use electrical signals to control light and encode information onto it.

The difficulty is that a BTO crystal can contain small regions, called domains, with different crystal orientations. Those regions can interact with light differently, so measuring them together blends their responses. That makes it harder to determine the material’s underlying optical properties and predict how it will behave in a device.

To reduce that mixing, the team led by Professor Min Seok Jang of KAIST’s School of Electrical Engineering examined two types of single-crystal BTO samples with relatively uniform domain orientations. The researchers used Mueller-matrix spectroscopic ellipsometry, a technique that measures changes in light’s polarization, or the orientation of its electric-field vibrations, when it reflects from or passes through a material. Those changes provide information about how the material affects light.

Their analysis covered wavelengths from 190 nanometers (nm) to 40 micrometers (μm), spanning the ultraviolet to the far-infrared. Because BTO interacts with light differently across that range, the researchers divided it into three spectral regions and used an analytical approach suited to each. They determined how the refractive index and absorption properties vary with both wavelength and crystal orientation.

The team also developed a method for calculating the overall optical response of a crystal containing differently oriented domains. Using the orientations and relative proportions of those domains, the method accounts for the mixed internal structure that had made BTO’s properties difficult to establish.

Even in the wavelength range where BTO is nearly transparent, the researchers were able to quantify very weak absorption. They combined ellipsometry with separate transmittance measurements, which record how much light passes through a sample, to determine extinction coefficients as low as approximately 10⁻⁵ in the 2–10 μm range. The extinction coefficient describes how strongly a material absorbs light, with smaller values indicating weaker absorption.

Together, these measurements help answer two practical questions about a waveguide, a structure that guides light through a device. The refractive index helps designers predict how the light will travel, while the extinction coefficient helps them estimate how much will be lost to absorption. Engineers can use the data to assess devices of different sizes and shapes before fabrication. Potential applications include communications modulators, devices that generate light at new wavelengths, and circuits that process quantum information using light.

KAIST, led by President Choongsik Bae, announced the work on November 8. The study was conducted in collaboration with Professor Harry A. Atwater’s team at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), the Korea Research Institute of Standards and Science (KRISS), and U.S.-based J.A. Woollam Co.

“This study reveals the optical response of barium titanate, which had long remained unclear, and provides a reliable reference for how the material interacts with light,” said Professor Min Seok Jang. He added that the findings are expected to contribute to optical communication devices that reduce light loss and enable faster data transmission, as well as quantum photonic devices that require precise control of light.

Reference: “Broadband Optical Characterization of Tetragonal Barium Titanate by Mueller-Matrix Spectroscopic Ellipsometry” by Jiwon Kang, Nina Hong, Christopher M. Yi, Yun Su Go, Martin Thomaschewski, Hwi Je Woo, Prachi Thureja, Junghoon Jahng, Harry A. Atwater and Min Seok Jang, 20 October 2026, ACS Photonics. DOI: 10.1021/acsphotonics.6c01514

#6325. AI Surveillance Could Be Harming Your Health. Here’s How.

Doctors from Harvard and Johns Hopkins warn that mass surveillance is a health hazard—and AI is making it much worse.

When CEOs and scientists wax poetic about the potential benefits of AI, the technology’s impact on human health often rises to the top—and in many ways, they’re not wrong. Artificial intelligence’s ability to sift through massive datasets makes these algorithms ideal for spotting early-stage cancer or discovering novel drugs. The United Nations even notes that AI-powered disease surveillance could detect potential outbreaks quickly and prevent crises from spiraling into global pandemics.

However, like any tool, artificial intelligence can also be used for nefarious purposes, and a new perspective published in the New England Journal of Medicine highlights a particularly insidious one and its potential impacts on human health: mass surveillance. Debates over how governments and companies collect our personal data are usually framed as civil liberties or national security issues. But experts from Massachusetts General Hospital, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, and Harvard Medical School say that being watched can make us sick, and in the age of AI, things could get much, much worse.

The authors identify at least three ways surveillance harms health. First, knowing (or even believing) that you’re constantly being monitored can lead to hypervigilance and chronic “anticipatory stress,” which takes a toll on both physical and mental health. Second, surveillance can scare vulnerable people away from essential health behaviors. This includes groups with a reasonable fear of persecution, such as undocumented immigrants or people seeking reproductive or gender-affirming care, who may avoid pharmacies and clinics, hold back details from their doctors, or even skip buying groceries. Third, surveillance data can be used to hand out things that shape our health, like insurance, housing, and jobs, unequally.

“Historically, mass surveillance programs in the United States have most often been organized by government agencies and subject to democratic oversight,” the authors write. “AI-enabled surveillance, however, relies on data ecosystems that are controlled primarily by private companies.”

That’s a big distinction. The Fourth Amendment’s protections are limited when people voluntarily share information with third parties, even if they don’t realize they’re doing so. HIPAA also generally doesn’t cover data collected by consumer-facing tech companies. As a result, AI companies and other private actors can access and analyze vast amounts of personal data, and they could share it with the government without your knowledge or permission. Traditional surveillance usually needed human oversight. AI, by contrast, can continuously comb through social media, search results, financial transactions, geolocation records, and camera footage, then combine it all into increasingly powerful predictions.

This concern isn’t without real-world precedent. The Denver-based Palantir Technologies, founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, developed AI-enabled tools for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), including a system known as ImmigrationOS. ICE has used these tools to combine information from multiple government databases, including visa histories and Medicaid records, to target people for immigration enforcement. Another tool, called Enhanced Leads Identification and Targeting for Enforcement (ELITE), pulls names, photos, addresses, and race and ethnicity data from Medicaid records to map areas with people who could be detained, according to reporting in The BMJ. It can reportedly even generate a “confidence score” for whether someone might be at home.

For the authors, all this surveillance amounts to a public health problem. When data collected for health care or social services can be repurposed for surveillance, trust erodes, and people may stop using vital programs. That’s why they argue that AI-enabled mass surveillance should be considered an emerging “structural determinant of health,” which they define as a social, political, environmental, or economic condition that shapes how health and illness are distributed across a population.

“We believe medicine has an urgent responsibility to confront these developments,” the authors write. “Decisions about AI-enabled mass surveillance are being made with limited input from health experts, even though these systems have clear consequences for population health.” Health care technologies can contribute to the problem, too. Clinicians increasingly recommend wearables and smartphone apps that continuously collect patient data, which means the medical system may be feeding the same data streams that could be used for surveillance.

The courts offer another option. More than 20 state attorneys general have sued the federal government for sharing Medicaid data with ICE and Palantir, and the authors say health care institutions can support these lawsuits by publicly opposing troubling data-sharing deals. Clinicians can also help by documenting patients’ fears about how their data is used and any resulting changes in whether they seek care, which gives litigators and policymakers evidence to work with.

AI surveillance could still be a boon to public health. The same ability to rapidly pull together data from different sources that makes it dangerous could also help health officials spot and respond to threats more effectively. In the end, AI is just a tool, and it’s up to us how we use it. But the authors warn that we may not have long to decide. By the time AI surveillance’s effects become fully apparent, its infrastructure “may already be deeply embedded in everyday life.” As they put it, “The norms established today could determine whether AI-enabled surveillance becomes a tool in service to population health or a driver of avoidable health inequities and structural harm.”

A new study supports a more nuanced approach to obesity diagnosis. Here's what to know.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Obesity is linked to a range of health problems ‪—‬ including heart disease, diabetes and early death ‪—‬ but it can be hard to know who is most at risk for these outcomes. Doctors and researchers often use body mass index (BMI) as a convenient tool to assess patients, but this metric does not account for individual differences in body composition, scientists have long argued.

"BMI misses a lot of information," Dr. Francesco Rubino, a professor of bariatric and metabolic surgery at King's College London, told Live Science.

Rubino recently chaired a team of 56 experts that was assembled to better define obesity and develop new diagnostic criteria for the condition. First proposed in January 2025, their new framework includes more body measurements beyond BMI and distinguishes between "preclinical" and "clinical" obesity.

Now, a new study published Wednesday (Nov. 11) in the journal Nature confirms that these new criteria could detect obesity with greater precision than BMI alone. In other words, with the new approach, more people would be accurately diagnosed with obesity and fewer people would be misdiagnosed than are with BMI alone.

Live Science spoke with Rubino and other experts to break down the new findings and learn what they mean for patients.

At the simplest level, obesity is excess body fat. There are special scans and exams that send weak electrical signals through the body to measure a person's body fat percentage directly, but criteria based on body measurements are more accessible across clinical settings.

BMI is the most common of these measurements, as it simply involves dividing a person's weight by their height squared. However, it does not account for individual differences in lean muscle mass or bone density.

BMI doesn't capture nuances and variation between patients, experts argue, and it limits what doctors can say about a given person's health risk.

Additionally, the different BMI categories — such as "overweight" and "obese" — don't carry the same risks for all patients. Certain racial and ethnic groups tend to experience health consequences, such as higher mortality rates, at different BMI levels than others do.

For a given patient being assessed for obesity, the proposed guidelines would suggest using at least one additional body measurement alongside BMI and having their doctor review their medical history for other signs of bodily or organ dysfunction.

The proposed body measurements are less influenced by a person's muscle mass or bone structure than BMI is. They include waist circumference, waist-to-hip ratio and waist-to-height ratio. Notably, because different ethnicities are associated with different fat distribution patterns in the body, the latest Nature study incorporated different waist circumference cutoffs based that varied by ethnicity.

In addition to these body measurements, the proposed criteria look at 18 conditions and signs of bodily or organ dysfunction that are related to obesity, such as cardiovascular diseases, joint pain and sleep apnea. (All 18 factors can be found detailed in this chart.)

Rubino and his colleagues — which together made up what's known as a Lancet Commission — defined "clinical obesity" as a disease state involving at least one of 18 forms of bodily dysfunction caused by excess fat tissue. Preclinical obesity, by contrast, is when a person is at risk of this disease state and may need interventions to avoid obesity-related dysfunction.

That means that two people with the same BMI, waist circumference and waist-to-height ratio may be classified differently, depending on whether they have other conditions. In the new study, between 77% and 91% of individuals with preclinical obesity did not progress to clinical obesity within 10 years, depending on the cohort analyzed.

This distinction can be complicated, though, as the diagnostic metrics for each form of dysfunction contain their own ambiguities.

"There needs to be more consensus on what's actually defining clinical obesity," said Dr. Aayush Visaria, an internal medicine instructor at Rutgers Robert Wood Johnson Medical School in New Jersey. Visaira was not involved in writing the new criteria but authored an analysis of the proposed measures.

The Lancet Commission argues that the categories of preclinical and clinical obesity could help doctors identify the people with the greatest need for treatment. The researchers tracked health outcomes using electronic health records from China, the United Kingdom, the United States and Spain, and they determined that their clinical obesity classification was better at flagging people's risk of death than BMI alone.

Changing the diagnostic criteria for obesity could, in turn, change who is recommended to receive weight-control medications.

They found no clear association between BMI and mortality risk, but clinical obesity was linked to a 69% greater risk of all-cause mortality, compared to no obesity.

The Lancet Commission's approach could drive a small net uptick in individuals diagnosed with obesity, according to the new study.

Under the current framework, "we are definitely missing some people who actually need obesity treatment but just did not meet the BMI criteria," said Dr. Jennifer Hwang, an instructor of medicine at the University of Chicago who has published her own analysis of the new criteria.

With the BMI-only approach, people with BMIs of 30 or higher are categorized as obese. With the new definition, some people with BMIs under 30 would be newly categorized as clinically obese, while a smaller group of people with high BMIs would suddenly not count as clinically obese, the Nature study predicted.

For instance, the former group might include people who have "overweight" BMIs but also have obesity-related dysfunction, while the latter group might include people with "obese" BMIs but without any dysfunction.

Overall, the new criteria would increase obesity prevalence by about 3.3% to 7.4%, the team predicted. The percentage varied depending on the group analyzed.

More research is needed to prove that the Lancet Commission's criteria would improve patient care and be practical to use in a clinical setting, Hwang said. She noted potential challenges in implementing both new aspects of the new framework. While the body measurements sound simple enough to use, clinicians would need training to perform them accurately.

Providers also may struggle with the new distinction between preclinical and clinical obesity. A 2025 analysis of the Lancet Commission framework noted that some patients who qualify for obesity medications under the Food and Drug Administration's guidelines may be recharacterized as having preclinical obesity and no longer receive a prescription.

Rubino and the rest of the Lancet Commission plan to continue validating their framework to see how it could best support personalized obesity treatment. For instance, they want to determine which forms of organ dysfunction are of greatest concern and develop a way of scoring each patient's level of risk.

#6323. A Simple Pill Could Cure a Common Cause of High Blood Pressure

Blood pressure stayed lower for up to two years after treatment ended in a small follow-up study, suggesting some people with hormone-driven hypertension could avoid lifelong medication.

For people with a common hormonal cause of high blood pressure, a cure has required surgery to remove an entire adrenal gland. Medication can keep their blood pressure under control, often with the prospect of taking it for life.

The condition, called primary aldosteronism, accounts for an estimated 5% to 10% of cases of high blood pressure, or hypertension, which affects millions of people worldwide. Benign nodules in the adrenal glands produce too much of the hormone aldosterone, causing the kidneys to retain excess salt and driving blood pressure up.

A study led by Queen Mary University of London now suggests that a limited course of medication could offer a lasting cure for some people with this condition. The approach, called extended aldosterone synthase inhibition (EASI), involves taking a new class of drugs for 6 to 12 months. These drugs block aldosterone synthase, an enzyme needed to make the hormone, targeting the excess production responsible for the hypertension.

The findings, published in the New England Journal of Medicine, came from follow-up measurements in 14 people treated at eight centers across the United States. They had participated in the first study of this drug class in people with primary aldosteronism, also led by Queen Mary and reported last year in the same journal. Researchers subsequently examined routine measurements of their blood pressure and hormone levels to see how they compared with values recorded before treatment.

For up to two years after treatment ended, hormone levels and blood pressure remained similar to, or lower than, those measured while participants were taking the drugs. The main marker of excess aldosterone production remained 99% below its pretreatment level, and blood pressure was, on average, 25 points lower. Researchers reported partial or complete resolution of hypertension, with almost a quarter of participants having normal blood pressure without taking any other medication.

Mason Freeman, Professor of Medicine at Harvard Medical School, initiated the original study while medical director at Cincor. He said, “This follow-up study led by Dr. Brown has generated some extraordinary and unexpected findings. The sustained remission in the biochemical markers of the hyperaldosterone state, combined with much improved blood pressure levels, offers the very exciting possibility that many patients with primary aldosteronism may be able to be treated with a once-a-day pill, perhaps for a limited period of time, and obtain similar benefits to what we now achieve only after invasive diagnostic testing and major adrenal surgery.”

Aldosterone synthase inhibitors had previously been tested in larger studies of people with hypertension. Those studies generally involved shorter treatment periods of 6 to 12 weeks, with outcomes measured while people were still taking the medication. Following patients after a 6- to 12-month course revealed the possibility that the treatment’s effects could outlast the medication itself.

One possible explanation dates to a 2005 experiment in mice. When scientists deleted the gene responsible for producing aldosterone synthase, the cells that make aldosterone disappeared. Researchers at Queen Mary predicted that blocking the enzyme for a prolonged period might have a similar effect in humans, potentially removing the source of excess hormone production.

Morris Brown, the study’s lead author and Professor of Endocrine Hypertension at Queen Mary, said, “While duly cautious about our findings because of the pragmatic nature of the study, they were predicted by previous experiments, and longer follow-up may justify a claim that a finite course of medication leads to infinite cure.

“EASI-treatment is unlikely to be the elixir for most patients with hypertension. But the possibility of tablets achieving a surgical cure has long been a holy grail for this common type of hypertension.”

The researchers are now leading a larger prospective clinical trial called ELIXIR to investigate whether EASI treatment can provide a lasting cure for people with primary aldosteronism. The trial will also use molecular imaging of the adrenal glands to examine whether prolonged treatment causes aldosterone-producing cells to disappear in humans.

Reference: “Hyperaldosteronism Remission after Extended Aldosterone Synthase Inhibition” by Morris J. Brown, Adina F. Turcu, Ramin Sam, Lawrence S. Kirschner, Oksana Hamidi, Aysegul Eren, Anat Ben-Shlomo, Wenyu Huang, Irina Bancos, Amir H. Hamrahian and Mason W. Freeman, 6 November 2026, New England Journal of Medicine. DOI: 10.1056/NEJMc2611265

#6322. A Viking Couple’s Grave May Reveal Who Really Settled This Strategic Island 1,100 Years Ago

Two metal detectorists searching the Isle of Man were surprised to find not one but two of the island’s most significant Viking finds.

Two metal detectorists searching the Isle of Man received double the surprise when they uncovered a 1,100-year-old double grave. It contained rare brooches typically worn by Scandinavian women and a sword that, according to one expert, would once have gleamed with a “bright silver” pommel. The site also produced intricately decorated trading weights, a Viking axe head, balance scales, and a ceremonial bronze ladle.

“This is an extraordinary discovery and one of the most significant groups of Viking Age objects found on the Isle of Man,” Allison Fox said in a statement. Fox is curator for archaeology at Manx National Heritage, a museum and heritage trust on the Isle of Man, a self-governing British Crown dependency in the Irish Sea between Great Britain and Ireland. “What makes it particularly exciting is the combination of finds, which gives us a rare opportunity to explore the lives of some of the island’s earliest Scandinavian settlers.”

Experts believe the metal detectorists, Daniel Crowe and Rhett Britton, came upon the double grave of a man and a woman who were buried with some of their finest possessions: three brooches for her and a sword for him. Fox said the date of the brooches suggests the grave may be the “earliest known female Viking Age burial” on the island. Together with the other finds, she said, the objects “help us build a picture of the people who lived here more than a thousand years ago, how they traded, and the connections they maintained across the Viking world.”

The find dates to around 900 C.E. That places it at the early end of the Viking Age on the Isle of Man, just as Scandinavian communities were becoming established there. Some of the objects are also the first of their kind found on the island.

Museum experts believe the Vikings first arrived on the island during the ninth century. Recognizing the strategic importance of its location in the Irish Sea, they established trading links before settling there. A rich Viking heritage remains across the island, and burials found in the past show evidence of pagan traditions. Viking influence still runs through Manx culture today. Tynwald, the island’s parliament, was founded during the Viking Age and is known as one of the world’s oldest continuous parliaments.

After making their discovery, Crowe and Britton didn’t try to clean the objects. Fox says this has allowed experts to fully appreciate the objects’ intricate details. She added that the brooches still have soil inside them, and the team is carefully excavating it in hopes of finding traces of textile.

Two of the brooches are a matching pair of oval “tortoise” brooches, the kind Scandinavian women wore to fasten their dresses at the shoulders. Both are covered in intricate interlocking animals, a hallmark of Viking art. According to Manx National Heritage, only one other pair like them has ever been found on the Isle of Man, and that was found by Daniel Crowe’s own father, John Crowe, along with fellow metal detectorist Craig Evans. The new pair is likely about 50 years older, which is why experts think this grave may be the island’s earliest known female Viking burial. The third brooch, decorated with spirals and a glass center, is the first of its kind found on the island.

The sword is the type a man would have carried, and it’s the 13th Viking sword found on the Isle of Man. Although the blade is badly corroded and parts of it are missing entirely, Fox said in a video from the heritage group that the pommel still shows “signs of the really intricate decorating that would have been on the pommel when it was buried.” X-ray analysis revealed traces of silver and copper wire inlaid into the iron, which makes it one of only three swords found on the island with such decoration.

“When this sword was buried,” she said, “this top part of the sword would have been really bright silver, a really high-status object.” In addition, traces of wood show that the sword’s handle was covered in wood rather than thread or horn.

Although 1,100 years in the ground caused much of the sword’s damage, experts believe the Vikings broke it on purpose as part of a burial ritual.

Because the brooches were found alongside the sword (items linked to a woman and a man, respectively), a double burial seems likely. Experts said, however, that they can’t be sure whether the grave goods came from one grave or from two graves placed close together.

Beyond the burial itself, the decorated lead weights and bronze balance scales found at the site highlight the Isle of Man’s role in Irish Sea trade. The weights are the first of their kind found on the island. One of them has a decorative bronze fitting, with artwork typical of Britain and Ireland, that may have been taken from another object.

The bronze ladle, another first for the island, was likely used in ceremonies.

Despite all the experts have gleaned from the discovery, there’s still much to be learned. “Although the original burial site has been disturbed,” Fox said, “further research may reveal much more about these objects and the people who owned them.”

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. #6321. Scientists Develop Injectable Glucose Sensor That Could Change Diabetes Care

An experimental injectable sensor could give people with diabetes a more affordable way to track blood sugar, with early tests showing that a cheaper sensing ingredient performed similarly to its costlier alternative.

For millions of people with diabetes, knowing how glucose levels are changing helps guide decisions about medication, meals, and daily activities. Continuous glucose monitors provide that information in real time, but their cost keeps the devices out of reach for some patients. Making monitoring more affordable requires attention to the materials inside a sensor, as well as how reliably they work.

Researchers at Texas A&M University have identified a less expensive ingredient for an experimental injectable glucose sensor. Their study, published in ACS Measurement Science AU, found that a sensing material costing roughly one-tenth as much as an alternative used in earlier versions delivered comparable performance.

The proposed sensor houses its sensing chemistry in a small hydrogel, a water-rich material that can be injected into tissue and sit beneath the skin. The gel provides a stable home for the sensing materials while allowing glucose to pass through. In testing, it retained more than 94% of the sensing mixture over seven days, demonstrating that the chemistry could function within an injectable platform.

“Our long-term goal is to develop a reliable, affordable injectable glucose sensor that can expand access to continuous glucose monitoring, particularly for people in under-resourced communities and those without adequate insurance coverage,” said Dr. Gérard L. Coté, the study’s principal investigator and a professor of biomedical engineering in Texas A&M’s College of Engineering. “Reducing the cost of the sensing materials is one step toward making these technologies accessible to more people who need them.”

To measure glucose, the platform uses changes in near-infrared fluorescence, a light signal beyond the visible range. Many glucose-monitoring systems rely on enzymes, which help chemical reactions occur. This approach instead detects glucose through a competition between molecules.

Glucose and a fluorescent sugar compound compete for available binding sites on a protein called concanavalin A, or ConA. As glucose concentrations rise, more glucose molecules enter that competition, changing the fluorescent signal. This process, known as competitive binding, allows the researchers to track glucose concentrations without enzymes.

The team compared several glucose-binding compounds, including two forms of a sugar called mannopentaose. Earlier versions of the technology used α-mannopentaose. The much less expensive β-mannopentaose provided comparable sensing performance and also performed well in artificial interstitial fluid, a solution designed to mimic the environment beneath the skin.

“The surprising part was how closely the lower-cost material matched the performance of the more expensive alternative,” said Dr. Sayantan Tripathy, an assistant research scientist in Texas A&M’s Optical and Bio-Sensing Laboratory and the study’s lead author. “In this case, the cheaper option wasn’t really a compromise, and that’s an important finding when you’re thinking about future glucose-monitoring technologies.”

The cost comparison concerns one sensing component. The technology remains at the proof-of-concept stage and needs additional development and testing before it could be considered for clinical use.

“Developing an affordable glucose sensor means considering the cost of the individual materials as well as how well they work together,” Coté said. “This study shows that we can substantially reduce the cost of one sensing component while maintaining comparable performance, giving us a promising foundation for further development.”

Reducing manufacturing costs could eventually help expand access to future diabetes-monitoring technologies. That possibility makes affordability a consideration throughout development, alongside technical performance.

“When new medical technologies are expensive, access can be limited,” said Dr. Melissa Grunlan, a study co-author, professor of biomedical engineering in the College of Engineering, and professor of chemistry in the College of Arts and Sciences. “Our goal is to develop sensors that are not only effective but affordable for the people who rely on them.”

The team plans to refine the platform and evaluate additional components that may improve its performance, longevity, and practicality.

“While the work remains in the research stage, the findings suggest that future glucose-monitoring technologies may not have to rely on expensive materials to deliver effective results,” Tripathy said.

Reference: “β-Anomeric Mannopentaose-Based Nonenzymatic NIR Glucose Sensor Enabling Cost-Effective Continuous Monitoring” by Sayantan Tripathy, Diana Al Husseini, Carolina I. Martinez, Anthony Dongchau, Samyucktha Ganesapandian, Melissa A Grunlan and Gerard L Cote, 19 August 2026, ACS Measurement Science Au. DOI: 10.1021/acsmeasuresciau.6c00076

This research was funded by the National Science Foundation (NSF) Engineering Research Center for Precise Advanced Technologies and Health Systems for Under-resourced Populations.
