Scientists have discovered that a known mushroom, Galerina indica, contains both psychedelic chemicals and deadly toxins.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A tiny brown mushroom found in Florida's swamps is the first known fungus to contain both psilocybin, the chemical compound in psychedelic mushrooms; and amatoxin, the poisonous substance in the world's deadliest mushrooms.

The species, Galerina indica, has been nicknamed the "dark magic mushroom" and was characterized in a study published Wednesday (Nov. 11) in the journal Current Biology.

"There is no species of mushroom anywhere, in any group, that has been known to produce both at the same time," study first author Andrew Kunik, a fungal biology researcher at the University of Florida, told Live Science. "So it's quite remarkable."

Exactly why the dark magic mushroom has evolved to contain these two compounds is unclear, but the authors told Live Science that they may give the fungus a powerful defense against being eaten.

The ability to produce either psychedelic or toxic chemicals has evolved multiple times across fungal lineages. A process called horizontal gene transfer, which is widespread among fungi, has played a part in that process.

In horizontal gene transfer an organism passes new genetic material to another, as opposed to vertical gene transfer, in which a parent passes genetic material to offspring. It can lead to unexpected genetic combinations and, in bacteria, plays a key role in the development of antibiotic resistance.

The tiny mushrooms seem to have acquired both psychedelic and toxic compounds via horizontal gene transfer.

Some of the world's deadliest mushrooms, from the Amanita genus, stop cells from producing proteins and can cause death through liver failure. Past work has shown these mushrooms shared the ability to produce their poisonous amatoxins via horizontal gene transfer with mushrooms from the unrelated genera Galerina and Lepiota. Some mushrooms have acquired the ability to produce psilocybin via horizontal gene transfer as well.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

But Kunik and colleagues weren't looking for specific chemicals when they began hunting for Galerina mushrooms in the swamps of Florida; they just wanted to learn more about the mushrooms' chemical makeup, as not all Florida Galerina mushrooms had been characterized before.

To find them both together in one mushroom, I never expected to find that.

They collected five specimens from Galerina, a genus that contains over 300 species worldwide, many of which are poisonous. Among the samples they collected were small G. indica specimens that grew on moss-covered palm trunks. The largest mushrooms were only about 0.2 inches (0.5 centimeters) tall, with caps up to about 0.1 inches (0.25 cm) wide.

Chemical analyses revealed that the dark magic mushroom contained both psilocybin and amatoxins, including one amatoxin that had never been documented in mushrooms. The new amatoxin wasn't wholly unexpected, given that other species of Galerina produce closely related amatoxins, Kunik said.

The production of psilocybin alongside the amatoxins was more of a surprise for the research team.

"To find them both together in one mushroom, I never expected to find that," study co-author Matthew E. Smith, a plant pathologist at the University of Florida, told Live Science. "We were shocked."

To understand how the tiny, deadly mushroom acquired its mind-altering, liver-poisoning abilities, the team compared the genes of G. indica with those of other psilocybin-producing mushrooms, finding the genes shared a common evolutionary origin — even though the mushrooms themselves are distantly related.

Scanning electron microscopy image of the spores from the “dark magic mushroom”.

The researchers also found G. indica’s psilocybin-producing genes are arranged in a different order than in other psilocybin-producing fungi, which suggests the gene cluster was rearranged during its evolutionary history, a clue that horizontal gene transfer happened.

G. indica seems to have acquired the ability to produce psilocybin via horizontal gene transfer from unrelated fungi about 15.5 million years ago, based on reconstructions of Galerina’s evolutionary history from DNA analysis, Smith said. However, it’s possible that psilocybin-producing genes entered the lineage through two separate horizontal gene transfer events, possibly as recently as 6 million years ago, Kunik noted. Collecting and sequencing more Galerina specimens could help untangle their evolutionary history.

The findings are surprising, said Hannah Reynolds, a fungal ecologist at Western Connecticut State University who was not involved with the new research. "What was exciting about this paper was seeing both of these [compounds] present, seeing that this gene cluster jumped in, got rearranged, maybe came in twice — it's very cool," Reynolds told Live Science.

The ability to produce two types of incapacitating chemicals could form a powerful defense against being eaten, because organisms that would normally eat them would have difficulty evolving defenses against both, Kunik speculated.

But the idea that this duo of compounds prevents the mushroom from being eaten is just a hypothesis. To buttress that idea, further research might tweak the genes of the dark magic mushroom to observe how removing one compound affects the species' role in the food web, Kunik suggested.

Tropical and subtropical mushrooms are historically understudied, so there is likely much more incredible fungal diversity right under our feet, Smith said.

Kunik et al. (2026). "The 'dark magic mushroom' co-produces amatoxins and psilocybin." Current Biology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2026.10.041

#6319. Scientists Discover How Exercise Could Help Protect the Brain From Parkinson’s

Exercise may benefit people with Parkinson’s disease in ways that go far beyond building strength and improving mobility. A review of 129 studies suggests that contracting muscles release chemical messengers capable of influencing brain health, potentially helping vulnerable nerve cells resist damage.

The research highlights how regular physical activity can improve movement, balance, mood, and cognitive function while reducing falls and disability. Scientists are also investigating whether the biological changes triggered by exercise could help slow aspects of the disease itself.

“Muscles do much more than move our body. They can act like an endocrine organ, producing hormone-like chemical messengers called ‘exerkines,’ which are released during exercise—just like the pancreas produces insulin or the thyroid gland produces thyroid hormones,” explains Dr. Miguel Germán Borda.

When muscles contract, they release signaling molecules known as exerkines that can travel through the bloodstream and influence organs throughout the body, including the brain, heart, liver, and immune system. Among the molecules examined in the review were brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), irisin, cathepsin B, myostatin, and growth/differentiation factor 15 (GDF15). These substances have different biological functions, and researchers are working to understand their individual contributions to brain health.

“So, the next question became, how do exerkines protect the brain?” says Dr. Salomón Páez-García. “We found that the exerkines act as a medium for the crosstalk between the muscle and the brain. Though the brain controls muscles, exercising muscles send beneficial signals back to the brain through exerkines,” he further explains.

Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a progressive neurological disorder characterized by the loss of dopamine-producing neurons, particularly in a brain region called the substantia nigra. This degeneration contributes to movement difficulties, while the disease can also affect thinking, mood, sleep, and other functions. With populations aging worldwide, Parkinson’s represents an increasing public health challenge.

The reviewed research suggests that certain exercise-related signaling molecules may reduce inflammation and oxidative stress, support mitochondrial function, and promote neuroplasticity, the brain’s ability to adapt and form new connections. Experimental findings indicate that these effects can help dopamine-producing neurons withstand cellular stress and damage. However, further clinical research is needed to establish whether these mechanisms meaningfully slow neurodegeneration in people with Parkinson’s.

Muscle health becomes increasingly important as Parkinson’s progresses. Sarcopenia, the gradual age-related loss of muscle mass, strength, and physical function, can contribute to frailty and disability. In people with Parkinson’s, it may also be associated with more frequent falls, greater cognitive impairment, poorer outcomes, and reduced quality of life.

The review identified benefits across several types of physical activity. Aerobic exercise, including walking and jogging, supports cardiovascular fitness, while resistance training, such as weightlifting and squats, builds muscle strength. Balance exercises, including Tai Chi and standing on one leg, improve stability. Programs combining these approaches can address multiple physical challenges simultaneously. Current Parkinson’s care guidelines recommend beginning exercise early, maintaining regular activity, and adjusting exercise programs to individual abilities as the disease progresses.

“Muscle is a biologically active tissue that has the potential to influence neural function. Building on this, we collected experimental, observational, and interventional data that evaluated the interplay between muscle status and exercise in PD,” says Dr. Salomón Páez-García, the study’s first author.

Although exercise is already an established component of Parkinson’s management, its potential neuroprotective effects remain under investigation. Researchers still need to determine which exercise types, intensities, and durations produce the greatest long-term benefits, as well as which exerkines are most responsible for the observed biological effects.

Reference: “Exercise, exerkines, and muscle–brain crosstalk in Parkinson’s disease” by Salomón Páez-García, Edgar Alvarado, Alejandro Cuevas, Laura Valverde, Eduardo Salinas, Kevin O’Hara-Veintimilla, María Cruz Rodríguez-Oroz and Miguel Germán Borda, 25 February 2026, Neuroprotection. DOI: 10.1002/nep3.70032

#6318. Record-low temperature created on China’s space station

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A Bose-Einstein condensate reached about 10 trillionths of a kelvin

An experiment on China's Tiangong space station (rendering shown) reached a record-low temperature in a state of matter called a Bose-Einstein condensate.

Shujianyang/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Science has reached a new low. Temperature, that is.

Scientists cooled a collection of atoms to about 10 picokelvins, or 10 trillionths of a kelvin. That’s barely a smidge above absolute zero (−273.15° Celsius). The atoms formed a Bose-Einstein condensate, a quantum state of matter, colder than any before, researchers report November 5 in Science.

To achieve that record-low chill, scientists took their work to space. The atoms orbited Earth aboard China’s Tiangong space station. There, researchers used laser-based traps to contain 20,000 rubidium atoms and reduce their motion, thereby cooling them. At an atomic level, temperature is tied to motion: Atoms and molecules in the air around us move more slowly when it’s colder. Similarly, in systems of cold atoms, scientists can define an effective temperature based on how slowly the atoms spread apart when they are allowed to expand.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

On Earth, gravitational forces cause clouds of atoms to sag, reducing the effectiveness of cooling. But on the space station, the atoms experienced microgravity, the apparent weightlessness of an object in free fall.

To make a Bose-Einstein condensate, a disorderly gaggle of atoms is cooled until the atoms all take on the same quantum state, acting as one entity. By experimenting with ultracold atoms, researchers can study exotic states of matter and other mysterious physics. And they can test fundamental concepts, such as the equivalence principle — the idea that explains why objects of different masses fall at the same rate in a vacuum.

Spacefaring Bose-Einstein condensates were previously made on the International Space Station, at effective temperatures as low as 52 picokelvins. And an experiment on Earth, in which atoms were dropped down a tower to induce weightlessness, reached 38 picokelvins. But drop tower experiments are limited by the time their free fall lasts. That’s not an issue for experiments in Earth’s orbit. So cold atoms in space are really taking off.

#6317. The 6 Best Electric Snow Shovels for Quickly Clearing Sidewalks and Driveways

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

These models deliver fast cleanup with minimal effort when there isn't enough accumulation to take out the snowblower. Here are our recommendations.

Winter will be here before you know it. Easily one of the most laborious and hated chores of that season is shoveling the snow. Not only that, it can be dangerous. Beyond the strain it puts on your back, the American Heart Association says it can increase the risk of a cardiac event for those with heart issues, and the cold weather can hide symptoms that otherwise would give you pause. That’s why the best electric snow shovels not only make the task easier, but safer, too, for those at risk.

Of course, you should not mistake these for full-blown snowblowers. Because of their compact size and throwing range, electric snow shovels are best used for small homes with shorter walkways and fewer steps. Like their larger counterparts, they use augers to scoop up snow (no more than 6 to 8 inches, ideally) and launch it up to 25 feet through the air so you don’t have to bend or lift as you dig out after a storm.

They also work well as supplemental tools for clearing out outdoor stairs, walkways, patios, decks, and anywhere else a snowblower may not be able to reach. If that sounds like it could help you out of a blizzard-induced jam this winter, we can steer you toward the best electric snow shovels that can make the chore as painless as possible.

Toro Power Shovel 60-Volt 12-Inch Electric Snow Shovel

Ego Power+ EGO POWER+ 12-Inch Electric Snow Shovel

We leaned on our personal experience with snow removal machines and conducted extensive research to inform our selections. Specifically, we looked at each machine’s clearing area, weight, battery life, and throwing distance. Because snow removal needs vary from property to property, we included larger models that can clear up to 6 inches of snow from two- to four-car driveways, along with lighter electric snow shovels that are easy to lift and maneuver in smaller areas, such as walkways and patios.

Though we still include one corded model as our best budget pick, we primarily focus on cordless models because for most people these days, the convenience of battery power beats having to drag a cord around on a cold day.

Most electric snow shovels max out with a fairly narrow clearing width and low clearing depth, potentially forcing you to do multiple passes to clear a proper path. This Earthwise model is an exception.

With a broad clearing width of 16 inches and a depth of 8 inches, it’s capable of clearing paths through deeper snow. And since it launches snow up to 32 feet away, you can use this machine to clear small driveways along with your walkways, deck, and patio.

On the other hand, this electric snow shovel is quite heavy. It has wheels, though, which make it easier to push and maneuver. It’s a tradeoff, but one that pays off if you live in an area that routinely gets 6 to 8 inches of snow in a night.

You may notice that our best overall is a bit cheaper than our best value pick. This is because we felt the wide clearing width and the fact that it has wheels to support your efforts made this a solid choice for many people.

Though higher in price than some of the other models on our list, there’s a lot that you get for the price, namely power and run time. With a larger battery than most, this electric shovel from Greenworks runs longer on a single battery than any other cordless electric snow shovel out there.

It packs a good amount of power with a large 80-volt 4.0-amp-hour battery powering a brushless motor; you’ll get about 45 minutes of run time on a single charge. This snow shovel clears a 12-inch path through up to 6 inches of snow, then blows it 25 feet away, making it ideal for uncovering a large area after a light snowfall.

Just remember that with great power and runtime comes great weight. With the battery loaded, this machine weighs more than 19 pounds, so moving it around for 45 minutes can turn into a real workout.

If you want the most clearing power possible from an electric snow shovel, Earthwise is your brand. This corded model can carve a 16-inch-wide path through snow up to 8 inches high, which is significantly more than what you can expect from other brands. It’s also significantly more powerful, moving up to 430 pounds of snow per minute.

For reference, most of our other picks move around 300 pounds per minute. As a result, it can handle deeper, slushier snow than most electric snow shovels. It also has a longer throwing distance than most corded or cordless electric snow shovels out there.

At 16 pounds, it’s pretty heavy, but like other heavy models, it has a pair of wheels so you can push it most of the time. In short, it offers the best snow removal capability of any machine this side of a snowblower.

Ryobi makes several types of cordless electric snow shovels, but this model is a head attachment for its Expand-It 40-Volt String Trimmer that you can swap in when the snow starts falling. The advantage here is that you aren’t limited to just one tool; you can swap in a variety of attachments to run on the same primary unit and battery. This makes a lot of sense if it only snows a couple of times where you live, and you only need a snow thrower infrequently.

During our testing, we were impressed with this tool’s performance. In mere minutes, we were able to clear a wide path through 8 inches of snow (more than the max height of 6 inches this model is rated for) on a patio outside our office. It was not fresh snow, either; it was densely packed after sitting for several days. There were times when the shovel head froze up while trying to push through too much at once, but this was quickly rectified by pulling back and pushing through again. The snow flies quite far, too, for such a small toolhead, at least 10 to 15 feet by our estimation.

Being able to fling snow that far is a good thing because this thrower can only send the snow straight forward (some models have adjustable fins that allow you to send it to either side). You need to be strategic about the direction you push to avoid creating more work for yourself if you have a long path to clear.

We must admit, too, that while this electric snow shovel makes the job easier than a manual shovel, it does take a bit of strength to operate, especially since it doesn’t have wheels to help you stay balanced and moving. You can move it along the ground, but you may need to lift it slightly if the snow is packed or icy at the lower levels, and it doesn’t come with a shoulder strap to help you do that. If you aim to greatly reduce the physical strain of snow removal, models from our list that feature wheels and directional fins may be a better option.

Overall, if you already have the Ryobi 40-volt-compatible string trimmer, adding this attachment to your arsenal would be a good move if you only need to clear snow from a small driveway, walkway, deck, or patio. The 40-volt, 4-amp-hour battery will give you up to an hour of power, which is more than enough for a small job like that, and buying into this multitool system will keep it from being a tool that just sits in the toolshed or basement for most of the time.

The lightweight design of this cordless electric snow shovel makes it a great option if other electric snow shovels are too heavy for you to manage. Whereas most electric snow shovels weigh around 18 pounds, this one weighs just 13.5 pounds.

Along with being lighter, the Snow Joe electric snow shovel also has a dual-handle design that allows you to operate it while standing up straight, taking pressure off your back. Despite its lighter weight, it can still clear a foot-wide path of snow up to 6 inches deep. The Snow Joe does have a shorter runtime than most, which limits it to lighter-duty snow removal, such as clearing walks, decks, and patios.

With its two 20-volt rechargeable batteries, the Worx electric snow shovel is both versatile and powerful. It can clear a path a foot wide and up to 6 inches deep and throw snow up to 25 feet, so it's suitable for clearing tighter spaces.

The two-battery design gives you the option to mix and match larger-capacity 20-volt Worx batteries to increase this shovel’s run time for larger jobs, such as clearing small driveways. It also comes with a dual charger, so you can charge both batteries simultaneously for a shorter turnaround time.

Another plus is that this model's batteries are compatible with other 20-volt Worx yard machines, making it a great option if you’ve already bought into the Worx product line.

We’d be remiss if we didn’t point out that this whole category of yard machines has some limitations. Most electric snow shovels can only handle snow depths up to 6 inches—8 inches if you’re lucky—and lack the power to handle heavier slushy snow. They are ideally suited to powdery snow on walkways, patios, decks, and maybe a small driveway. If you see heavy snowfalls regularly or have a large number of driveways and parking spaces to clear, get a snowblower before you buy an electric snow shovel. For big jobs, go with a gas snowblower. An electric snowblower works for small to moderate-sized driveways.

When push comes to shove, we recommend looking for a cordless electric snow shovel rather than a corded one. Having the freedom to move without worrying about a cord makes the whole shoveling or snowblowing process much easier. That said, if you’re on a tight budget or only need to clear a short walk or a small patio or deck that’s near an outdoor outlet, you can get by with a corded model.

Much like a snowblower, electric snow shovels are rated by how much snow they can move. The wider the shovel, the fewer passes it takes to clear an area. Most electric snow shovels move a 10- to 16-inch-wide path of snow. A small, narrow shovel is lighter and more nimble, making it useful for creating pathways. Wider, larger models are better equipped for clearing a patio or driveway, but are also heavier and more difficult to maneuver in tighter spaces.

Electric snow shovels can handle snowbanks around 4 to 8 inches high, depending on their clearing depth. Technically, you can remove deeper snowfall with these machines, but you’ll have to make more passes to do so.

For an electric snow shovel to be useful, it should be able to propel the snow far enough that it’s off the deck, walkway, or driveway that you’re clearing. Most electric snow shovels launch their snow between 20 and 30 feet, which is on par with entry-level, corded electric snowblowers, but shorter than cordless and gas snowblowers that can throw snow a distance of 40 feet or more. With that in mind, consider the route you plan to take while clearing, and make sure you’re moving the snow somewhere out of the way so it can sit until spring arrives.

Electric snow shovels process and throw snow like a snowblower, so you won’t need to bend over and scoop up snow as you would with a shovel. However, you should still look for the lightest possible option. While you won’t have to lift and throw snow as you would with a conventional snow shovel, you have to hold it upright and apply some force to push it through the snow. At the very least, you should look for a shovel that you can lift easily whenever you need to clear steps or multiple levels of patio.

Electric snow shovels typically weigh between 10 and 20 pounds. As you might expect, more powerful shovels that can move more snow and feature large batteries tend to be heavier than smaller, narrower models. Some large electric snow shovels have a set of wheels mounted to the rear of the base for standing upright on their own, so you can maneuver the machine with minimal lifting.

Similar to standard snow shovels, electric models come in both straight and curved handle varieties. A curved handle allows for standing more upright while operating the machine, putting less strain on your lower back and decreasing the risk of injury. A straight handle gives you more leverage for lifting loads of snow, but since an electric snow shovel has an auger that lifts and blows the snow for you, it’s not an advantage for electric models.

Electric snow shovels operate similarly to single-stage snow blowers. The shovel end of the machine has an auger that’s powered by an electric motor. As you push the shovel through the snow, the rotating auger collects snow, mashes it up, and then propels it through a shoot that throws the snow off to the side

The average electric snow shovel can churn through about 300 pounds of snow per minute. That means a snow shovel with a 12-inch wide intake and a clearing depth of 6 inches can remove about 4 inches of powdery snow from a 1,000 square foot driveway in about 20 minutes.

Just keep in mind that a shovel’s snow-clearing ability varies depending on certain conditions, such as the heft of the snow itself.

It’s never a bad idea to have a standard snow shovel around. While the electric snow shovel can reach most spaces that a standard push-behind snowblower can’t, it may not always be able to clear hardened snow or wet slush.

Plus, a manual shovel ensures that you can always dig out in an emergency, like when you’ve lost power after a snowstorm.

#6315. A 3-Million-Year-Old Fossil Is Turning the Story of Human Evolution Upside Down

Nearly 3 million years after the Taung Child lived, its fossil is challenging long-held assumptions about humanity’s origins, suggesting our ancient family tree was far more diverse than scientists once believed.

A century ago, a child’s fossil helped establish Africa as the birthplace of humanity. Now, that same discovery is raising another question about our origins: How many early human species have scientists been treating as one?

Discovered in South Africa in 1924, the Taung Child became the defining fossil, or “type specimen,” of Australopithecus africanus. It provided the first concrete evidence of human origins in Africa. Yet because no definitive criteria were established for classifying later discoveries, the Taung Child remains the only fossil conclusively assigned to the species.

A new study published in Nature dates the fossil to between 2.96 and 3.03 million years ago and suggests that several supposed members of its species may have belonged to different branches of the human family tree.

Led by Professor Gabriele Macho of the Archaeology, Environmental Changes and Geo-Chemistry (AMGC) research group at Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB), an international team examined tooth structure and patterns of brain and dental development during growth.

Several adult fossils traditionally classified as Australopithecus africanus did not match the Taung Child’s developmental trajectory. Differences in brain development were particularly revealing, suggesting that multiple hominin species may have occupied South Africa’s Sterkfontein region, either alongside one another or at different times.

“For over 100 years, we assumed the Taung Child was just one of many similar fossils from the era,” says Professor Gabriele Macho. “Our findings turn that on its head. The human family tree wasn’t a neat, straight trunk—it was a chaotic, tangled bush driven by climate shifts.”

The environment in which these ancient human relatives lived may help explain their diversity. Fossilized pollen indicates that the Taung Child inhabited a much wetter, more forested landscape than modern South Africa. Some of the trees growing there are now found hundreds of kilometers to the northeast.

Over millions of years, alternating wet and dry periods repeatedly transformed the region. As forests and other habitats expanded or contracted, hominin populations may have become isolated, evolved separately, and later encountered one another again. The researchers suggest these shifting conditions encouraged interbreeding and adaptations to different predators and pathogens.

Southern Africa’s position between tropical and temperate ecosystems made it a potential meeting ground for populations that had followed different evolutionary paths.

Rather than a straightforward progression from one ancestor to the next, the findings suggest that the emergence of our genus, Homo, involved a complex network of ancient populations repeatedly separated and reunited by a changing climate.

Reference: “The Taung child and the biogeographic and palaeoclimatic drivers of southern African hominin diversity” by Gabriele A. Macho, Simon Neubauer, Clement Zanolli, Pieter Vermeesch, Kevin L. Kuykendall, Andreas Koutsodendris, Laurin S. Kolb and Thibaut Caley, 5 November 2026, npj Palaeoecosystems. DOI: 10.1038/s44513-026-00008-2

#6314. Archaeologists Uncover 3,800-Year-Old Burial Mystery on Spain’s Coast

A burial ground on Spain’s southern coast suggests ancient communities may have continued building massive shared tombs during the Bronze Age, rather than simply reusing older monuments.

A 3,800-year-old burial mystery on Spain’s southern coast is challenging what archaeologists thought they knew about prehistoric burial traditions.

At a time when communities across the Iberian Peninsula were abandoning massive communal tombs in favor of smaller, individual graves, people near the Strait of Gibraltar appear to have continued burying their dead together. Even more puzzling, the stone monuments they used may have been newly constructed rather than inherited from earlier generations.

The discovery comes from the Trafalgar necropolis, where archaeologists investigated two collective tombs containing the remains of multiple individuals.

Radiocarbon dating of 16 individuals places the use of these tombs between 1875 and 1625 BC, making them among the latest known examples of collective megalithic burial in Iberia.

But the age of the human remains is only part of the mystery. Archaeologists also found no evidence of earlier occupation at the site, raising the possibility that the monuments themselves were constructed during the Bronze Age, when such building traditions were thought to be fading.

The study, published November 11, 2026, in the open-access journal PLOS One, was conducted by Eduardo Vijande-Vila of the University of Cádiz in Spain and colleagues.

Determining when a tomb was used is not the same as establishing when it was built. Elsewhere in Iberia, Bronze Age communities sometimes buried their dead inside monuments dating back to the Copper Age, making it difficult to distinguish new construction from the reuse of older structures.

Trafalgar may represent an important exception. The absence of evidence for an earlier burial ground suggests the cemetery could have been established in the early second millennium BC. However, additional dating methods are needed to determine when the monuments were originally constructed.

The authors explain, “The Trafalgar megalithic necropolis has revealed a highly significant finding. During the Bronze Age, an entirely new funerary space was constructed in a landscape dominated by the sea. We propose this hypothesis based on the absence of archaeological evidence for earlier occupation in the surrounding area. Until now, the evidence available for this period has primarily pointed to the reuse of megalithic monuments built during the Copper Age. This discovery offers a new perspective on funerary practices during this period and would demonstrate that new monumental burial spaces continued to be constructed.”

The excavations also uncovered grave goods, including gold and copper earrings, silver beads, and an ivory comb, offering additional clues about the people buried at the site.

If further research confirms that the monuments were newly built during the Bronze Age, Trafalgar would provide rare evidence that monumental communal burial traditions survived longer than previously recognized.

Researchers believe additional tombs may remain undiscovered, potentially offering further insight into ancient Iberian burial traditions. However, strong coastal winds and shifting sands threaten to bury the site beneath the dunes again, making continued preservation essential for future excavations.

Reference: “The last builders of megaliths in the South of the Iberian peninsula? The Bronze Age necropolis of Trafalgar (Barbate, Cádiz, Spain)” by Eduardo Vijande-Vila, Serafín Becerra-Martín, Berta Morell-Rovira, Marta Díaz-Zorita Bonilla, Eduardo Molina-Piernas, Alejandro Muñoz-Muñoz, Adolfo Moreno-Márquez, Pablo González-Fernández, Salvador Domínguez-Bella, María Leticia Gómez-Sánchez, Diego Salvador Fernández-Sánchez, José Luis Ramírez-Amador, José María Corona-Borrego, María Carmona-Gil, Jesús Corrales Díaz and Juan Jesús Cantillo-Duarte, 11 November 2026, PLOS ONE. DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0359220

A proposed tabletop quantum sensor could match the precision of the best satellite measurements of frame dragging, a subtle effect predicted by Einstein's general relativity.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have proposed a new tabletop device to detect the subtle way Earth's daily spin on its axis twists the space-time around it ‪—‬ an effect predicted by Einstein's general relativity.

If built, the sensor could measure the quantum effect known as frame dragging with the same precision as the best satellite experiments, but in minutes instead of years, the researchers proposed in a new study.

The research, published Sept. 17 in the journal Physical Review Letters, aimed to address a classic mismatch in physics. Picture a ring of clocks bolted to a spinning merry-go-round. You synchronize each clock with its neighbor around the ring. Then, you compare the last clock with the first. They don't match.

"It is impossible to synchronize that collection of clocks when you're in a rotating frame," Kai-Isaak Ellers, a physics graduate student at the University of California, Berkeley (UC Berkeley) and first author of the study, told Live Science.

A photo of scientists working on NASA's Gravity Probe B in 2003. This device measured Earth's frame-dragging from space, confirming Einstein's predictions with an 18% margin of error.

Einstein's theory of general relativity predicts that a massive, spinning object drags the fabric of space-time along with it, just like a spoon twirling in honey. The effect is clearly visible around supermassive objects, like the Milky Way's central black hole. But around Earth, the effect is very faint.

So far, scientists have measured Earth's frame dragging only from orbit. They tracked how the twisting of space-time slowly shifts spinning gyroscopes or the paths of satellites. In 2011, NASA's Gravity Probe B satellite, which carried four gyroscopes, confirmed Einstein's prediction with a margin of error of about 18%. Satellites tracked with lasers have since done even better. In July, researchers reported in the journal Nature that the LARES-2 satellite had shrunk that margin of error to just 0.2%.

However, that took about three years of laser tracking. Researchers also had to account for the fact that Earth bulges at the equator and its mass is spread unevenly, which gives the planet’s gravity small irregularities that tug on satellites far more strongly than frame dragging does. To subtract those tugs, the team relied on detailed maps of Earth's gravity made by other satellites.

Measuring frame dragging more precisely is a way to stress-test general relativity. Several alternative theories of gravity predict a slightly different amount of twisting, and a lab-based measurement would also be free of the modeling assumptions that satellite experiments depend on, Ellers said.

The new device is a loop of superfluid helium-4 — helium chilled until it flows without friction and behaves like a single, giant quantum object. The loop is interrupted by a thin barrier riddled with tiny holes, called a Josephson junction. Superfluid helium can slip through the holes, but ordinary liquid helium cannot.

"That's where the quantum behavior comes from," said K. Birgitta Whaley, a quantum physicist at UC Berkeley and a co-author of the study.

As Earth spins and drags space-time, it nudges the quantum state of the helium flowing through the junction. That nudge shifts the frequency at which the helium sloshes back and forth in the loop, which the researchers could detect.

A visualization of Earth's uneven gravity field taken by NASA's Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment in 2009. The lumpiness of our planet's gravitational field makes it harder to precisely measure relativistic effects.

Superfluid devices, many of them built at UC Berkeley, have detected Earth's rotation since the late 1990s. But the helium-4 versions built around a Josephson junction, like the new design, have worked within about a hundredth of a degree of 2.17 K (minus 455.76 Fahrenheit, or minus 270.98 Celsius), the temperature at which helium-4 becomes a superfluid. At that temperature, a lingering fraction of "normal" helium mixed in with the superfluid adds noise.

Instead, the team calculated how the device would behave at a few thousandths of a degree above absolute zero. Below 0.7 K, the noise changed character, and the team found it drops sharply as the helium gets colder. One key finding in the new paper is the result of the team's thermal noise analysis, which showed how sensitive these devices could be at millikelvin temperatures, Elles said.

The catch is the barrier. Earlier helium-4 devices used holes about 90 nanometers wide. Working at these frigid temperatures demands much smaller holes, about 1 nanometer across ‪—‬ roughly the size of a helium atom. Keith Schwab, a physicist at Caltech and co-author of the study, and his collaborators are developing such materials, but they haven't been built into a working sensor yet.

If they can be, the researchers calculate that the device could measure frame dragging to 0.2% precision in about 35 minutes. If its vibrating membrane were made from the lowest-loss crystals, such as quartz or sapphire, that could drop to about one second, they said.

"This seems to be a very serendipitous discovery that at millikelvin, we can get this high sensitivity," Whaley told Live Science.

The signal corresponds to a time difference of about 10-35 seconds between helium flowing one way around the loop and the other — the same mismatch as the clocks on the metaphorical merry-go-round.

"The interesting thing about it is just how small it is," Whaley said. "It's not so far off from the Planck time," about 10-44 seconds, the shortest slice of time before the known laws of physics are expected to break down. This experiment is still a billion times too large to reach that limit, Whaley said. But future helium experiments could help explore whether time flows smoothly, like a ramp, or ticks forward in tiny, indivisible jumps, like the frames of a movie.

Ellers, K.-I., Christodoulou, M., Schwab, K. C., & Whaley, K. B. (2026). Quantum sensing of gravitational frame dragging with a superfluid ⁴He gyrometer. Physical Review Letters, 137(12), 121404. https://doi.org/10.1103/q3v9-rjm9

#6311. A Strange Liquid Is Helping Scientists Overcome a Major Barrier in Nanotechnology

By filling the tiny pores of fragile materials with an unusual liquid, scientists have found a way to create intricate patterns without destroying their structures.

Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) contain networks of tiny pores that can trap gases, capture pollutants, and support chemical reactions. These properties make them attractive for advanced sensors and electronic devices, but their fragile structures are easily damaged by the processes used to manufacture such devices. Researchers in Japan have now developed a way to carve precise patterns into these materials at room temperature without causing the extensive structural damage normally associated with the process.

The technique, developed at Tokyo University of Science (TUS), involves filling the pores of MOFs with an ionic liquid before exposing them to a focused ion beam. In experiments, the liquid strengthened a copper-based MOF and substantially reduced damage, allowing researchers to produce intricate features only a few hundred nanometers wide.

The origins of MOFs trace back to 1974, when University of Melbourne chemistry professor Richard Robson began exploring whether molecules and chemical bonds could replace the wooden balls and metal rods used in structural models. His experiments with copper ions connected by four-armed organic molecules helped establish the foundations of a new class of porous materials. Today, approximately 100,000 MOFs are known, with potential applications ranging from gas storage and chemical separation to pollution control.

Turning these materials into functional devices requires precise fabrication, often involving dry etching, which removes material using energetic particles such as ions. Unfortunately, ion beams can disrupt the delicate crystalline frameworks and produce unwanted cavities. Cryogenic etching has offered a way to limit this damage, but it requires specialized cooling equipment and liquid nitrogen.

Led by Assistant Professor Yumeng Zheng and Professor Kentaro Kinoshita from TUS’s Department of Applied Physics, the researchers investigated whether ionic liquids could make MOFs more resistant to ion beam damage. Their approach builds on earlier findings from Kinoshita’s team showing that these liquids can improve the mechanical stability of MOFs. The study was scheduled for publication in Communications Materials.

The team tested four imidazolium-based ionic liquids in Cu3BTC2, a copper-based MOF containing benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylic acid (BTC). Each liquid occupied approximately 50% to 60% of the material’s pore volume. The researchers then used a focused gallium ion beam to etch patterns into the samples at room temperature.

Untreated MOFs suffered substantial structural damage, including the formation of large cavities. Samples containing ionic liquids showed considerably less visible microstructural damage under the same conditions. The researchers successfully etched a square measuring 5 × 5 micrometers (approximately 0.0002 × 0.0002 inches), a pillar, and a Chinese character with lines just 130 to 300 nanometers (about 5 to 12 millionths of an inch) wide.

“In this study, we developed a simple method for room-temperature dry etching of this fragile class of materials. By infiltrating MOFs with ionic liquids, their mechanical stability is greatly improved, and the damage from electron and ion beams is reduced, achieving harmless ion beam etching,” says Dr. Zheng.

The researchers propose that ionic liquids protect MOFs through a combination of thermal and electrical effects. The liquids may absorb heat generated during ion bombardment, reducing local temperature changes, while their mobile ions could help redistribute accumulated electrical charge and screen local electric fields. These mechanisms remain proposed explanations rather than directly established causes of the reduced damage.

Additional measurements confirmed that all four ionic liquid treatments increased the MOF’s hardness without substantially changing its stiffness. Thermal analysis also showed that treated samples decomposed at higher temperatures than untreated material, indicating improved thermal stability.

Although the experiments focused on a single copper-based MOF, the researchers believe the approach could potentially work with other frameworks. If its effectiveness extends to additional materials, room-temperature etching could provide a more accessible route to manufacturing MOF-based devices without the cooling requirements of cryogenic processing.

“We can foresee applications in high-sensitivity sensors, separation and analysis devices, and catalytic devices. This technology has the potential to become a foundational technology for bridging the exceptional material functionalities of MOFs with their use in practical devices,” says Prof. Kinoshita.

Reference: “Ionic-liquid-assisted room-temperature dry etching of metal–organic frameworks” by Yumeng Zheng, Momoka Muraoka, Koki Egawa and Kentaro Kinoshita, 10 November 2026, Communications Materials. DOI: 10.1038/s43246-026-01396-3

This work was partly supported by JSPS KAKENHI Grant Number 26K00987.

#6310. A NASA Veteran Claims to Have Used Mind-Bending Physics to Conquer Gravity

Charles Buhler’s claim could change how spacecraft fly. But experiments show how much work it takes to establish that a mysterious push is real.

In April 2024, Charles Buhler, an electrostatics specialist who helped establish a laboratory at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center, made a remarkable claim. His company, Exodus Propulsion Technologies, had built a device that could produce thrust without expelling propellant. He attributed the push to what he called a “New Force.”

As we reported in our earlier coverage, Buhler’s claim would have big consequences for spaceflight. That promise depends on whether researchers outside Exodus can reproduce the push and rule out an ordinary explanation.

One physicist has spent years investigating similar claims. Martin Tajmar, a professor and chair of space systems at Dresden University of Technology in Germany, has spent two decades measuring the forces produced by charged capacitors, including lopsided ones like the designs Buhler describes.

“It’s all negative,” he tells Popular Mechanics. Meaning, his tests found no evidence of that force within the limits of his equipment. He hasn’t tested Exodus’s hardware, but his experiments show what an independent test would need to account for.

A capacitor stores electric charge. Apply a high enough voltage to certain designs, and they can set the surrounding air moving, producing a push on the device itself. Tajmar calls this corona wind, “a discharge in air that drags air molecules with it.” In those cases, the device moves by pushing air backward, much as a fan does.

Tajmar’s team wanted to see whether a capacitor would still produce a push with almost all the air removed. For their 2024 study in Scientific Reports, they put the capacitor and its battery-powered electrical equipment together on a sensitive balance inside a vacuum chamber. At 10,000 volts, an asymmetric capacitor produced no clear sign of an unexplained force, even with instruments sensitive enough to detect a push measured in billionths of a newton.

Exodus hasn’t sent Tajmar a device, so he built his own capacitors for those experiments. He says his asymmetric design follows the principles in the company’s patent, though he doesn’t know the exact dimensions of its hardware.

“It’s Exodus who have to say why my asymmetric capacitor does not produce any thrust,” he says.

He believes his results challenge the company’s explanation, but he’d need its hardware to put its particular device through the same checks.

Keeping the battery and high-voltage equipment on the balance removes outside power cables that could interfere with the reading. Researchers also have to watch for electromagnetic forces or parts shifting as they heat up, either of which could look like thrust.

Tajmar also recommends swapping the device for an electrical dummy that draws power but should produce no thrust. If the balance still registers a push, something else in the setup is causing it. Researchers would need to track that down before treating the reading as evidence of a working drive.

Buhler has also said the devices can keep producing thrust after the power is switched off. Electrical charge can linger in insulating materials, leaving an electric field even after the supply is disconnected. Researchers would need to work out whether that leftover charge explains the reading and, if there really is a push, where it comes from.

In a short white paper, Exodus says other experimenters have reproduced the effect and argues that the device pushes against the vacuum itself, allowing momentum to be conserved. But it doesn’t include their laboratory reports. Without those details, readers can’t tell how the experiments were done or whether the researchers ruled out other causes of the push.

What leaving the propellant behind could change

Spacecraft have to bring along the propellant they’ll use to speed up, slow down or change course. That adds weight, which takes more propellant to move. The rocket equation puts numbers to that trade-off, showing how much a spacecraft can change its speed with the supply it carries.

If a drive could produce useful thrust without using up propellant, engineers could plan missions differently. A spacecraft could keep changing course as long as it had enough power and the drive kept working. Some of the weight now devoted to propellant tanks and their contents could go toward other equipment.

But the drive would bring its own baggage. It would need a power source and a way to get rid of waste heat, and all of that would have to travel with it. Engineers would need to find out whether the thrust was worth the weight of the complete system. Getting a reliable push in the lab would give them a reason to start working that out.

Light can give a spacecraft a push, too. When a laser sends light in one direction, the laser gets a tiny push in the other, because light carries momentum. Tajmar points out that this already offers a way to produce thrust without using up material propellant.

“If you just power a laser with the power that we use in our experiments, the thrust is also propellantless and actually already exists,” he says.

The catch is how much power it takes. To hold up a 1.2-ounce object, roughly the weight of the devices Buhler described, a laser would need to send about 100 million watts of light downward. A drive that produced a useful push with much less power would be worth engineers’ attention. Researchers would also have to explain what carries momentum in the opposite direction, as the light does for a laser.

“You have to test it in an independent laboratory. And then with a different method,” Tajmar says. He wants the results published so other experts can examine the work, including the equipment itself. Getting the same push on a different instrument would help show that the device deserves the credit.

Nobody needs to make the whole apparatus float. Even a small sideways push would warrant attention if it survived those checks and other researchers could reliably reproduce it. Then engineers could start asking whether it was strong enough to put to work aboard a spacecraft.

Buhler’s claim promises freedom from the propellant tank, which would change how we travel through space. The next move is closer to home. Put the drive in another lab, let someone else take the controls, and see whether the promise still has any push behind it.

#6308. How octopuses squeeze through tiny openings, step by step

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The cephalopod how-to guide involves three or four moves, depending on a hole’s size

Octopuses are famous for fleeing tanks by squeezing through narrow slits and impossibly tiny holes. Now scientists have studied the sequences some cephalopods like this Mayan octopus use to make such great escapes.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Octopuses have made many a great escape. Remember Inky, who fled from New Zealand’s national aquarium?

The cephalopods can Houdini their way out of tanks and off boats by squeezing through narrow slits and incredibly tiny holes. Now researchers know exactly how some octopuses pull it off. These masterful getaways involve a consistent, step-by-step game plan, researchers report November 5 in the Journal of Experimental Biology.

Octopuses are mostly squishy muscle, allowing them to shape-shift, though they do have some rigid body parts. Not many scientists have studied how these animals squirm through small openings, says Robyn Crook, an evolutionary biologist at San Francisco State University who was not involved in the research. “It’s one of the most characteristic behaviors of octopuses in popular awareness, but the strategies octopuses use have not really been examined systematically.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Sneaking through small spaces isn’t just a party trick for octopuses, says Michael Kuba, a biologist at the University of Naples Federico II in Italy. The animals use that skill to find hidden food and to avoid becoming food themselves.

Kuba and his colleagues observed how three common octopuses (Octopus vulgaris) and four Mayan octopuses (Octopus maya) approached small holes. For each individual, the team measured the distance between the octopus’s eyes as an indicator of the size of their most rigid cartilage around their brain. Then the researchers designed acrylic boxes with holes that were slightly smaller or larger than that eye-to-eye measurement. They plopped the octopuses inside and watched what happened.

Octopuses have slightly different escape how-tos, depending on the size of the hole they are squeezing through. Here, a common octopus (Octopus vulgaris) wriggles through a space just a little bit bigger than their most rigid body parts. It takes just three steps for the octopus to free itself from the acrylic box.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Common octopuses used one of two escape strategies depending on the hole’s size. When the hole was wider than the distance between their eyes, the octopuses pushed themselves through it in three steps. First, they snuck one or two arms through the hole and then threaded a couple more arms through. Finally, they used the arms that they had already snaked through the hole to push against the box and yank their head and the rest of their arms through in one fell swoop. The whole operation took a few seconds.

When the hole was narrower, common octopuses added a fourth step. They shoved all of their arms through the hole first and then squished their head and bulbous mantle through.

When a hole is smaller than their most rigid body parts, common octopuses add a fourth step to wrestle their bodies through an opening.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Mayan octopuses behaved more cautiously than the common octopuses. When confronted with the narrower hole, Mayan octopuses didn’t even attempt to fit inside of it. They usually ignored it. This difference between the species could stem from their biology or how they’ve adapted to their environments, Kuba says. Mayan octopuses live in sandy, rocky areas, so while they might disappear under rocks, they don’t often need to cram through holes, he says.

The team hopes these escape artists will inspire new soft robots that can morph their shape to fit through tiny spaces, says Wenci Xin, a robotics researcher at the National University of Singapore. “This incredible capability could enable robots to overcome environmental limitations and enter spaces that are difficult to reach.”

Studying how octopuses navigate different types of holes may provide additional clues for robots, Crook says. For instance, the cephalopods may take a different tack for openings that are more like slits or tubes than holes.

Currently, robots built to fit through tiny holes tend to be snake-shaped, but further research on these eight-armed contortionists could unlock other configurations.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

W. Xin et al. Overcoming environmental constraints: octopus uses 3-step or 4-step strategies to squeeze through small holes. Journal of Experimental Biology. 2026. doi: 10.1242/jeb.252825

#6307. Powerful New Weight-Loss Drug Could Change How Millions Treat Painful Knee Arthritis

An experimental weight-loss injection may offer more than a way to shed pounds, with clinical trials suggesting it could also ease the burden of painful knee arthritis.

Losing weight can help relieve knee osteoarthritis, yet the condition often makes weight loss difficult in the first place. When walking, climbing stairs, or simply standing up from a chair causes pain, getting enough exercise can become a challenge.

For the roughly 15 million Americans living with painful knee osteoarthritis, treatment options remain limited. Physical therapy, topical medications, anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen and Voltaren, opioids, and corticosteroid injections can help manage symptoms, although steroid injections typically provide only short-term relief.

Previous research has shown that losing just 5% to 10% of body weight through diet and exercise can improve symptoms. Losing more than 10%, however, is difficult through lifestyle changes alone, particularly for people whose knees already limit their movement.

An experimental weight-loss injection called retatrutide may offer another way to address this problem. In two large clinical trials led by Northwestern University, participants who were overweight or had obesity experienced substantial weight loss alongside significant reductions in knee pain.

The phase 3 trials, published in the New England Journal of Medicine, involved more than 1,000 participants combined. Those receiving the highest dose of retatrutide lost approximately 25% of their body weight on average. A pooled analysis found that about two-thirds of participants receiving the drug reported at least a 50% reduction in knee pain, compared with 38% of those given a placebo.

Researchers tracked these changes using the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Arthritis Index (WOMAC), which asks patients to rate their pain from 0 to 10. Participants also recorded their daily pain levels through an app.

“The findings are really saying for people who are overweight and have OA, if you lose a significant amount of weight with this treatment, there is a good chance that you’re going to get a meaningful reduction in your knee pain,” said corresponding author Dr. Thomas Schnitzer, a professor of physical medicine and rehabilitation, anesthesiology and medicine (rheumatology) at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine. “A major factor is that you’re loading your knees less and therefore, there’s less pain and it allows you to increase your function.”

Developed by Eli Lilly, retatrutide is a once-weekly injection that activates receptors for three naturally occurring hormones involved in metabolism. Existing weight-loss medications such as semaglutide and tirzepatide target one or two receptors and typically produce weight reductions of 10% to 20%. Retatrutide produced losses of approximately 20% to 25% in these trials.

“Participants had remarkable responses,” Schnitzer said. “Many of the people in this study lost considerable amounts of weight, with a few losing up to a hundred pounds or more.”

The improvements also extended beyond body weight and joint pain. Participants experienced lower blood pressure, reduced blood lipid levels, and less systemic inflammation, suggesting broader metabolic benefits.

Scientists from Eli Lilly were among the study’s co-authors. Philip Conaghan, professor of musculoskeletal medicine at the University of Leeds in the United Kingdom, presented results from the TRIUMPH-4 trial at the American College of Rheumatology annual meeting in Orlando, Florida. Findings from the second trial, TRIUMPH-1-OA, were presented separately during a poster session.

Despite the promising results, retatrutide remains experimental and would require approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration before becoming a treatment option. Schnitzer emphasized that diet, exercise, and lifestyle changes should remain the first approach because they are less expensive and avoid potential side effects associated with GLP-1 medications, including gastrointestinal problems and muscle loss. Preserving muscle is especially important for patients with knee osteoarthritis because it helps stabilize the joint.

The trials also left a crucial question unanswered. Although retatrutide significantly reduced pain, researchers do not yet know whether it slows the underlying progression of osteoarthritis or could help patients avoid knee replacement surgery. People who already needed knee replacements were excluded from the studies.

“That would be the goal here to say you can reduce people’s pain, and you can stop the progression of their osteoarthritis,” Schnitzer said.

Further research must also determine whether retatrutide could benefit people with knee osteoarthritis who are not overweight, since they were not included in the trials. Scientists are particularly interested in whether the drug’s potential anti-inflammatory effects contribute to pain relief independently of weight loss.

“These drugs are believed to have significant anti-inflammatory activity, but the mechanism is not entirely known,” Schnitzer said. “Whether cutting down inflammation in the joint is also important in addition to reducing load needs more research, so this is still a first step, in my view. I’ve been working in the OA field for a long time, and I think this opens up opportunities to do a lot more studies to understand the condition better.”

Reference: “Retatrutide Once Weekly in Adults with Knee Osteoarthritis Pain and Obesity” by Thomas J. Schnitzer, David J. Hunter, Philip G. Conaghan, Arya M. Sharma, Sue D. Pedersen, Kaiyi Chen, So Young Park, Nune Makarova, Kathryn Giblin and Tammy Forrester, 7 November 2026, New England Journal of Medicine. DOI: 10.1056/NEJMoa2610676

Funding for the study was provided by Eli Lilly and Company.
