#6270. Tadpoles are dying in waves in Brazil, and scientists have found a clue

Scientists linked recurring tadpole deaths in a Brazilian pond to ranavirus, with outbreaks more likely after weeks of low humidity.

Before January 2024, the only tadpole deaths recorded at a small pond in Brazil’s Atlantic Forest were isolated cases involving predators.

Since then deaths at the pond have occurred in repeated waves. Outbreaks were reported in three consecutive breeding seasons.

According to the research team, the cause was ranavirus. This virus is known to infect amphibians and reptiles as well as fish. Outbreaks were found to be more likely after periods in which the air had been dry for some weeks.

Most of the dead tadpoles (315 of 324) belonged to the monkey frog (Phyllomedusa distincta). This leaf frog is found only in the Atlantic Forest.

The authors reported that this was the first confirmed ranavirus die-off among wild native amphibians in the American tropics.

Researchers also recorded a sharp decline in egg-laying compared with counts from two decades earlier.

The authors believe the virus is the most likely explanation for the decline. A gap of more than 20 years in the egg counts makes a direct link difficult to establish.

The study was carried out by Aline Fonseca as part of her doctoral research at the Federal University of Paraná (UFPR).

Her colleagues included the owners of the reserve: Germano Woehl Jr. and Elza Nishimura Woehl of the Rã-Bugio Institute.

The work took place at the Rã-Bugio Sanctuary, a protected reserve of about 12 acres (4.75 hectares) in Guaramirim in the state of Santa Catarina.

The pond itself is fed by two springs. It is roughly two-thirds the size of a tennis court and has been kept free of fish so that frogs are able to breed in it.

Monkey frog tadpoles tend to hang upright at the surface of the water. As a result, dead tadpoles were relatively easy to find and count.

Three outbreak periods were recorded. The first ran from January to April 2024 and the second from November 2024 to January 2025. The third lasted from late November 2025 to March 2026.

Of the 324 dead tadpoles that were collected, 315 were monkey frogs and nine were Bischoff’s tree frogs (Boana bischoffi). Ranavirus DNA was detected in 287 of them (about 89%).

Redness and swelling were commonly observed in the infected tadpoles along with bleeding beneath the skin. Bleeding inside the eye was noted in some individuals.

The presence of a virus in a dead animal does not by itself establish the cause of death.

Liver tissue from 13 infected tadpoles was therefore also examined under a microscope and large areas of dead cells were found.

No sick tadpoles were observed in a second pond that lies about 1,500 feet (450 meters) away and is separated from the first by intact forest.

Measurements made at the affected pond during the first outbreak showed that water acidity was normal. No signs of contamination were detected.

On several occasions the discovery of a first dead tadpole was followed within a short time by many more.

Tadpoles that were dying were seen floating at the surface and were unable to swim down. In most cases, death followed within 30 minutes.

Tadpoles that hatched early or late in the breeding season survived better than those that hatched in the middle of it.

The pond was most crowded in the middle of the breeding season, when nearly all tadpoles died.

Most of the bodies that were recovered belonged to young tadpoles whose back legs had only begun to form.

However, older tadpoles carried about the same amount of virus. This suggests that heavier infection was not the reason the young made up most of the dead.

The authors believe timing is a more likely explanation. Most tadpoles in the pond were still young when the outbreaks occurred.

It is also possible that larger dead tadpoles were eaten by predators and scavengers before they could be counted.

Monkey frogs lay their eggs on leaves above the water.

The female folds each leaf around the clutch (a group of eggs). When the eggs hatch, the tadpoles drop into the pond below.

Between August 1999 and February 2004, the Woehls searched leaves, stems and tree trunks around the pond every morning during the breeding season.

Each new clutch was marked so that it would not be counted twice.

The same daily counts were repeated from August 2025 to February 2026 after the second outbreak season.

Egg-laying was estimated to have fallen by about 83% (with the likely decline lying between 70% and 90%).

Clutch counts were lower throughout the breeding season.

The decline therefore could not be explained by a change in the timing of laying.

The researchers suggest that fewer young frogs surviving to adulthood could help explain the decline in egg-laying.

Daily records from the three outbreak seasons were compared with weather data. Humidity (the amount of moisture in the air) was found to be the strongest predictor of deaths.

Temperature did not help to predict them. Rainfall added no further information once humidity had been taken into account.

When average humidity over the previous two weeks was 65%, the team’s model estimated a nearly 98% chance of finding dead tadpoles on a given day. When it was 90%, the estimate fell to about 7%.

“The virus is likely present in the environment at all times without causing disease, but low humidity may cause it to increase its own replication and trigger an outbreak,” Fonseca said.

As water levels fall the tadpoles are crowded into less space. This may make it easier for the virus to spread between them.

It has also been suggested by the authors that dry conditions may place the animals under stress and weaken their immune defenses.

Dry weeks may help to explain when outbreaks occurred.

But the researchers also had to consider whether longer-term changes in the weather could account for the decline in egg-laying.

For this reason, weather records covering the period from 1999 to 2026 were examined.

No clear long-term trend was detected in temperature or rainfall or humidity. Average temperature rose by about 0.27°F (0.15°C) per decade.

This increase was not statistically significant. The records therefore did not establish a clear warming trend.

Whether egg counts came from before or after the outbreaks explained the decline better than any of the weather measures. Adding weather data to that comparison improved it only slightly.

It should be noted that the weather data were not collected at the pond. They were taken from a global dataset in which each area measures about 7 by 6 miles (11 by 10 km).

No clutch counts were made between 2004 and 2025. As a result the point at which the decline began cannot be determined.

Although no signs of pollution were found at the reserve, other threats to the frogs cannot be ruled out.

Ranavirus is regarded by the authors as the strongest explanation for the fall in egg-laying. But it has not been shown to be the cause.

Six stretches of the virus’s genes were sequenced and were found to be identical in every sample analyzed. All of them matched the frog virus 3 group.

That group is known to infect amphibians and reptiles and fish on several continents. Because the match is so close, the origin of the outbreak is difficult to trace.

Ranavirus has previously killed wood frog tadpoles in North America. In South America most confirmed die-offs had until now involved bullfrogs raised on farms.

Frog virus 3 has caused repeated losses at farms in the Atlantic Forest region that raise American bullfrogs.

The authors suggest that wastewater from crowded farms could carry the virus into wild ponds. It has not been established that this occurred at the reserve.

The virus may have arrived in the forest recently, or it may have been present for many years.

Co-author Luís Felipe Toledo of the State University of Campinas (UNICAMP) has spent more than a decade studying chytrid fungus.

The fungus is another threat to amphibians. His group has found evidence of the fungus on Brazilian amphibians dating back to 1916.

“Perhaps the ranavirus has also been here for a long time. It remains to be seen what changed for it to become a threat,” Toledo said.

Climate forecasts for the Atlantic Forest indicate that droughts are likely to become more frequent and more severe.

The authors warn that if dry weeks do help to trigger these outbreaks then losses of this kind could occur more often and become more serious.

The UFPR team plans to collect samples from nearby areas in order to find out where else the virus is present. Toledo has also pointed to museum collections as a possible source of clues.

Testing preserved frogs could help to establish how long ranavirus has been in the region.

The study is published in the journal Biodiversity and Conservation.

Scientists on China's Tiangong space station used a laser trap to cool a clump of atoms to just above absolute zero, setting a new record.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have cooled atoms to the coldest temperature ever recorded, using a laser trap aboard China's Tiangong space station.

Tiangong included an experiment in which atoms were cooled to 10 picokelvins, which is barely above absolute zero, the coldest theoretical temperature possible in physics. Absolute zero is minus 459.67 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 273.15 degrees Celsius) and the threshold at which all particles in an object are believed to stop moving.

Scientists hit the mark using "optical tweezers," known more formally as an optical-dipole trap (ODT), which hold atoms in a laser beam," the scientists reported Nov. 5 in the journal Science.

The team placed 20,000 rubidium atoms in the trap in order to restrict their motion. This reduced motion, along with the weightlessness induced by the low-gravity environment aboard the space station, caused the cloud of atoms to cool to much lower temperatures than are possible on Earth.

The experiment's results could help improve future space-based research, the team said.

"This record-low temperature could stimulate a new generation of ODT-based experiments in quantum simulation and precision measurements in space," the researchers wrote in the paper.

Despite this achievement, it's doubtful that scientists could ever hit absolute zero. One interpretation of the third law of thermodynamics, which looks at how systems behave when they approach absolute zero, is that the particles would always have a bit of entropy (disorder) associated with them, making absolute zero unachievable.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"One version of the third law states that it would require an infinite number of steps to reach absolute zero, which means you will never get there," Saibal Mitra, a professor of physics at Missouri State University, told Live Science in a 2024 interview.

The second law of thermodynamics, which states that entropy always increases, would also be violated if scientists could reach absolute zero, he added. "If you had a heat sink at absolute zero, then you could build a machine that was 100% efficient," Mitra said.

That said, space makes it easier to get close to absolute zero because microgravity allows atoms to "float" and become more efficient at cooling, Science News reported. The researchers took their weightless collection of atoms and created a quantum state of matter known as a Bose-Einstein condensate, in which very cold atoms clump and create a "fifth state" of matter as they behave akin to a single atom.

Tiangong's very cold clump follows similar experiments on the International Space Station that reached 52 picokelvins and from a weightless fall induced by a drop from a tall tower, in which atoms hit 38 picokelvins, Science News added.

#6268. Webb captures a galaxy still reeling from an ancient collision

Webb’s infrared view of the Cartwheel Galaxy reveals how an ancient collision reshaped its structure and sparked waves of star formation.

Today’s Image of the Day features the Cartwheel Galaxy, where a bright ring of stars surrounds a glowing center and curved strands of dust stretch between them like spokes.

The striking shape emerged from a violent collision that disrupted a spiral galaxy hundreds of millions of years ago.

New stars now shine along the outer ring, while traces of the galaxy’s earlier structure remain woven through the scene.

The view comes from the James Webb Space Telescope, which combined observations from two infrared instruments to reveal stars and dust in extraordinary detail.

Released on August 2, 2022, the image also includes two smaller companion galaxies and a background scattered with more distant galaxies.

Located roughly 500 million light-years away in the constellation Sculptor, the Cartwheel belongs to an unusual class known as ring galaxies.

Its appearance differs sharply from the familiar spiral arms of our Milky Way.

Astronomers attribute that shape to a high-speed collision between a large spiral galaxy and a smaller galaxy.

The smaller galaxy responsible for the impact is outside this image, so neither of the two prominent companions should be mistaken for the intruder.

The encounter sent disturbances outward through the larger galaxy, producing a bright inner ring and a much broader outer ring.

NASA compares their expansion to ripples spreading across a pond after a stone hits the water.

Those enormous ripples have reshaped the galaxy over hundreds of millions of years. What appears to be a finished wheel is still undergoing change.

The outer ring marks a region where the collision’s effects continue to unfold. As it expands into surrounding gas, it triggers the formation of new stars.

NASA estimates that this outer structure has been expanding for about 440 million years.

Star formation and supernovas, the explosions of dying stars, help make it an especially active part of the galaxy.

The center has its own concentrations of activity. Hot dust fills the bright core, and its most luminous areas contain enormous clusters of young stars.

Together, these regions show how a galactic collision can do more than rearrange existing material.

It can also change where new generations of stars emerge, leaving a pattern that remains visible long after the original encounter.

Earlier observations, including images from the Hubble Space Telescope, had already revealed the Cartwheel’s unusual structure. But dust obscures parts of the galaxy when viewed in visible light.

Webb observes infrared wavelengths, allowing astronomers to examine stars that are harder to distinguish through that dusty veil.

Its Near-Infrared Camera, or NIRCam, reveals points of starlight and pockets of star formation.

It also helps distinguish the smoother distribution of older stars from the clumpier regions associated with younger populations.

The Mid-Infrared Instrument, known as MIRI, adds a different perspective by detecting emission from dust and revealing material rich in hydrocarbons and silicate compounds.

Combining the instruments brings the stellar populations and dusty structures into the same view.

Each contributes information that would be harder to recognize from the other instrument alone.

The image’s colors translate infrared observations into a form human eyes can see. They help separate different features rather than reproduce the view an astronaut would see through a window.

Blue points mark individual stars or regions of star formation.

Bright red strands trace glowing dust, including the curved spokes that connect the inner and outer portions of the galaxy.

Those spokes preserve something of the spiral galaxy that existed before the collision.

Despite the disruption, the Cartwheel retained rotating arms, linking its present appearance to its earlier form.

Similar glowing dust also appears in the companion spiral galaxy toward the upper left, giving viewers another structure to explore beyond the dominant ring.

The Cartwheel’s eventual shape remains uncertain.

Its expanding rings and surviving spiral features capture a galaxy in transition, with its past still visible inside the changes set in motion by the collision.

That makes the image more than a portrait of an unusual object.

Across its bright rim and dusty spokes, the Cartwheel records how one encounter can influence a galaxy for hundreds of millions of years.

The collision has passed. The galaxy is still responding.

#6267. Rising seas could threaten coastal homes sooner than flood maps suggest

A study of Oʻahu finds that waves and erosion could threaten homes, roads, and sewage systems earlier than simple sea level rise maps suggest.

Most sea level rise maps assume that only land below the future ocean level will flood.

A new study of Oʻahu found that this approach misses 62% to 73% of the land at risk when sea levels rise by less than 4 feet (1.2 meters).

Anna Mikkelsen, a graduate student in the Department of Earth Sciences at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa, led the study, which was carried out with colleagues at the university’s Climate Resilience Collaborative.

Waves and coastal erosion could threaten homes, roads, and sewage systems on the Hawaiian island long before rising water floods these areas.

The researchers used computer models to estimate exposure rather than actual damage. They assumed that no new defenses would be built and that no buildings or residents would move between 2022 and 2150.

Planners often use a method called passive flooding in regions where little data is available.

The model raises the sea surface and marks land below the projected water level.

Mikkelsen’s team combined two other hazards with passive flooding. The team used an erosion model to project shoreline retreat along 9,523 survey lines around the island.

A separate wave model estimated coastal flooding from the largest waves of a typical year.

The three hazard maps were placed over public records of buildings, land parcels, roads, schools, hospitals, parks, sewer mains, and cesspools.

The researchers repeated the comparison at 1-foot (0.3-meter) increments of sea level rise, up to 6 feet (1.8 meters).

The dates for each step came from federal sea level projections issued in 2022 for the Honolulu tide gauge.

Under the Intermediate scenario, the sea stands 3.8 feet (1.16 meters) above its 2000 level by 2100.

Under the Intermediate-High scenario, which assumes rapid loss of ice sheets, it stands 5.8 feet (1.78 meters) above that level.

The ocean already reaches some of the island’s buildings.

In 2022, 544 buildings housing about 2,700 residents lay within zones exposed to erosion, high tides, or yearly high waves.

Passive flood maps would have missed nearly all 544 buildings. Waves alone affected 84% of them, while erosion affected the remaining 16%.

Passive flood maps also miss most threatened cesspools. Of the 54 cesspools already lying inside a hazard zone, 82% are threatened by erosion and 98% are left off passive flood maps.

On Oʻahu, waves and erosion threaten coastal areas before permanent flooding does.

The higher waterline is expected to become the main hazard after 3 to 4 feet of sea level rise.

The team estimates that 74% of the affected buildings and 87% of the affected cesspools would still be left off a passive map even when the sea has been raised by 4 feet.

“This tells us that it is critical to use multiple hazard models, and that areas with little data, such as other Pacific Islands, that rely on simpler passive flood model estimates may be underestimating the risk to their coastal infrastructure,” said Mikkelsen.

Exposure increases gradually through the first 3 feet (0.9 meters) of sea level rise. It then roughly doubles over the next foot.

The models project that the number of affected buildings goes from about 5,900 to about 11,100 between 3 and 4 feet of rise. Affected residents go from about 27,800 to 58,100 on an island of roughly 1 million people.

The length of affected road grows from 57 miles (92 kilometers) to 130 miles (210 kilometers). Affected sewer mains grow from 38 miles (61 kilometers) to 94 miles (151 kilometers).

The timing depends on the scenario. Sea levels are projected to rise 3 feet by 2073 under the Intermediate-High scenario and 4 feet by 2102 under the Intermediate scenario.

“Sea-level rise will not come to O‘ahu as a slow, harmless rise in the water level,” said Chip Fletcher, the paper’s senior author and director of the Climate Resilience Collaborative.

“Waves and erosion are already damaging homes, roads and wastewater systems, and our results show a threshold, somewhere between 0.9 and 1.2 meters of rise, where scattered local problems become widespread infrastructure failure.”

Honolulu has the largest number of exposed buildings and residents, and low streets in parts of the city are already flooded by high tides.

Honolulu’s dense street network gives drivers other routes around flooded blocks. But many rural coastal communities depend on a single highway.

The models project that erosion will make about 650 feet (200 meters) of Kamehameha Highway impassable in Kaʻaʻawa on the east side.

The models project this loss at just 1 foot of sea level rise, expected around 2051 under the Intermediate scenario. No alternative route runs along that shore.

Residents who live north of Kaʻaʻawa now reach central Honolulu in about 35 minutes, and that travel time would be tripled by a detour around the rest of the island.

Farrington Highway carries as many as 40,000 vehicles a day along the west side, and no public alternative exists for it.

Impassable sections are projected by the models at 3 feet of rise and 15% of the highway is projected to be impassable at 4 feet.

Earlier studies of managed retreat in Hawaii put the cost of relocating a major road and its buried utilities at about $279,210 per meter in 2025 dollars.

The authors applied that figure to the 31 miles (50 kilometers) of major road exposed by 2100. The estimated cost came to nearly $14 billion.

Many households on Oʻahu are not connected to a sewer and send their wastewater into one of the island’s roughly 8,000 cesspools.

A cesspool is an unlined pit that releases untreated sewage into the surrounding soil. A 2017 state law requires all cesspools to be phased out by 2050.

The number of cesspools inside a hazard zone is projected by the models to rise from 54 in 2022 to 92 at 1 foot of sea level rise and to 738 at 4 feet.

Cesspools and septic systems already leak sewage into coastal waters around Oʻahu. This pollution damages coral reefs and increases the risk of waterborne illness.

“These pathways would increase as sea levels rise because the groundwater also rises, and these systems may become flooded or unable to function properly,” Mikkelsen said.

The central sewer network also faces risks. High tides already push contaminated water from the Ala Wai Canal through Honolulu’s storm drains and into its streets.

The models project that the number of affected sewage pump stations could rise from one today to 16 after 4 feet of sea level rise.

The main threat also varies from one coast to another.

In Honolulu, passive flooding and wave flooding account for most exposure. Erosion accounts for roughly half on the North Shore, while yearly high waves dominate along the Waiʻanae coast in the west.

A building was counted as affected whenever any part of its footprint was touched by a hazard zone.

This approach shows which buildings face flooding or erosion. It does not measure how badly each building might be damaged.

The models also left out rainfall, storms, sinking land, and rising groundwater.

Groundwater already floods some basements in Honolulu, but the maps do not show these buildings as affected until sea levels rise by 6 feet. For this reason, the authors say their estimates may be too low.

Another modeling assumption could overstate erosion risk.

The erosion model did not account for seawalls and other barriers that line 27% to 29% of Oʻahu’s sandy shoreline, so it may overstate erosion wherever those structures continue to hold.

The researchers also did not examine how the three hazards affect one another.

They ran each model independently, so the flood models retained the current shoreline even where the erosion model projected beach loss.

The University of Hawaiʻi has made every hazard layer public in its SOEST Climate Viewer. These results update estimates from a 2017 state report on sea level rise used by state and county planners.

The full study was published in the journal Environmental Research: Climate.

#6266. The 8 Best Handheld Vacuums for Cleaning Small Messes

Keep your upright vacuum in the closet and opt for this convenient appliance instead to tackle everyday dirt, dust, and debris.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Cleaning is soothing for some, but for others, it’s simply another task to add to an overwhelming to-do list. Hauling your clunky upright vacuum out of the closet every time you need to tidy up a minor spill or dust bunny makes the task of cleaning even more inconvenient. That’s why handheld vacuums are such a practical companion to your regular vacuum. They help you reach narrow spaces such as stairs, corners, under car seats, and around furniture and cut down on how much large, clunky equipment you need to carry around.

But don't retire your go-to vacuum just yet. Handheld vacs are better suited for tackling small messes in between your deeper cleans. Since they have lower dustbin capacities and less suction power, they aren’t equipped to handle whole rooms or entire floors and can’t penetrate deep enough into your carpet fibers. However, if you’re looking for a machine that can supplement your usual cleaning tools, then a handheld vacuum might be right for you.

We evaluated a host of handheld vacuums from top brands like Black+Decker, Dyson, and Shark. We looked at their capability, features, and capacities to find the best devices to help you maintain cleanliness. These are the eight models we recommend, along with expert insight and valuable tips before you shop.

For handheld vacuums that we tested ourselves, we evaluated their performance around the house on a mix of surfaces and different types of furniture, paying attention to how well they handled everyday messes and how easy they were to maneuver. We also considered some of the more practical details like emptying the dustbin, maintaining the filter, and overall ease of use.

For models we haven’t tested firsthand, we drew on our extensive vacuum-testing knowledge, researching leading contenders and focusing on key features like battery life, filtration, suction performance, and attachments.

We prioritized cordless, rechargeable handheld vacuums that work well for a range of messes, such as pet hair and crumbs. This list reflects our top selections for handling everyday messes and more demanding cleanup jobs.

Lightweight, user-friendly, and full of power, the Dustbuster HHVK515J is an excellent vacuum to take on an array of tasks across the home, the shop, and even inside your car.

The nozzle at the end of the vacuum stretches an additional 7.5 inches—all you have to do is pull it forward to get into all the hidden nooks and crannies. It has two cleaning speeds, one of which is a power boost in case you need to maximize suction for a bigger mess.

The Dustbuster uses a foam filter and a pre-filter to trap debris and other common allergens, both of which you can wash from time to time. This vacuum doesn't come with any additional attachments besides the adjustable nozzle, so it might be best used for immediate messes that you need to clean up right away.

The Black+Decker Dustbuster AdvancedClean is reasonably priced, lightweight, compact, and has a good amount of suction power. The battery only lasts for about 15 minutes off of a single charge, but that's more than enough time to clean up a workspace, countertop messes, and other light debris.

Even with its smaller build, the Dustbuster comes with a built-in flip-up dusting brush and crevice tool, so you don’t have to deal with storing any attachments. It uses a washable pleated filter, but it’s not HEPA, so some dust and allergen particles may not be trapped completely.

The dustbin holds about half a liter of debris at a time, and it empties with a quick press of a button. The Dustbuster comes with a wall mount for quick and convenient storage.

What we appreciate about this handheld vacuum is that Shark has packed in similar features to some of the pet hair vacuums we love, like a paddled roller brush for scooping up deeply embedded hair and making continuous contact with surfaces. Alongside these features, you also get a self-cleaning brush roll.

This handheld vacuum uses two cyclonic air streams, one for powerful suction and one to separate debris away from the motor to protect its lifespan. When it's time to empty the dustbin, just hit the eject latch and the chamber door falls open, discharging dust and hair. You don’t have to touch any of the gunk.

We also like how the design uses a two-stage filter, and you can wash and use it again. The vacuum runs for up to 10 minutes off of its rechargeable lithium-ion battery.

The Dyson Car+Boat is a handheld vacuum that can easily alternate between detailing the interior of your car and cleaning small messes from bare floors, carpet, and furniture. Plus, it offers up to 50 minutes of fade-free suction in standard mode, which is more than any other handheld vacuum on this list (besides the corded option, that is).

Similar to Dyson cordless stick models, the Car+Boat uses a fully sealed filtration system to pick up and trap almost 100 percent of airborne particles as small as 0.3 microns.

It also comes with a mini motorized brush, a crevice tool, and a combination tool for messes both big and small. The main caveat is that you have to keep a trigger button depressed for the duration of your cleaning session in order for the vacuum to stay powered on.

The DeWalt DCV517B stands up to tough chores, tackling anything like a bowl of breakfast cereal dumped on the floor (milk and all), or a handful of metal shavings on top of your garage workbench.

The HEPA filter traps debris of varying sizes effectively, and the vacuum has two cleaning modes so you can alternate between the nozzle head and extendable hose. This model also has a half-gallon tank that easily detaches for emptying.

The DCV517B uses DeWalt-brand batteries, which may add some considerable heft to the body itself (it weighs 4.5 pounds to start). But a high-capacity battery gives superior vacuuming strength and provides the suction needed to clean both wet and dry messes.

The Shark Wandvac is the sleek, modern hand vacuum that could just as easily serve as an accent piece in your living room as it does for cleaning up spills. While the exterior might be flashy, the bones of the machine are solid as well.

The large mouth is great for big messes, and the powerful suction means even serious dirt or food spills will be pulled up without much issue. Beyond this, the Wandvac has multiple attachments including the Multi-Surface Pet Tool and Duster Crevice Tool.

During our testing, the Duster Crevice Tool was quite effective for hard-to-reach corners, ceilings and otherwise ignored spaces like under the fridge, but we were most impressed by the Surface Pet Tool. In combination with a bit of elbow grease, it lifted tons of hair and dander out of carpets, furniture, and other upholstery. Just note that the dustbin is a little small, which means frequent emptying.

The Bissell Pet Hair Eraser is the only thing that worked to remove embedded pet hair, litter paw prints, and dander from my black polyester couches (and I tried plenty of other methods). Suction is consistent and strong, and the motorized pet tool provided the power I needed to get rid of wiry hairs that had found themselves looped in the fabric.

The Pet Hair Eraser has a pleated post-motor filter, a washable inner foam filter, and a mesh pre-filter for trapping dust and allergens. The dustbin is easy to empty once you remove the filter, and you can give it a quick rinse if you want to remove any lingering debris. The vacuum lasts for up to 17 minutes, but it takes a long time to fully recharge.

Don’t want to deal with rechargeable batteries? A corded handheld vacuum is a great option if you prefer to have continuous power for your cleaning tools. The Dirt Devil Scorpion has a 15-foot power cable so you don’t have to always be within range of an outlet, along with a 2.5-foot detachable hose and built-in crevice tool for picking up dirt and debris in hard-to-reach areas.

The dustbin holds a little less than half a liter, which is right around the capacity we recommend to cut down on trips to the trash can. This model also uses a washable filter to reduce the amount of maintenance and replacements needed.

Use this alongside your corded upright, and you’ll have the suction power you need to tackle tough household messes. We just wish it came with some more attachments to really take it to the next level.

A quality handheld vac should be ready to use whenever you need it, which means having a dependable battery with a run time that lasts long enough so you don’t lose power mid-clean. Many of our selections use a lithium-ion battery that can last anywhere from around 10 to 50 minutes between charges. Just be prepared that some models take several hours to go from fully dead to fully charged, so keeping the vacuum docked and hooked up to power consistently is important.

Handheld vacuums have a smaller dustbin capacity and fill up faster than full-size, upright versions, but that’s because they handle light spills, not whole-home cleaning. If you regularly reach for your handheld vacuum, look for models that hold up to half a liter or more of debris, so you don’t have to make as many trips to the garbage can.

A handheld vacuum with multiple attachments may be a worthwhile investment if you have kids that are prone to dropping crumbs or furry friends that shed profusely. Crevice tools get into the nooks and crannies of the couch, whereas bristled or motorized brushes pick up stubborn pet hair.

Additional hose pieces can also be beneficial if you need extended reach. These types of attachments focus airflow and suction to a designated area, and may be used on different surfaces like upholstery, carpet, and hardwood floors.

Handheld vacuums often come with cloth, foam, or pleated filters that trap dust, hair, grime, and allergen particles—and most of these versions are washable to avoid buying replacements all the time.

Some handheld vacuums include an additional filter, called the pre-filter, which traps larger particles before they reach the main filter. Others might have a HEPA filter that removes up to 99.7 percent of airborne particles and is useful for allergy sufferers.

We recommend shopping for a handheld vacuum with at least a two-step filtration system or a HEPA filter if you’re trying to keep your home or car clear of common allergens like pollen and pet dander. Otherwise, a washable filter will do just fine for general cleaning tasks.

What is a good suction power rating for a handheld vacuum?

First, it’s important to note that brands don’t all advertise suction power the same way. Some list air watts (AW), some use pascals (Pa), and some don’t provide a suction rating at all and focus more on the motor.

These measurements aren’t directly interchangeable, but for everyday messes and light debris I would look for a handheld vacuum rated around 20 to 40AW or between 5,000 to 10,000Pa.

How often should I clean or replace the filter?

A light cleaning should be done every few weeks or whenever you notice reduced suction power. Foam and felt filters can be washed every 1 to 3 months, and should be replaced every 3 to 6 months.

HEPA filters are not washable unless specified by the vacuum manufacturer and should be replaced between 6 to 12 months. You can adjust the frequency of maintenance based on your cleaning needs and how much debris you typically pick up

There’s no one-size-fits all for how long a handheld vacuum lasts because it largely depends on build quality, frequency of use, battery health, and maintenance. Cleaning the filter and dustbin regularly helps preserve the battery and motor, too, but if the vacuum is losing suction or the battery can’t hold a charge, it might be time for a replacement.

#6265. Just like humans, orangutans prefer experiences they learned about while hearing laughter because it puts them in a good mood

Orangutans preferred a reward associated with laughter a day after learning about it, suggesting mood may shape what they value later.

Grandma’s pancakes may taste especially good because of the happy moments associated with them. Our mood during an experience can influence how much we value it later.

Now the same thing has turned up in orangutans, the least social of the great apes.

In a zoo test, six orangutans learned to dig a nut out of one material right after hearing other orangutans laugh. They learned to find a nut in a second material after hearing wind.

Both materials offered the same reward, yet a day after the last lesson, the apes preferred the material associated with laughter.

Daan Laméris, a postdoctoral researcher at Indiana University, led the work with Erica Cartmill, a professor at IU Bloomington.

Five of the orangutans live at ZOO Planckendael in Belgium, where Laméris ran most of the sessions, and the sixth lives at the Indianapolis Zoo.

Six animals is a small group, as ape studies usually are. And the good mood is the researchers’ reading of what the apes chose, since an orangutan can’t say how it feels.

In an interview with Earth.com, Cartmill said her lab’s earlier studies had already given evidence that hearing laughter puts apes in a positive mood.

“For me, the most important take-away from our study is that emotions influence learning,” she said. “In particular, if an orangutan is in a more positive mood when they learn something new, they will value that thing more strongly.”

On each trial, the experimenter set two plywood platforms in front of an orangutan.

Each held a bowl of a different material, shredded paper and yarn, for example, and an almond or a cashew was buried in one of the bowls, out of sight.

Once an ape pushed a finger into one bowl, the other platform was pulled away.

The apes learned two pairings over four days. The nut was always under one material on days one and three, and under a new material on days two and four.

A session ended once an ape chose right six times in a row, or after 30 trials.

Before each session, the ape spent five minutes beside two speakers, encouraged to stay nearby through familiar care routines and a bit of fruit every 10 to 15 seconds.

Ahead of one pairing, the apes heard laughter and play squeaks recorded from young orangutans they had never met. Ahead of the other, they heard wind noise at the same volume.

On day five, the two rewarded materials came back together for 30 trials. A nut was hidden under each on a random third of them, so the apes had nothing new to learn.

All six orangutans chose the laughter-paired material more often than the wind-paired one. For four of the six, the preference was strong enough that chance is an unlikely explanation.

On average, the apes picked the laughter-paired material on about two out of every three choices.

Unlike the other great apes, orangutans don’t live in stable groups. They meet up now and then in temporary parties, so they have fewer chances than chimpanzees, bonobos, or gorillas to hear another ape laugh.

Cartmill’s lab had already found that bonobos responded more optimistically to ambiguous situations after hearing laughter, in a 2025 study. Orangutans looked like the harder case.

“It is surprising to find these effects with orangutans, because they are the least social of all the great apes,” Laméris said. “So even among relatively non-social animals, laughter is important.”

Laméris told Earth.com that the result suggests the effect of positive social signals on thinking may run deeper in great apes than their social lives alone would predict.

“It also highlights that being relatively solitary doesn’t mean being socially or emotionally insensitive,” he said.

Before the laughter test, the team checked that the task could detect value at all. The routine was the same five days, but one material hid three nuts and the other hid one.

Four of the six apes later preferred the three-nut material, and the group as a whole did too. With six animals, though, the statistics behind that check were less firm than the laughter result.

The check matters because it shows what a preference in this task means. The apes’ choices on day five tracked how much a hiding place had been worth to them.

The preference associated with laughter was comparable in size to the preference associated with a larger reward.

Neither laughter nor the bigger reward made the apes learn faster. They reached six correct choices in a row at about the same pace whichever sound they had heard and whatever the payout.

What did speed them up was practice, since second sessions went faster than first ones.

The findings suggest that laughter influenced how much the apes valued what they had learned, without changing how quickly they learned it.

People show the same pattern, and it hadn’t been tested in another great ape before.

Laughter spreads between people, and great apes copy each other’s play faces and play sounds. Yet none of the orangutans laughed in response to the recordings.

“One important finding of our study is that the orangutans did not start laughing themselves after hearing play vocalizations,” Laméris said.

“While laughter can be contagious in humans, we did not observe this.”

The shift happened without any visible copying, the authors wrote. Feeling along with another animal and mirroring its expression usually happen together, and this result pulls them apart.

Orangutans do catch each other’s yawns and scratching, so they aren’t immune to copying. Here, though, the effect showed up in their choices rather than in laughter or other visible mimicry.

Laméris said the method is a way to study feelings in animals that can’t report them.

Rather than relying only on visible behavior, researchers can measure how an experience changes what an animal later chooses.

That approach, he said, could lead to better ways of assessing animal welfare.

The researchers adapted a test originally developed for rats, whose later choices can shift after play sessions or tickling by a handler.

Whether five minutes of recorded laughter changes how an orangutan learns anything outside a test, or how well it lives, is an open question.

Laméris said the team doesn’t know yet whether the effect carries over to everyday learning or welfare, though an environment that promotes positive states “is likely to enhance learning, and more broadly improve the welfare of animals.”

The group is part of a larger project on joy in animals. Laméris said a study of how laughter changes what chimpanzees pay attention to is already complete.

Cartmill said a version of the orangutan test is now under way with pet dogs.

Those results could help reveal whether the effect extends to animals more distantly related to humans.

The full study was published in the journal Biology Letters.

Over 300 Live Science readers responded to a recent poll about whether they'd train themselves to lucid dream if they could.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Lucid dreaming describes when you realize you're in a dream as it's unfolding. Sometimes, people can control the content of their dreams from this state of awareness.

Recently, researchers claimed that they found a way to "train" people to lucid dream by having them meditate and complete virtual-reality-augmented exercises while they were awake. Following the release of that study, Live Science asked its readers whether they would learn to lucid dream if they could.

Over 300 readers weighed in, with 77% saying "Yes, I'd want to try to control my dreams." Additionally, 17% of respondents said "No, I already lucid dream enough without training," 3% said "No, I don't see the point," and the final 3% said they weren't sure.

In the comments, one reader shared that they'd once experimented with hypnagogic napping, a technique famously used by Thomas Edison and Salvador Dalí in which the famous luminaries would wake themselves up just as they were drifting to sleep. Edison claimed that this helped him access a creative sweet spot at the edge of sleep and wakefulness.

"When I was experimenting with the hypnagogic state (using the Edison method) I started having spontaneous lucid dreams," the reader wrote. "I can confidently say, that there were some of the most profound experiences of my life, so the answer is definitely yes."

Another reader reported having lucid dreams "about once or twice a year," adding that they typically wake up shortly after realizing it's a dream. "My most recent one was of my recently deceased wife. I became very sad when I realized she wasn't supposed to be there," the reader wrote. "I hugged her and told her I don't want to be without her. She replied that I could live a long life if I took care of myself (This was a very typical response from her...lol). I feel very blessed to have had that dream."

Other readers chimed in on Facebook. "Already have it [lucid dreaming], but if I didn't I would certainly practice to do so," one wrote. "Hell yes," another said, in response to the idea of training themselves to lucid dream.

Other readers noted that they already lucid dream quite often or that they can consistently control their dreams, with one even saying that all of their dreams are lucid. Another said, "Some nights I interrupt it [my dream] like Monty Python — 'Too silly!' and start over."

But while one person compared lucid dreaming to "writing and directing your own movie," another noted that "lucid dreams can be boring, repetitive, annoying." So while many people would practice lucid dreaming if they could, not everyone sees the appeal.

Nicoletta Lanese is the health channel editor at Live Science and was previously a news editor and staff writer at the site. She is a recipient of the 2026 AHCJ International Health Study Fellowship, with a project focused on antibiotic stewardship practices in Japan and the U.S. They hold a graduate certificate in science communication from UC Santa Cruz and degrees in neuroscience and dance from the University of Florida. Beyond Live Science, Lanese's work has appeared in The Scientist, Science News, the Mercury News, Mongabay and Stanford Medicine Magazine, among other outlets. Based in NYC, she also remains involved in dance and performs in local choreographers' work.

#6263. Science to restore speech is moving fast. Here’s what’s next

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A Michigan woman uses a brain implant to speak with her neurosurgeon. Efforts to restore speech highlight what’s at stake when we lose opportunities to talk.

Scientists are racing to restore people’s ability to communicate. Powerful AI-based methods to decode speech signals and predict words, along with advances in technology, promise success.

This episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me takes listeners through the breadth of scientific efforts to restore words, emotions and even gestures to people who can’t move or talk.

We’ll hear from Casey Harrell, a man with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis who can no longer talk. A user of today’s technology, Harrell has a unique perspective on what he’d like to see improved for the technology of tomorrow.

And as season two wraps up, listeners will be left with a reminder of the power of a voice: a piece of comedy from Jules Rodriguez, performed with his voice clone in front of a live crowd.

“Being backstage and then seeing him come out, like, roll out his wheelchair, and everybody goes nuts because they’re like, ‘What is going on here? This doesn’t make sense,’” says Jules’ wife, Maria Aleandra Fernandez. “And every time I was like, ‘This is life. This is love. This is passion. What else is there?’ I don’t know that there’s anything else more powerful than what this guy is doing here.”

Laura Sanders: OK, I want to ask who your favorite comedians are and why. Who makes you all laugh?

Jules Rodriguez: Pete Holmes and Mike Birbiglia are some of my favorites.

[Audio] He was just like, I’m a bear, et cetera.

[Audio] The best part of sleep is falling asleep. That’s the only part you’re there for.Jules: Their styles are different, but I have always gravitated towards their authenticity.

Sanders: There’s another comedian who is extra meaningful for Jules: Conan O’Brien.

[Audio] Today is a bit of a different sort of episode. I’ll be talking to Jules and Maria.

Sanders: After MA had reached out, Conan invited the couple onto his podcast, where they connected about comedy. Conan still checks in on Jules every so often.

[Audio] It’s incredible to me that in our conversations, you’re very frank about the pain that you go through, and how intense it is. But you’re also always so positive and funny and, frankly, you give me a lot of [beep]. Which I find to be, well I hate it, by the way, first of all. Oh, get over it, Conan.

Jules: Conan is very special to me. Watching and listening to him helped me disconnect from the harsh reality of my life. And when I got to meet him and chat with him, it meant the world to me.

Maria Aleandra Fernandez: Having the most normal conversation with Conan O’Brien is something I will never get over.

[Audio] So he has a bunch of banked phrases. He’s going to play a few of our favorites. OK. I’m fine. I’m perfectly [beep] fine. [laughter] Come on man, are we doing this or not? Oh my God, oh my God. I’m destroying this marriage. MA: He really is so genuine and like, not only willing to talk to us, but really looks forward to talking. Like, I love talking to you guys. I’m not just doing it to be a nice person, which feels, you know, feels wonderful.

[Audio] You have my love, my respect and we’re thinking about you guys all the time.

Sanders: As you were talking earlier, it made me think about what it means to make somebody laugh and to entertain them, and like how actually very, very special that must be. Just kind of, at its heart, it’s, it is joy and humans connecting. And so, extra special.

MA: That’s the other thing I’ve learned mainly through Jules, about humor and comedy. And who were we watching yesterday? The NPR interview with Dave Chappelle. [Audio] Dave Chappelle says he is very clear about his role as a comedian.

MA: And Dave Chappelle said something that is so spot-on. He said that comedians are how people metabolize things.

[Audio] We’re like the nation’s kidney. We help everyone metabolize not just facts, but feelings around facts, or ideas. And jokes are just a shorthand for all of that.

MA: And I’m also a nerd and I’ve been reading some Greek tragedies and studying about how, you know, that’s also like the artists that help people metabolize feelings and emotions. And when he said that, I was like, that’s exactly it. And that’s what Jules has done.

It’s something that heals. And it’s not even like it’s self-deprecating. It’s not like, oh, let’s make fun. And the way he does it is so smart and genuine, but also not taking himself seriously. It just disarms everything. You’re just like, oh, OK. And that idea of metabolizing the really hard feelings that come around grief, mortality, losing a person, seeing how he’s trapped in his body, but he chooses not to be trapped in that really big way is so profound.

Sanders: Science is iterative. It builds. It may take a wrong turn or two, but overall, it’s moving toward a deeper understanding of our world and of ourselves.

By using their voices, by telling their stories, by telling their jokes, Jules and MA are helping me, and maybe you too, metabolize the pain – and the joy – of living. Welcome to The Deep End, Talk to Me.

[Voices] Hey mom, can I tell you something? Hi. Do you want to talk? That added layer of it being you. Hello? Your voice. Hi.

Sanders: I’m Laura Sanders and today, we’re going to look ahead to what’s coming next for the human voice and efforts to restore it.

Sanders: In some ways, this podcast is a story of progress, of figuring out, little by little, more about the brain, and more about technology and more about people. Today, Jules can type with his eyes, and his son can hear his dad’s voice say I love you. In earlier episodes, you heard from Casey Harrell. Casey can think about saying a word to his daughter, and boom, they’re off playing a game together.

Casey Harrell: So this has kept me still in touch with people and the world, and it is not hyperbole to frame it this way.

Sanders: Casey has ALS and can no longer speak. He volunteered for a clinical trial, and now he has a device implanted in his brain that detects neural patterns as he tries to say a word. This system has changed his life.

Casey: It is the ability to parent my daughter. It is the ability to connect with my wife. It is the ability to make a wry joke with my friends. Timing is everything, and that is why having nothing, this is completely revolutionary.

Sanders: But there aren’t many people like Casey. Leigh Hochberg is the director of the BrainGate clinical trials consortium, the trial that Casey is participating in. I asked him how many people might have participated in similar sorts of research projects. How many people have electrodes in their brain that can help them speak?

Leigh Hochberg: In terms of actually decoding attempted speech, I’m almost sure it’s still less than 10. It may be closer to five or six, so far, and that number undoubtedly is going to increase fairly quickly.

Sanders: So this is a small but growing number. Growing, because we now have a solid scientific understanding of the brain’s speech signals, and other signals too. And neurotech companies are very interested.

Hochberg: About 10 years ago or so, the academic research had de-risked this field sufficiently that it allowed for the entry of now likely a dozen or more companies that are actively pursuing their own version of an implantable brain-computer interface.

What I anticipate will happen, what I guess I hope will happen, is that the companies will continue to very carefully, thoughtfully and in a very focused manner, create their systems, and test them rigorously. And hopefully they’ll be demonstrated to be safe and effective. And at the same time, the academic groups have the opportunity to continue to demonstrate what’s possible, to push beyond that, and to show hopefully what those medical devices, once they’re actually available to market, might be able to do next.

Sanders: I talked with Vikash Gilja, a neural engineer who works at a company called Paradromics. He sees this momentum that Hochberg describes too.

Vikash Gilja: And, you know, we can see all the pieces coming together. These tools weren’t available even five years ago. And what we’re seeing is like, you know, month over month, there are new tools available. So we’re able to leverage those and move faster.

Sanders: Paradromics has developed its own brain-computer interface for communication. The device is about the size of a dime, and it sits on the motor cortex. That’s the part of the brain that creates speech signals. The chip then detects these signals as a person thinks about saying a word.

Matthew Willsey: So the cortical module has 421 tiny little sensors.

Sanders: That’s neurosurgeon and biomedical engineer Matthew Willsey, of the University of Michigan Health. He’s describing the device from Paradromics here.

Willsey: They’re about one and a half millimeters long. And you know, it’s smaller than your thumbnail, like kind of all the way around. It’s like a cylinder. And at the bottom of the cylinder are the electrodes, is what we call them. And we get them really close to the brain. And then when we deploy it, what it does is it pushes those electrodes down into the brain.

Sanders: Those tiny sensors are listening to the nearby neurons that control the muscles required for speech.

Willsey: The principle is to try and get these things as small as possible to disrupt the least amount of tissue as possible, and then to get them really, really close to the individual cells, the neurons themselves that have the information we’re trying to record.

Sanders: The goal here is to restore a person’s ability to talk.

Willsey: So in the ideal situation, the electrodes would sit, you know, right next to those neurons. This type of technology that’s very intuitive, that can record activity from the brain in kind of a high-throughput way, can put the words up at a good speed and a good accuracy, allows them to kind of regain the ability to communicate with others close to how they maybe were before they had the illness. So that truly is very powerful.

Sanders: You might remember that Casey’s implant, called the BrainGate 2 system, requires ports on his head that are connected to external wires.

Casey: What is annoying about this device is really easy to answer. It is not portable, and it is not implanted only inside my head.

Sanders: Unlike Casey’s implant, the Paradromics device is fully implantable. That means it’s wireless. This summer, Willsey implanted Paradromic’s device in a volunteer’s brain. The brain belonged to a 68-year-old woman who lives in Michigan. She has primary lateral sclerosis, a disease that has taken away most of her ability to talk. So far, the Paradromics system is up and running, and the volunteer is testing her abilities out.

Here she is talking with Willsey and other researchers in a video provided by Paradromics. You’ll hear her natural voice, which is hard to understand, and then a digital voice speaking the words her brain implant decoded.

[Audio] I love the change of seasons in Michigan. And my favorite one is the fall. I love the change of seasons in Michigan. And my favorite one is the fall. Yeah, it’s good.

Sanders: This volunteer has used the device to talk to her grandkids on the phone. But this is just the very beginning for this research project. There’s so much more to test.Casey is still working on his system, too — particularly, streamlining the process. When Casey uses his brain-computer interface, it decodes speech signals from his brain, then puts words on a screen. Casey then selects a button, using his eye movements or his brain-computer interface, to say these words out loud with a digital voice. Here’s Casey.

Casey: It is not fast enough to provide enough instant conversation with other people that need to slow down to talk to me.

Sanders: But scientists want to skip this middle part — the words written on a screen. They want instead to go straight to speech, and perhaps make conversations faster. Casey says this goal to go directly from brain signals to a speaking digital voice would be his top priority.

Casey: That one is the holy grail of what this will become in terms of speech. It will allow you to have a seamless conversation. I am talking about, yes, I will intend to talk, and then it will just translate that automatically into speech, like we do, and you are doing right now.

Sanders: In an earlier episode, we talked about attempts to do just this with Casey’s system, to push it to do what they call brain-to-voice. Early attempts were hard to decipher. But it has already improved, by a lot. In the latest tests, this brain-to-voice process produces words that are understandable – reaching about 95 percent accuracy for listeners. Here’s Casey speaking test sentences. It comes from a preprint manuscript posted on the website bioRxiv.

[Audio] The day is not over yet. Please come in with me.

Sanders: Scientists have another thing on their to-do list. And this one goes beyond the words themselves. Here’s Gilja, from Paradromics.

Gilja: Let’s say I identify whether a sentence is a statement or a question. Well, now you can pass that information on to speech synthesis, so that you get these two different versions.

Sanders: The same words could be a statement or a question. You see what he means. You see what he means? And that information can be pulled out from a person’s brain activity.

Gilja: If I’m decoding prosodic information, if I’m decoding speed, when a word is meant to appear, that can also be passed on to modern speech synthesis systems, so that you’re more accurately capturing the prosody that somebody intends. Same thing with loudness, right? So you can see how as that information becomes available from the neural channels, it can be provided to the AI speech synthesis to get closer to the intended voice in the moment that the individual wants to generate.

Sanders: All of these signals can be collected and used to build a more accurate voice — one that says things exactly how a person intends to say them, like a Minnesotan’s ooftah or a slow southern hey y’all. Now, today’s voice clones can add these emotional layers onto words already. Here’s what Jules told me when I asked him about whether his voice clone can do it.

Jules: Oh, there are plenty of things it does that are all the above. But one thing in particular is how it inserts tone and inflections on words. Sometimes my wife will get mad because my response can come off with some sass.

Sanders: So there’s loudness, emphasis, pitch — all of these things contribute to what words means. But imagine if a brain implant can pick up these cues directly — no typing required. Here’s Hochberg.

Hochberg: There’s a lot that can be conveyed through the emphasis, through the tone, through even the humor that can sometimes be conveyed by the way that somebody who’s able-bodied may speak a particular sentence. All of those, I think, really can be captured by these implantable brain-computer interfaces by harnessing the rich neural activity that’s available from the brain. We should be able to restore a lot of that.

Sanders: Sergey Stavisky is one of the UC Davis researchers working with Casey and Hochberg. He and his colleagues are working on some of these ideas.

Stavisky: And even now we’re continuing to improve that and actually adding additional layers. So we have one forward-looking project where we can maybe decode the kind of emotional valence of how he’s trying to say it. Is he trying to say something in an angry way or in a surprised way or in a happy-sounding way, to kind of further make it more expressive.

Sanders: They’re even trying  to decode singing. Well, OK, it’s really more of a hum at this point, he says. But those sorts of tone shifts could, in theory, be deciphered.

Stavisky: We definitely have our work cut out for us on the singing and melody side of things.

Sanders: All sorts of voice signals could be pulled from brain activity.

Stavisky: Ultimately, we want people to be in full control of what they’re communicating. This should come from their intent. So, yeah, we are trying to decode all of the aspects of his voice, whether it’s the pitch, the timbre, the loudness, the intonation, which word he’s stressing. All of that, ideally, we would decode from brain activity, including kind of all of that emotional nuance.

Sanders: Voice clones can speak with various emotions. You heard my voice clone do just that in earlier episodes. But the difference here is that a person wouldn’t have to type in the instructions. They would come straight from their brain, seamlessly. Other nonverbal signals can be pulled from the brain, too.

Samantha Brosler: In the past five years or so, there have been a lot of advancements in the field of BCIs for restoring individual functions to people with paralysis.

Sanders: That’s Samantha Brosler, a bioengineer at the University of California, San Francisco. Some brain-computer interfaces can pick up movements. We haven’t talked much about them, but these implants have their own very successful research history. They’ve allowed people to control a robotic arm, for instance.

Brosler: Most of these devices so far have been designed to restore one function at a time, whereas in reality, frequently people who are paralyzed are missing both the ability to speak and perform body movements. And so in this study, we asked whether a single brain implant could be used to decode both speech and movement at the same time.

Sanders: It turns out, it could. She and her colleagues were able to decode gestures for communication — things like thumbs up, or a head nodding yes — and words. This combo approach is a more natural way of getting a point across.

Brosler: We naturally use gestures alongside our speech. So for example, some gestures can substitute for speech entirely, like nodding yes, shaking your head no, waving, shrugging, giving a thumbs up. But they can also add or change the meaning of what we’re saying. So for example, if you say maybe combined with nod head yes, that has a very different, you know, meaning than if you say maybe and shrug or shake your head no.

Sanders: My kids know that a slow maybe with a skeptical eyebrow raise is much closer to a no than my fast upbeat maybe with a little head nod. There is so much subtext in our body language.

Brosler: So I think of, you know, gestures and body movements as an additional communication channel that can work together with speech to add expressivity to what we’re trying to say.

Sanders: In the study, the output was a digital avatar who looked like the person. Success looked like the avatar moving and getting the word right.

Brosler: And the idea is that we enable the participants to use speech and gestures alone or together. So in theory, someone could say hello while waving.

Sanders: The researchers started simple, with just a few phrases — hello, bye, good idea, how’s it going, let’s go — and just a few gestures, like a shrug or a point, a fist pump, thumbs up.

Brosler: Of course, ultimately, we’re hoping to expand this to even larger vocabulary and more range of body movements across the whole body to help allow people more expression in their communication.

Sanders: The sheer number of different approaches to restoring communication is a sign that this neurotechnology is coming fast. Here’s Willsey.

Willsey: I think it’s good. There’s a lot of players that are entering into the field that have a variety of different ideas where they can run the clinical trials and see how these different devices stack up.

Sanders: There are lots of reasons to be optimistic about the future here, and it’s a future that isn’t even that far off. Here’s David Brandman, one of the researchers at UC Davis who works with Casey. He’s also the neurosurgeon who implanted Casey’s device.

Brandman: I think I’m about five years away from being able to meet a patient with ALS and having the following conversation, and saying, you know, Ms. Smith, I’m sorry you’ve been diagnosed with ALS. I don’t have a cure for you, but I do have a device that I can implant that can help you communicate despite facing a future of paralysis. It’s a device that would be implanted. It’s fully wirelessly. It’s cosmetically invisible, and you’d be able to use it to communicate your needs and have a meaningful conversation with friends and family. So I think that kind of conversation is about five to 10 years away.

Sanders: It’s a beautiful vision. When you’ve been a reporter as long as I have, you’re skeptical when scientists say something big is just five to 10 years away. But in this case, I see it.

It’s easy to get drawn into the technical details here. Different types of implants, the decoding processes, AI-powered voice clones and what they can do and can’t do — what they should do and shouldn’t do. But if you step back and really look, you’ll see that this research is all propelled by a very simple and powerful fact: The human voice is too important to lose.

Casey: What does my voice mean to me? It means so much. I think it is the most important thing that I have lost in this whole disease.

Sanders: So now we are here, in this moment, as Jules would say, right here, right now. And right now, the human voice is shifting and changing, expanding in ways that were completely unthinkable even just a few years ago. The future of the human voice and its many replicas is anybody’s guess.

Sanders: In one of Jules’ comedy sets, the one he did in November of 2024, he wheels out onto the stage as the song “Walking on Sunshine” plays.

As the crowd settles and finishes their clapping and woo-ing, Jules pauses. You can’t see this, but he wiggles his eyebrows — a lot. The crowd goes crazy every time. He hasn’t said a single word yet. After another pause, he deadpans with his voice clone: “That is all the time I have. My Make-A-Wish covered only a few minutes. Goodnight, everybody.”

And with that, Jules takes control and he’s off on a tear, ripping through stories of a weatherman who seems too happy about standing out in hurricanes, the exquisite guilt trips lovingly crafted by his Cuban parents, and the indignities of having body parts shaved with his sister right there in the room. Jules has the audience laughing so hard. It’s magnificent.

MA: And being backstage and then seeing him come out, like roll out in his wheelchair and everybody go nuts because they’re like, what is going on here? Like, this doesn’t make sense. And every time I was like, this is like life. This is love. This is passion. This is like, what else is there? Like, I don’t know that there’s anything else more powerful than what this guy is doing here and what I can help him do.

Sanders: I get what MA meant when she said that comedy is something that heals. When his set actually does come to a close, he tells the audience. [Audio] Now you have to watch me slowly get off this stage. Goodnight, everybody.

Sanders: It’s hilarious. It’s happy. It’s sad. It’s perfect.

This is The Deep End, Talk to Me. I’m Laura Sanders. If you like this podcast, tell your friends and leave us a review. It helps the show a lot. Send us your questions and your comments at podcasts@sciencenews.org.

#6262. Strange new material pulses in perfect rhythm to make future robots feel more alive

Dozens of motorized cells that start vibrating at random merge into one slow pulse, forming a mechanical time crystal that holds its rhythm.

A few musicians can hold a beat together, but an orchestra with no conductor tends to drift apart. Physicists have now built a sheet of material that does the opposite, and ends up making unified waves.

Nudge it, and dozens of small motorized cells begin to twitch on their own, each at its own pace. Over a few seconds the twitches merge into one slow pulse that the whole sheet keeps, and there’s no clock telling it when.

The team at the University of Amsterdam and the University of Birmingham calls the merging process wave coarsening.

The final state is what physicists call a time crystal: matter that repeats a motion in time the way an ordinary crystal repeats a pattern in space.

“Our research provides a striking example of spontaneous organization – tiny vibrations organizing themselves until an entire material moves in a coordinated way,” said Jack Binysh of Birmingham, a co-lead author who began the work in Amsterdam.

“Like musicians gradually finding the same beat, individual parts of an active material can organize their movements until the whole structure moves together.”

Each cell of the material is a trio of elastic hexagons wired to a small circuit board. A sensor reads how each hexagon is squeezed, and a voice-coil actuator, the kind found in a loudspeaker, pushes on it.

The board follows one rule. When a hexagon is compressed, its clockwise neighbor is compressed too, and its counterclockwise neighbor is stretched.

The rule breaks a symmetry that ordinary materials obey. Push on a spring and it pushes back the same way whichever end you push.

These cells respond differently depending on direction, which physicists call non-reciprocal. They can only do it because each one has its own power.

The team built 37 of these cells into a honeycomb and set it on a glass plate slicked with Teflon so it could slide freely. Then they turned the pushback strength past the point where a single cell starts to oscillate on its own.

Given a shake, each cell began vibrating at about 30 times a second. Then something slower took over.

A longer wave crept around the edge of the material in one direction, growing in wavelength, in period, and in size, until it drowned out the fast twitching. A few seconds in, every cell was shearing back and forth together on one steady rhythm.

The team ran the experiment six times, each from a different random jolt. Each time, the distance over which cells moved in step grew by a power law while the vibration’s energy rose.

A mathematical model of the sheet reproduced the same growth on a line and on a grid. In the model, energy is pumped in without pushing or spinning the sheet as a whole.

The last step is what makes the words time crystal apply.

In simulations, the team subjected the final oscillation to noise. The larger the sheet, the longer its rhythm held, a sign that the order survives at scale rather than being washed out by small disturbances.

To check that the effect was not a quirk of one design, the team built a second material. It was an elastic ring carrying 24 small torque motors that twist in response to their neighbors, floated on an air table.

Any small disturbance of the material set off short waves around the ring, which merged into longer ones.

The ring’s shapes took turns. A six-lobed pattern grew first and briefly dominated, then a five-lobed one caught up and overtook it, then four, each dying as the next longer shape took over.

In the end the ring settled into a slow cycle around a flattened, pancake-like shape.

“Wave coarsening could be exploited as a way of controlling shape changes and directed motion – proving useful in robotics, active matter and optomechanics,” Binysh said.

“Our discovery could form a key step towards the development of biology-inspired multifunctional robots.”

The coarsening stops if the material can push against something. When the team removed the Teflon so the honeycomb rubbed on the glass, the short waves kept circling and never merged into the whole-sheet pulse.

In the model, friction sets the wavelength at which the waves get stuck.

The team also simulated a much larger disc of 5,813 cells. There, coarsening started everywhere at once, but waves along the rim soon took over.

They ran in one direction around the edge, the way currents run around the edge of certain quantum materials.

On a ring-shaped disc, the inner and outer edges carried waves in opposite directions and, with friction added, the two stayed at the edges instead of invading the middle.

Both the model and the simulations of growing size confirmed the time crystal. The physical sheets of material had 37 and 24 cells. The honeycomb is flat and only shears.

What wave coarsening does in a three-dimensional material that can bend and twist is untested, and that is what the team wants to build next.

The applied question is whether one material can hold several stable rhythms and switch between them. Co-lead author Jonas Veenstra, now at ENS de Lyon, said the group has started to think about it.

Each pattern could get a different job, such as a shape change or a direction of travel, and a single material could then do the work of several machines.

Such a material would be a step toward robots that coordinate the way flocks and fireflies do, with no central controller, a direction the Amsterdam group has already explored.

Corentin Coulais leads that group, with Anton Souslov of the University of Cambridge as co-corresponding author and co-authors at Delft University of Technology and Leiden University. The materials, Coulais said, carried more than 100 sensors and actuators.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.
