#6261. Almost all of Europe’s wild bee species still exist, but their shrinking habitats tell a much darker story

A century of records shows European pollinator decline is uneven. Nearly all wild bee species persist, but most have lost range since 1921.

At first glance, the survival of Europe’s wild bees looks like a success story. Records show that almost every bee species seen in the last century is still alive somewhere today.

However, when scientists map out exactly where these bees are actually living, it becomes clear that their territories are rapidly disappearing.

Most wild bee species occupy less of Europe than they did a century ago. Among the species with enough records to track, the average bee has lost about a third of its range since 1921.

The authors call it a reshuffling rather than an extinction wave: sensitive species are thinning out while a resilient few spread.

Carlos Martínez-Núñez of the Doñana Biological Station in Sevilla, part of Spain’s national research council, CSIC, led the analysis.

His co-authors include Ignasi Bartomeus at Doñana, who designed the study with him, and researchers at the University of Mons in Belgium and the University of Novi Sad in Serbia.

The records they used were gathered opportunistically over a century, not in a planned survey. They come from museum drawers, expert collections, published papers and online databases.

So the team had to correct for a century of uneven collecting, and it could estimate trends for only about 40 percent of species.

The dataset holds more than four million records of wild bees and hoverflies collected across Europe between 1921 and 2020, each one checked by taxonomists.

Hoverflies are flower-visiting flies and Europe’s other big group of insect pollinators.

Between them, the records cover 1,898 wild bee species and 784 hoverfly species. That’s 88 percent of the 3,051 known on the continent.

To turn scattered records into trends, the team divided Europe into hexagonal cells with sides about 31 miles (50 kilometers) long.

For each species and each year, the models estimated which cells it occupied. They also estimated how likely a species was to be recorded at all, so a decade with few collectors wouldn’t read as a decade with few bees.

About 91 percent of the species in the dataset have at least one record from 2001 onward. The rest, at most 9 percent, could be candidates for extinction across the continent.

However, most of them were extremely rare a century ago too, and the IUCN’s European Red Lists name only 14 bee species and one hoverfly as possibly extinct.

Counting species, region by region, gave a mostly stable picture as well. The Atlantic region, which takes in the United Kingdom, Belgium, the Netherlands and western France, lost wild bee and hoverfly species steadily across the century.

In the Continental region of central and eastern Europe, the historical decline in bees slowed while hoverflies fell in recent decades.

Most of what scientists know about pollinator decline comes from the Atlantic region, where farmland was transformed over the past century. The authors wrote that declines that steep may not hold across the rest of Europe.

The species-by-species view is where the reassurance ends. In every region except the Alpine one, more bee species were shrinking their range than expanding it.

In an interview with Earth.com, Martínez-Núñez said that gap is what surprised him most, and that a count of species alone can hide big changes.

“Species may still be present, but their declining occupancy can provide an early warning of broader environmental change, long before they become extinct,” he said.

Averaged across Europe, bee occupancy fell by 0.42 percent a year, a 34 percent drop over the century.

For hoverflies, the pattern looked different: species expanding and contracting were roughly balanced, and the continental average rose.

“Hoverflies show a contrasting positive trend at the European scale, highlighting the importance of looking beyond broad generalizations about pollinator decline,” Martínez-Núñez told Earth.com.

But that rise came mostly from a small number of species with very large gains, and from the early decades, when records are thin. When the team began the analysis in 1971 instead, the hoverfly increase flattened to no change.

For bees, the later start changed where the losses showed up. The Atlantic decline disappeared, which fits damage done early by agricultural intensification. Declines in the cold Boreal north and the warm Mediterranean south grew steeper.

The Alpine region was the exception: declining bee species didn’t outnumber expanding ones there, and among hoverflies the expanding species dominated.

The authors read that as warm-adapted species moving uphill as the climate warms.

Body size, diet, social habits and climate preference together explained less than 1 percent of the variation in how a species did.

However, one weak pattern held. Bee species tied to warmer climates tended to expand their range, and cold-adapted groups, bumblebees among them, tended to contract, with wide differences inside each group. Hoverfly declines clustered in cold-adapted genera as well.

Some genera of parasitic bees, which lay their eggs in other bees’ nests, declined consistently, and so did some bees that collect pollen from a narrow group of plants. Others of the same kind did fine.

The team found a weak link between a parasitic species’ trend and its host’s.

The regions that worry Martínez-Núñez most are the Atlantic and Continental ones, where bee and hoverfly diversity has declined.

“I’m also concerned about specialist and parasitic bees, which may be particularly vulnerable to environmental change.”

Bee species the IUCN Red List classes as Critically Endangered showed the steepest declines of all.

Species the list marks as Data Deficient, meaning too poorly known to assess, also had consistently low trends. The authors took that as a sign that little-studied species may be declining without anyone noticing.

Occupancy tracks where a species is found, not how many individuals live there. A bee could be vanishing from most of a cell and still count as present. The models worked for 1,225 of the roughly 1,940 species with enough records to try.

Records are sparse in the first half of the century studied. Some regions have thin coverage, and the recent downturn in Alpine hoverflies shifted when the team changed the model, so they called it too early to confirm.

Whether the reshuffling is already costing Europe pollination is the open question. The authors wrote that the consequences of this kind of species turnover are rarely tested.

Asked what can be done now, Martínez-Núñez said farmers can keep hedgerows, field margins and flower-rich habitats. City planners can link up green spaces planted with native species.

“Gardeners can plant native flowers that bloom throughout the year and avoid pesticides,” said Martínez-Núñez.

The authors expect their trend data to feed the next Red List assessments, including for pollinators now listed as of Least Concern that are in decline.

Long-term monitoring of Europe’s wild pollinators is still missing, so a century of museum drawers is the only long view there is.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#6260. The 6 Best Inflatable Hot Tubs for Backyard Relaxation

Bliss out with one of these affordable inflatable hot tubs for the ultimate at-home spa experience.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Nothing beats a warm, bubbly soak under the stars, but not everyone has the space—or budget—to install a permanent hot tub in their backyard. That’s where inflatable hot tubs come into play.

They cost less than their hard-sided counterparts—some four-person models are under $500, if you can believe it—and are easy to store in the off-season. Another plus: inflatable hot tubs come with everything you need to get them up and running, so you just fill them with water and crank up the temperature.

Whether you’re looking for a small option for two or a larger model to soak with friends and family, read on for our best inflatable hot tub recommendations and the essentials to consider before you shop.

Looking for more ways to upgrade your backyard? Check out our stories on the best outdoor sectionals, cantilever umbrellas, and smokeless fire pits.

We scoured user reviews and chose options across sizes, styles, and price points, from value-packed to high-end. We spent a lot of time weighing different hot tub models—both permanent and inflatable—so we used our expertise to recommend only durable, comfortable options. As mentioned above, there are plenty of features to consider when shopping for an inflatable hot tub, and we highlighted the most notable ones for each model we cover.

The Intex PureSpace Plus gives you the jet count and water capacity of pricier six-person inflatables for less. It holds 290 gallons and lists a six-person capacity, though four adults is more realistic if everyone wants ample legroom. The 170 air jets run along the walls and floor for a full-body massage, but they’re fixed, so you can’t aim them at a sore spot.

The tub can inflate in a few minutes with the included hose, no tools needed. Heating is slow, though, with the pump reaching a 104-degree Fahrenheit maximum over several hours, so start it in the morning if you want to relax by dinner time. A built-in hard-water treatment system softens the water as it fills, which slows the mineral scale that otherwise builds up inside the heater and pump.

A multicolor LED light is great for nighttime soaks, and two spare filter cartridges and a floating chlorine dispenser keep the water clear. It also includes a ground cloth and insulated cover to help retain heat between uses. Two removable headrests are included, so you can really relax after a long day.

The Miami is built for two people who want a hot tub without much fuss or yard space. It’s round, 71 inches across, holds 177, and fits two adults comfortably or four if everyone doesn’t mind a snugger fit.

The insulated EnergySense cover and liner retain heat, and Coleman rates the tub 40 percent more energy-efficient than comparable inflatables, so it uses less power over a season of use. A Freeze Shield feature turns the heater on automatically when the water temperature nears freezing, so the pump and liner won’t ice up. A power-saving timer also lets you schedule heating for when you’ll actually use it.

The 120 air jets are spaced around the seating area, so the bubbles reach your back and legs. Setup needs no tools, and the box includes the heater pump, a ChemConnect chemical dispenser, a Type VI filter cartridge, and the insulated cover. The one compromise is size. At 26 inches tall with a 52-inch interior, it’s shallower and snugger than some of the six-person tubs on this list.

For large groups, you can’t go wrong with this Bestway inflatable hot tub, designed for up to eight adults. What I love most about this model is that the pump doesn’t hang off the side—it’s integrated, built directly into the liner. A control panel extends above the rim, so you don’t need to get out of the tub to change the temperature or massage system. It’s a big improvement over models with exterior pumps that have hard-to-reach control panels on top. And, if you’re sitting on the opposite side of the tub and want to make an adjustment, you can do so through the brand’s app.

Another plus is this hot tub’s energy-efficient design, with insulated walls and an included cover, plus the three-layer material is said to be durable enough to withstand punctures. The hot tub features 190 jets, a 380-gallon capacity, and a power-saving timer.

Made of laminate PVC and polyester mesh, this 222-gallon hot tub seats four people—perfect for a backyard gathering. This hot tub is similar to the 6- to 8-person model we wrote about above, just smaller and without some of the higher-end features, including an upgraded pump.

The 4- to 6-person model has 140 high-powered jets, an all-in-one heater and filtration system, and a pump mounted high off the ground for easy access to the digital panel.

There’s also a floating chlorine dispenser to regulate the amount of chemicals in the water, plus two filter cartridges and a carrying bag. The insulated cover and thermal ground cloth help keep your hot tub warm when you aren’t using it, so you can spend less money heating it every time.

The Intex PureSpa Greystone Deluxe is designed to hold its heat when the weather turns cold. The cover is filled with high-density thermal foam instead of air, and Intex rates it up to 50 percent more efficient at retaining heat, so the heater cycles on less often. The heater covers 50 to 104 degrees Fahrenheit, and the Intex Link app lets you schedule heating ahead of time, so the water is ready when you get home from work.

The control panel is wireless. You can take it off its dock and adjust the temperature, jets, or multicolor LED light without fully climbing out. The blower heats the air before it reaches 140 bubble jets, so running the jets doesn’t cool the water as much. The square shell is 69 inches on each side and holds 120 gallons, and Intex rates it for four people. It also has a built-in hard-water treatment system to reduce mineral buildup and extend the life of the heater and pump.

With a name like Palm Springs, it’s no surprise this Coleman inflatable hot tub performs better in milder climates. Coleman says the tub can’t run when the air drops below 39 degrees Fahrenheit, so it suits patios in states where it doesn’t snow for much of the year.

Its EnergySense cover traps heat, and Coleman rates it 40 percent more efficient than covers on similar inflatables. Free Shield turns the heater on automatically if the water nears freezing, protecting the pump during an unexpected cold snap.

The tub is 77 inches across and holds 242 gallons, with 140 AirJet bubble jets in a ring around the floor. The DuraPlus walls have three layers and stretch 56 percent further than PVC before tearing, so a stray branch or a dog’s claw is less likely to cause a leak.

Budget aside, if you’re in the market for a hot tub, first nail down how many people you’ll need to accommodate. Most options comfortably fit four to six people, including our best overall pick, the Intex PureSpa Plus 6-Person Inflatable Hot Tub.

Larger models seat eight or more adults, and extra-small hot tubs are ideal for two. Square inflatable hot tubs generally offer more room to stretch out, but they’re typically harder to find than round models.

Most inflatable hot tubs are made of PVC and vinyl, and the best models have three-layer outer walls (often labeled as TriTech) to prevent punctures.

It may surprise you that more jets aren’t always better. It’s more important to consider jet placement, whether they’re adjustable, and whether they vary in size and function.

All inflatable hot tubs typically include a pump, heater, filtration system, and cover, and many also come with ground cloths, extra filter cartridges, chlorine regulators, and carrying bags. Nice-to-have extras include cup holders, multicolor LED lights, and removable headrests.

#6259. Ocean research has a data problem, but a new tool could help

Free software called oceandatr brings scattered ocean datasets together, helping marine scientists prepare maps and plan conservation research.

Information about water depth and underwater mountains around a Pacific island may already exist, but finding and combining it can be difficult.

For a marine scientist, finding it and getting it into a usable form can take as much effort as the research it was supposed to support.

A new free software package brings those scattered datasets together with one command. In one test, it assembled the data for a Pacific conservation planning exercise in a little over two minutes.

The package is called oceandatr. Jason Flower, a project scientist at the Environmental Markets Lab at the University of California, Santa Barbara, led the work.

Colleagues at the University of Queensland, the Waitt Institute, and four other institutions joined him.

“This paper is unique, in that we weren’t trying to answer a specific research question,” said co-author Echelle Burns, a project scientist at the lab.

“We were building a tool for marine scientists like us, who find themselves using the same data-pulling and organizing workflow over and over again.”

The ocean’s measurements sit on many websites, run by many groups.

Seafloor depth comes from one international compilation, and the locations of underwater mountains from a separate catalog.

Maps of coral habitat come from another source. Records of where boats fish come from Global Fishing Watch, which tracks them by satellite.

Each source stores its data at a different scale and in a different format.

Before any of it can go on the same map, a researcher has to download it, trim it to the area of interest, and reshape it so the grids match.

Flower and his colleagues had written that code so many times that they turned their scripts into ready-made functions and published them.

The tool works in R, a programming language that environmental scientists already use widely. It asks for three things in order.

First, a boundary for the area of interest, which can be a country, an ocean, or the zone a nation controls offshore. Second, a grid laid over that boundary.

Third, the data, which the tool fetches from each source and drops into the grid.

Depth comes from the GEBCO global terrain model. The tool downloads it in chunks, so it can process datasets too large to load into memory all at once.

Smaller datasets that exist only as single global files, such as the seamount and coral maps, ride along in a companion package.

That way they don’t have to be downloaded again with every update.

“The package could be used in any marine science project that requires spatial data,” Flower said. Researchers can also feed in their own measurements, and the tool fits them to the same grid.

To show the tool working, the team drew a planning region in the high seas of the western Pacific. They cut it into 8,142 squares, each 6.2 miles (10 kilometers) across.

For every square, oceandatr gathered depth, seafloor landforms, seamounts, coral habitat, and environmental zones, along with how much fishing happened there during the year 2022.

On an ordinary desktop PC, that took 2 minutes and 16 seconds. That is the step that used to mean writing fresh code for every dataset.

The team then fed the result into a conservation planning tool that picks protected areas while keeping the cost to fishing low. The target was to set aside 20% of each habitat type.

In a second test, the team modeled where fishing happens across the waters of the Federated States of Micronesia, using seafloor depth, distance to port, sea temperature, and dissolved oxygen.

The model accounted for about half of the differences in fishing effort from place to place.

The authors wrote that it was a demonstration of the data pipeline, not a finished fisheries model. A rigorous one, they wrote, would go through a formal process of choosing which variables to keep.

The tool is only as good as the datasets behind it. The global depth map can be coarser than what a local survey holds, which is why the package lets a user swap in their own depth file instead.

The team built the tool partly through marine planning work with the Waitt Institute in small island nations.

Users must judge whether the global datasets provide enough detail to study an individual island’s reef. They can supply local data when finer detail is needed.

The code is public on GitHub. The authors plan to add daily sea surface temperature alongside the long-term averages, and to make the package run faster on older computers.

“R packages are constantly evolving, and oceandatr will evolve with them,” Burns said. “It’s a ‘living package’ that’s going to continue to be updated and refined in the coming years.”

The full study was published in the journal Ecology and Evolution.

A new AI model, called Brain-IT, can transform brain scans into images and reverse the process, turning images into what they'd look like as brain activity.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

An artificial intelligence (AI) tool can use brain scans to recreate the images people looked at with eerie accuracy.

The system, called Brain-IT, uses data from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to measure activity in the visual cortex, the part of the brain that processes visual input. A computer model then predicts both the broad layout of an image and high-level information about its content. It then passes those predictions to an AI image generator, researchers explained in a study uploaded to the preprint database arXiv. The research was presented at the ICLR 2026 conference, held April 23-25, and publicized by its authors in September.

Brain-IT builds on an approach called the Universal Brain Encoder. That model begins with an image and then predicts the fMRI response that would be expected in individual "voxels" ‪—‬ small 3D units ‪—‬ in a brain scan.

"The key idea is that every voxel, a tiny cube of brain tissue, gets its own learned vector that captures what it cares about in images," said study first author Roman Beliy, a doctoral candidate in the Department of Computer Science and Applied Mathematics at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel.

Some voxels may be tuned to relatively simple elements of an image, such as edges, textures or locations. Others might be responding to higher-level abstract categories, like faces, bodies or scenes.

Traditional image-to-fMRI systems have generally been custom trained for each participant and dataset. The Universal Brain Encoder is more flexible. It learns from data from multiple people and can transfer information across participants, datasets or different MRI systems with varying magnetic-field strengths, according to the study.

A voxel can determine which parts of an image are relevant to it based on its learned profile, essentially saying, "I recognize edges. Which parts of this image are edges?"

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The Universal Brain Encoder starts with an image and predicts brain activity; Brain-IT starts with measured brain activity and reconstructs the image the person saw. In other words,it asks "based on this brain activity, what was the subject looking at?". It sorts thousands of tiny brain-scan measurements from the visual cortex into 128 groups based on the kinds of visual information they tend to carry.

The system then lets those groups share clues with one another, allowing it to combine, for example, information about a scene's shape, color and possible objects, to build a more complete picture of the image, Beliy explained.

The decoder produces two types of visual predictions. One captures semantic information ‪—‬ the features associated with what is likely in a scene; for an image of a dog standing in grass, for instance, this would include things like the features of a dog and an outdoor, grassy setting. The other captures structural information, like the broad visual layout or how forms are arranged.

In the above example, this would be aspects like the outline of the dog or where it was positioned in the frame. The structural prediction gives the generator a starting point for the image, rather than beginning from pure noise, while the semantic info guides an image generator that removes the remaining static until the image emerges.

Although the new tool can recreate what people see, it can't reproduce memories or imagined scenes.

"We're not reading people's thoughts," study co-author Michal Irani, a computer scientist at the Weizmann Institute of Science, told Live Science. "The images we do manage to recover from fMRI require people's cooperation and full intended collaboration."

The original image of a baseball game (left) and the reconstruction (right) generated by the Brain-IT AI model based on the brain activity of a person viewing the image.

Brain-IT's synthetic images were compared with the images that participants saw. Brain-IT surpassed prior leading methods on standard objective reconstruction metrics and produced more faithful results, the study authors wrote. The system shined when limited fMRI data from a new participant was available, with just one hour of data from a new participant producing results as accurately as earlier approaches that had been trained on 40 hours of recordings.

A high-scoring or realistic-looking output should not be mistaken for a perfect copy of what someone saw, however.

In the final stage of processing, the system uses an off-the-shelf diffusion generator trained on massive numbers of images. Models like this generate plausible images and can smooth textures, sharpen facial features or fill in missing details.

Beliy said this "beautification" can make reconstructions more polished and convincing and introduce details that don't necessarily come from the brain data itself. In other words, the scan constrains the generated picture, but the AI model supplies some of its realism from learned patterns in photographs.

While the new system produces impressive results for seen images, it can't be used to reconstruct an imagined or remembered image.

"Brain-IT relies on how the brain processes a seen image," Irani said. "Information flows from the eyes to the primary visual cortex and onward through a series of visual areas that recognize objects and scenes."

In a controlled experiment, researchers also know precisely which image was shown, giving the model a target during training and evaluation. In contrast, memories and imagined images do not offer the same clean reference. They can be vague and shaped by brain networks involved in memory and thought, with only partial and weaker reactivation of visual regions, Irani said. One limitation that would prevent this technology from being widely deployed is that the only way to get reliable results is from fMRI scanning, which is cumbersome and expensive. The team is currently experimenting with using easier-to-collect electroencephalogram (EEG) data, which is obtained via electrodes on the head, but that work is in the very preliminary stages, according to Irani.

The new system could help brain researchers better understand which visual information is represented in different brain regions, how those regions interact and how individuals’ patterns differ. Such tools could eventually reveal differences in visual processing that could help clinicians spot neurological, neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions.

"There are numerous useful medical applications which we are currently striving toward," Irani said. "These include using our brain encoder/decoder to detect and analyze brain disorders such as MS, PTSD, autism and psychiatric disorders."

Beliy, R., Zalcher, A., Kogman, J., Wasserman, N., & Irani, M. (2025, October 29). Brain-IT: Image Reconstruction from fMRI via Brain-Interaction Transformer. arXiv.org. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.25976

#6257. Light is hard to block from every direction. This physicist found a way

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Mandana Tadayon, Anna Mattson and Emily Conover

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Physicist Stefano Martiniani has designed an entirely new class of materials that blurs the line between order and chaos. Called gyromorphs, these metamaterials rely on crystal-like geometric structure and liquidlike randomness to block light from penetrating at any angle.

Physicists thought, structurally speaking, that they could not create such hybrid materials. “But this is evidence that you can, under certain constraints,” says Martiniani, of New York University. He likens the gyromorphs’ disorderliness to a crowd of people. You could see through the crowd if individuals stood still in straight lines, but not if they are clustered together in random groups. But there’s order too: From anywhere you stand in a gyromorph crowd, you’ll see a ring of people at a given distance.

Gyromorphs are a type of metamaterial, a substance with a structure designed to give it properties not found in naturally occurring materials. Metamaterials can control light, sound or other waves, and are often used in smartphones, medical imaging and computers. Martiniani says gyromorphs could be used to make more energy-efficient optical computers, which use light to process and store data.

To design a gyromorph, Martiniani needed to find a way to achieve the perfect structural balance. He turned to FReSCo, a program his lab created that designs molecular structures to meet researchers’ specifications, for help. “We had an algorithm, we gave it an objective, and then it was able to solve that objective, finding a solution that we were not expecting,” he says. “That is the best kind of discovery.”

#6256. In 1991, NASA sent 2,478 jellyfish into space, and some born in orbit came back pulsing abnormally

In 1991, NASA sent moon jellyfish into space aboard Columbia. Those formed in orbit showed abnormal pulsing after returning to Earth's gravity.

In June 1991, the space shuttle Columbia carried thousands of tiny moon jellyfish, Aurelia aurita, into orbit. NASA’s life sciences records list 2,478 of them on the flight.

Some of the young jellyfish formed in orbit. Back on Earth, 18.3 percent of them pulsed abnormally, compared with 2.9 percent of those that developed on the ground.

Dorothy Spangenberg of Eastern Virginia Medical School in Norfolk led the experiment. Her goal was to learn whether the animals’ gravity sensors could form normally without gravity.

Columbia launched on June 5, 1991, on the STS-40 mission and landed at Edwards Air Force Base in California on June 14. The flight, commanded by Bryan O’Connor with a crew of seven, lasted nine days, two hours and 14 minutes.

It carried Spacelab Life Sciences 1 (SLS-1), the first Spacelab mission dedicated solely to life sciences.

Of its 18 investigations, ten involved humans, seven involved rodents and one used jellyfish. Six body systems were studied in all, from the heart and lungs to the blood, bones and muscles.

The neurovestibular system, which helps people sense gravity and balance, was one of them.

Both polyps and young jellyfish flew. Polyps are a stalk-like stage that lives attached to a surface, and they can metamorphose into tiny, free-swimming ephyrae.

Ephyrae on the mission measured about 0.04 to 0.08 inch (1 to 2 millimeters) across, according to a 1997 NASA report on jellyfish thyroxine by Spangenberg.

Before the flight, about 25,000 polyps were mixed together and divided into flight and ground control groups. A NASA educational guide to the experiment says 60,000 jellyfish were grown for the mission.

The team triggered metamorphosis with iodine or the hormone thyroxine at 82 degrees Fahrenheit (28 degrees Celsius). Some groups were treated 48 or 24 hours before launch, and others eight hours after liftoff.

Ephyrae formed in orbit as well as on the ground, so the jellyfish apparently could still make the hormone needed for metamorphosis in space. Even two groups of polyps that received no trigger formed ephyrae there.

Some ephyrae were preserved on the eighth day of the mission. Others were preserved after landing for study under light microscopes and scanning and transmission electron microscopes.

Under the microscope, the flight ephyrae looked very similar to those raised on Earth. Counts of their arms showed no significant differences.

Like adult moon jellyfish, ephyrae swim by pulsing, rhythmically contracting their bodies. That movement is where the space-grown animals stood out.

The abnormal pulsing suggested problems in the development of the gravity receptors or the neuromuscular system, or in how the two worked together.

The 1997 report raised another possibility. The animals may have been unable to readjust to Earth’s gravity after landing.

Ephyrae in microgravity also showed more looping and circling behavior than ephyrae on Earth, Spangenberg and colleagues reported in a 1996 study of touch-plate formation. That paper drew on SLS-1 and a later flight.

Sensory hair cells in ephyrae that developed in microgravity also had fewer lipid droplets near their bases than those of ground controls.

Moon jellyfish sense gravity with organs called rhopalia, found around the edge of the bell. Each holds a statocyst filled with tiny crystals called statoliths.

Space-grown ephyrae formed rhopalia that looked much like those of ground controls. They had statocysts with statoliths, light-sensing ocelli, ciliated mechanoreceptor cells and immature touch-plates, according to a 1994 study of graviceptor development.

The number of rhopalia per arm did not differ significantly between the groups. Ephyrae induced to form in space with iodine even made more statoliths per rhopalium than one set of controls.

But statolith loss from the rhopalia was significantly higher in ephyrae kept in space in artificial seawater, compared with their controls on the ground.

Normal pulsing depends on normal development and function of the rhopalia.

Humans have similar calcium-containing crystals, called otoconia, in the inner ear. They help people keep their balance.

When Columbia flew, the effect of microgravity on human otoconia had not been studied, the NASA guide noted.

Many developing jellyfish structures resemble human ones but are less complicated. That could help predict what happens to the embryos of more complex animals during spaceflight.

Jellyfish flew again on the later IML-2 mission. Spangenberg suspected that a buildup of the jellyfish version of thyroxine might be linked to the statolith loss.

On Earth, thyroxine given to the animals increases statolith demineralization. A planned third experiment would have measured the jellyfish hormone in space-grown ephyrae, but NASA deselected it in August 1997.

The study was published in the journal Advances in Space Research.

#6255. The 4 Best Nugget Ice Makers to Get Soft, Chewable Ice at Home

We tried out the best versions that sit on your countertop and churn out several pounds of ice per day.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

If you’re a fan of soft, crunchy, chewable ice, a countertop nugget ice maker can bring that sought-after texture right to your kitchen. Also known as pellet or “Sonic” ice, nugget ice is made of compacted flakes that are soft, airy, and easy to munch on and slow to melt. It’s especially good for soaking up the flavor of whatever you’re drinking, making it a favorite for everything from sodas and cocktails to iced coffee and just plain, old water.

Nugget ice makers have become increasingly popular home appliances, but the machines themselves can be relatively advanced. They require more complex internal components than basic ice makers, and thus tend to cost more—often starting around $400 for a high-quality design. Depending on the appliance, you’ll also find features like large ice baskets, water reservoirs, self-cleaning cycles, and high daily production.

To help you find the right machine for your kitchen and budget, we researched, tested, and reviewed the best nugget ice makers from manufacturers such as GE, Euhomy, and Gevi. Whether you’re entertaining friends or just ready to retire the built-in ice maker on your fridge, these are the models we recommend.

The selection of countertop nugget ice makers available from trusted and reliable brands is limited, so we dug to find and test the best options by considering product specs, capabilities, and prices. During testing, we ran cleaning cycles to get the systems ready to go. We then timed how long it took for each machine to produce one batch of ice, and again for how long it took to fill the ice basket completely.

Throughout our setup and testing, we evaluated each model’s ease of use, reliability, and the quality of the ice they made. We took note of any cool or unique features like app compatibility, storage options, and more.

Our home appliance writer, Nick Hilden, also spoke with Jessica Randhawa, founder and head chef at the Forked Spoon, and Yu Jiang Zhao, mixologist, about what to keep in mind when choosing a nugget ice maker.

This was the nugget ice maker that made our tester throw out their ice trays once and for all. It takes everything we liked about the previous version, GE Profile Opal 2.0, and boosts the ice production speed, upgrades a smattering of components and functions to make it easier to clean and enhance its lifespan, and includes an external water tank and ice scoop to boot.

We’ve found that it churns out ice at a rapid enough pace to keep round after round of cold beverages for a sizable gathering. It has an easy-to-use app that offers smart functions such as scheduling alerts for maintenance. Additionally, its sleek design has a timeless vibe that won’t look dated two years from now.

It’s got a footprint nearly that of two shoeboxes side by side, which is a bit big for a smaller kitchen. It can also get somewhat noisy when it’s actively producing ice—about the volume of a loud refrigerator—though it’s basically silent when it’s just keeping it cool. But if you’re looking for reliable, convenient ice on demand, there’s none better.

Full GE Profile Opal 2.0 Ultra Nugget Ice Maker Review

This little unit packs a surprising amount of ice production power, churning out as much or more than any of the larger models on our list (40 pounds per day). Additionally, its compact size makes it perfect when you have less countertop real estate to spare, or if you want portable ice production for a backyard barbecue or camping in an RV.

Our testing found that it churns out ice fast, with the first batch in under ten minutes. Its operation is as straightforward as they come, and its cleaning is easier than most other machines, with an automatic cleaning mode that requires little effort on your part besides draining out the water that runs through the system.

All told, it’s a great ice maker for anyone who wants a no-fuss model that will look nice in the kitchen without taking up too much space. It also offers similar performance to larger, more expensive models, minus the roomy storage capacity.

Full Euhomy Smart Countertop Nugget Ice Maker Review

The Gevi 2.0 is the kind of ice maker you won’t mind taking up prime countertop real estate, given its polished design. The bin holds almost five pounds of ice (the largest capacity on our list), and the machine has thick insulation on all sides to keep cubes frozen for longer.

One of our favorite features is the door on the ice maker that opens to a 90-degree angle. To achieve this, the Gevi ditches the viewing window that’s present on other models, but this design choice allows you to pull the ice basket forward. This made it very simple to scoop our pellet ice once the container was full.

The instruction manual says that it takes about 15 to 30 minutes for the first cubes to form, but I noticed a couple of pellets had dropped around the 9-minute and 20-second mark. They were fairly wet to start but began forming more compactly over time and were the perfect, crunchy texture. However, it takes a few hours to get a full basket, which is tricky if you need ice immediately.

The water reservoir is kind of awkward to access with the door style, but the Gevi also comes with a hose that hooks up to your tap if you want it to fill automatically.

Ice makers require regular cleaning to ensure both quality ice and a long lifespan for the unit, and we found that the Silonn Nugget Ice Maker makes it easier than the rest. Most notable is its self-cleaning function, which is as effortless as it gets: Push a button to start the clean cycle, and let it do its thing. This is unlike other models that require removing a lot of parts or going through a complex series of steps. We also like that you can just toss its removable water reservoir and ice bin in the dishwasher, with no hoses or bottles to clean.

In terms of operation, it delivers most everything you want from a solid ice maker. It produces a hefty 44 pounds of ice a day, and its 2.6-pound bin holds plenty of ice for several rounds of drinks. It’s straightforward and intuitive to use—all you need to do is fill it with water—and is somewhere in the middle in terms of countertop footprint.

It does produce more noise than other popular models. Most nugget ice makers crank the volume up when actually producing ice, but this one has a noticeable hum even when on standby. For reliable ice with no-hassle cleaning, however, it’s hard to beat.

One of the key benefits to a good nugget ice maker is that it can churn out upward of 30 or even 40 pounds a day, making it ideal for hosting large, thirsty groups. The best models can have the first cubes ready within about 10 minutes, and will have a full bin within an hour or so.

A countertop machine, of course, can’t store three dozen pounds of ice. Most ice bins hold 1 to 3 pounds, which will replenish as depleted. It’s rare to go through a full bin, so unless you expect to host a particularly large number of people, this may not be the most pressing concern.

The vast majority of home nugget ice makers are equipped with a built-in water reservoir. These are great for at-home use as they don’t require installation and are highly portable, making it easy to pack them away for storage.

The larger the tank, the more ice the machine will produce. However, this also means that it will require more counter space. Models with smaller water reservoirs eat up less room, but require you to refill them frequently.

You can plug some models directly into your home plumbing system, which eliminates the need to fill a tank as it will draw water continuously. These, however, may require expert installation depending on your DIY skills, and will usually end up in a cabinet or closet rather than on your countertop.

The bigger the ice maker, the more countertop space it uses, so consider how much room you have in your kitchen. Our top pick, the GE Opal 2.0, is a great ice maker, but it has a pretty big footprint for a kitchen with limited counter real estate. When measuring dimensions, don’t forget about the inch or two of clearance that you’ll need for the fan, which keeps the motor from overheating.

If you have the space for it, Randhawa recommends placing the model in the pantry. This not only keeps your countertops open, but can muffle the operating noise.

“With most nugget ice machines you should expect some sound when operating on standby, but they can get pretty noisy when producing ice,” says Randhawa. “That might not matter in the din and clatter of cocktail hour, but could be more bothersome when things quiet down.”

It’s difficult to determine how loud a particular model will be without actually hearing it as there is no standardized noise rating. Your best bet is to check reviews for what previous buyers or reviewers have to say.

Nugget ice makers use a large metal cylinder with an auger inside that freezes as the machine runs. Water then pours into the cylinder and starts to freeze along the walls, producing a thin sheet of ice that the auger scrapes and pushes through the machine as ice flakes.

The machine then squeezes the flakes to push out excess water and compacts them into small, airy pieces so that what you end up with is a soft, porous nugget of ice that (probably) won’t crack your teeth when you chew it. They’re ideal for beverages because they take on the flavor of the drink, and there’s really nothing quite like that taste and texture.

Unfortunately, nugget ice makers aren’t ready to use right out of the box. Once you’ve gotten your unit, it’s best to let it sit upright on a level surface for at least two hours before plugging it in. This helps the refrigerant settle. The time may vary depending on the model you have, so it’s best to refer to the manual for the specific time.

You should also run the self-cleaning or sanitizing cycle before getting started. A combination of equal parts water and vinegar can get the job done. By doing this, you’re clearing the machine of any lingering residue or grime that could affect the clarity and taste of the ice. After completing a cycle with the solution, you can run another one with just water for a full wash-down.

Nugget ice makers are not a set-it-and-forget-it machine—they require regular cleaning and additional upkeep. One of the main concerns with these appliances is calcium buildup, or limescale, which accumulates if you have hard tap water.

To prevent this, it’s a good rule of thumb to occasionally descale your ice maker. You can make a 1:1 solution of distilled white vinegar and water, put it in the reservoir, and run it through the machine for a few cycles. Another tip is to use filtered water.

Self-cleaning modes should be run at least once a month, but if you’re a frequent party host, every other week couldn’t hurt. If you’re using a nugget ice maker that hooks up to a water line, you would benefit from an inline filter. Vacuuming the fan and blowing out the condenser also prevents clogs from dust and debris that may cause overheating.

Nugget ice makers make anywhere from 24 to 44 pounds of ice in a 24-hour period. They start up relatively quickly (as little as 10 minutes) but may take up to an hour to fully fill the ice bin.

Models with large capacity bins are best for big groups, while smaller ones are good for home bars and entertaining a couple of friends. Some options have ice bins that are insulated to keep ice from melting, while others just have an acrylic bucket in which ice melts faster.

For those that regularly host large gatherings or just don’t want to run out of nugget ice, we suggest running your nugget ice maker the day before and storing nugget ice in the freezer. Alternatively, you could stockpile extra nugget ice just in case you’re burning through more than expected the day of your event.

Most nugget ice machines are countertop units, so special installation isn’t necessary. We’ve specifically recommended models that don’t require you to install them, as the vast majority of owners will want something user-friendly and easy to store when not in use. Typically speaking, ice makers that require installation are heavy-duty, professional-grade units for serving large groups of people.

According to Randhawa, “Most nugget ice machines just use a standard outlet and require space around it to vent per the instructions.” Without proper ventilation space, your unit could overheat and break down.

“[Nugget ice makers] run compressors constantly and consume more power than people think it should for a countertop appliance,” says Zhao. “If energy consumption is a concern to you, look for those with an Energy Star rating, and factor in that it will likely be running a good portion of the day.”

Newer models tend to need about 0.05 to 1 kilowatt-hour per day, depending on your ice use. The more ice you make, the more power you’ll need. That’s roughly the equivalent of an energy-efficient fridge, which increases electric bills by about $10 to $15 a month.

If you always want ice at the ready, then you’ll have to run your nugget ice maker at all times, but it’ll likely shut off once the bin is full. “This is a normal operating procedure,” says Zhao. “Turning it off and on [manually] every day reduces its life and means you are waiting 15 to 20 minutes for your first batch every day.”

However, these machines don’t technically need to run year-round if you’re worried about possibly running up your electric bill. “You can turn them off and put them away when you don’t plan on using them,” says Randhawa. “We put ours away during vacations and over the winter, after the temperature drops, which is generally when we don’t want ice in our drinks.”

#6254. Scientists want to improve photosynthesis to help feed the world, but it isn’t so simple

Scientists screened about 15,000 bacterial Rubisco variants, revealing promising changes and unexpected obstacles to improving photosynthesis.

Plants look like experts at turning air and sunlight into food. But a key enzyme in that process, Rubisco, is slow and sometimes captures the wrong gas.

Scientists have now tried to improve a faster bacterial version of that enzyme, and the single changes that helped often stopped helping once they were combined.

Even the computer models built to predict such changes struggled to say which combinations would work.

The team screened about 15,000 altered versions of the enzyme inside living photosynthetic cells. What came out is a long list of which changes help and which hurt.

The list comes with a limit: the enzyme was bacterial, not a plant’s, and any use in a crop would need further testing in plant cells and whole plants first.

Paul Hudson, a professor of systems biology at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm, led the work with Ute Hoffmann and Axel Knave, who share first authorship.

Colleagues at SciLifeLab, the University of the Balearic Islands in Spain and Kobe University in Japan took part.

Every plant carries Rubisco, and so do some bacteria.

Sunlight supplies the power, and the enzyme captures carbon dioxide from the air and attaches it to a sugar, the first step in building the rest of the plant.

When Rubisco captures oxygen instead, it produces a byproduct the cell has to break down and recycle, which costs energy.

Plant Rubisco is a 16-piece assembly that is hard to produce and alter in the lab. Some bacteria carry a simpler form, built from identical copies of one piece, that fixes carbon faster.

Versions like it have been proposed as replacements for the plant enzyme in crops.

Hudson’s team chose one from a bacterium called Gallionella. This type of Rubisco evolved mainly in places with little oxygen.

Chemists call capturing carbon dioxide carboxylation and capturing oxygen oxygenation, and the fast bacterial enzyme does more of both.

“But they also catalyze the oxygenation reaction more readily, meaning that they are less selective for carbon dioxide,” Hudson said.

“Our idea was to take these fast Rubiscos and make them even faster, or at least reduce their oxygenation rate while retaining a high carboxylation rate.”

The team put the altered enzymes into Synechocystis, a photosynthetic bacterium, or cyanobacterium.

Its own Rubisco had been switched almost entirely off, so each cell could grow only as fast as the bacterial Rubisco it carried allowed.

Each altered gene also carried a 20-letter DNA tag. These tags let researchers track which variants became more common as the cells grew together in one pooled culture.

The library had two parts. One tested individual changes at selected positions in the enzyme.

The other combined changes at seven positions, with 16,200 possible combinations in its design.

None of the positions was a guess. Most came from two programs that compare the enzyme with thousands of related Rubiscos and flag the spots most likely to tolerate change.

The pooled cells then grew for 12 generations in bioreactors, with or without oxygen in the gas feed. The cyanobacteria grew more slowly whenever oxygen was present.

Cells carrying about 8% of the single-swap variants grew faster than cells carrying the starting enzyme, compared with under 1% of the multi-change variants. The helpful swaps clustered in a few places.

Two of them were in a flexible loop beside the enzyme’s active site, a stretch thought to help Rubisco tell carbon dioxide from oxygen.

Another helpful swap was at the seam where two copies of the enzyme meet, beside a tunnel that runs between the two active sites.

Swaps there helped more when oxygen was present.

One short stretch couldn’t be changed at all: it forms a helix above the opening where the enzyme’s sugar partner enters and leaves, and every swap there made growth worse.

To check the tag readings, the team grew six of the best variants on their own. Cells carrying each of the six variants outgrew cells carrying either the starting enzyme or the natural enzyme.

The cells held about the same amount of each enzyme, which argues against the idea that they were simply making more Rubisco.

The obvious next step is to combine the winners, and it mostly didn’t work. On average, the more changes a variant carried, the worse the cells holding it grew.

Cells carrying one variant with three particular changes grew more slowly than cells carrying the starting enzyme. Cells carrying a fourth change on its own also grew more slowly.

Put all four together, and the cells grew noticeably better.

The computer models struggled with combinations too. Three programs that score a mutation by how it fits the pattern across related Rubiscos did reasonably well on single swaps.

On variants with several changes, their predictions pointed the wrong way, largely because of one swap they kept recommending that hurt every variant it appeared in.

A model trained on the team’s own data did better at predicting the combinations already in the dataset.

But when the team built 11 new variants it recommended, each with six to 12 changes, eight of them didn’t support growth at all. Only two beat the starting enzyme.

The best enzyme in the whole study, called Ad1, came from the simpler approach of adding proven changes together. Give Ad1 one more swap that had helped on its own, and growth collapsed.

The team purified Ad1 and a six-change variant called C6 and measured them in the test tube with radioactive carbon dioxide.

Both reacted with oxygen more slowly than the starting enzyme, and Ad1 was choosier about carbon dioxide over oxygen.

Carbon-fixing speed changed in opposite directions, with C6 about 25% faster than the starting enzyme and Ad1 about 15% slower.

There was a cost. Both variants needed more carbon dioxide around them to work at full speed, so their overall efficiency at fixing carbon was lower too.

The better growers the team tested were also generally less heat-stable than the starting enzyme, which the authors wrote may reflect a looser fit between the two halves.

Inside the cells, the Ad1 strain held less of the sugar Rubisco works on and more of the product it makes. That fits a smaller bottleneck at that step.

The strain also grew better than the starting enzyme’s cells in ordinary air, not only in the carbon-rich bioreactors.

The cells were cyanobacteria, not plants, and the enzyme was bacterial.

Moving a bacterial Rubisco into a crop would also mean moving the machinery that concentrates carbon dioxide around it, which the authors call an outstanding challenge.

The starting enzyme was itself a slower version of the natural one, and even Ad1 still fixed carbon more slowly than the natural enzyme.

The pooled screening also ran at 5% carbon dioxide, far above the level in air, which may have hidden differences in how the enzymes handle scarcer carbon dioxide.

And the team measured only two enzymes in detail, so it can’t yet say that less reaction with oxygen is what sped up growth.

Next, Hudson’s team wants to cut the oxygen reaction further in the promising variants and work out which parts of the enzyme help it choose carbon dioxide.

With funding from the European Union, the researchers are also testing new enzymes in plant cells and in cyanobacteria engineered to produce useful chemicals.

They have publicly shared their analysis code and results, including successful and unsuccessful changes, so others can train their own models.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

A tiny asteroid entered Earth's orbit in April and is expected to leave in January. Meet the minimoon 2026 QQ8.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Earth and its moon will have company this holiday season. In April, our planet picked up a passing "minimoon," pulling the space rock into a temporary orbit, astronomers have confirmed.

The object, dubbed 2026 QQ8, was first observed by Hungarian researcher Krisztián Sárneczky in August. It was officially reported by the International Astronomical Union's (IAU) Minor Planet Center — the body that logs and confirms new solar system objects — on Oct. 29. This extraterrestrial traveler is expected to stick around until January 2027, extending its stay through the holidays before breaking free of our planet's influence.

2026 QQ8 is tiny — only about 6 feet (2 meters) across, according to the IAU. If it got too close to Earth, it would likely burn up in our planet's atmosphere. However, researchers don't think there is much chance of that happening, since 2026 QQ8 is currently orbiting at around 1.5 times the average distance of the moon.

2026 QQ8 takes 359 days — almost a full Earth year — to orbit the sun. It comes close to our planet every 10 years or so. This minimoon is classified as an Aten asteroid; this population of space rocks occasionally cross into Earth's orbit and have semimajor axes smaller than Earth's, meaning they typically orbit closer to the sun than our planet does. Large Aten asteroids are considered the most dangerous type of asteroid, as they can easily get lost in the sun's glare before speeding toward Earth — but, again, our new mini companion is far too small to pose a threat.

2026 QQ8 is not the first minimoon discovered circling Earth. That distinction belongs to 1991 VG, which was around 30 feet (10 meters) in diameter when it was detected in November 1991. Astronomers now think Earth grabs minimoons pretty frequently; we are likely to have at least one at any given time. Most of the space rocks stay around for less than a year, although a handful may remain in Earth's gravitational pull for decades.

New telescopes ‪are expected to help researchers spot more minimoons as they enter and leave Earth's orbit. These include the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile, which began operation earlier this year. The Rubin observatory, which takes a full scan of the entire Southern Hemisphere sky every few days, has already spotted what may be a new dwarf planet lurking in the outer solar system, as well as a new satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. Over its planned 10-year mission, the observatory is expected to detect millions of previously unknown moving objects in space.

#6252. Does everyone carry disease-linked DNA variants? What nearly a million genomes revealed

The average human genome holds about 5 million variants, and one to three of them are already labeled as causing a genetic disease.

A DNA test may flag a variant linked to disease, but that result alone does not mean you will develop the condition.

The typical adult carries one to three rare variants already labeled as causing a genetic disease, plus about 50 more whose meaning is still uncertain.

Most of them do not cause disease in the person carrying them.

The counts come from the largest attempt so far to describe the average human genome.

Caroline Wright, a professor at the University of Exeter, led a team that read the full genomes of nearly a million adults in two large health studies.

The volunteers in UK Biobank and the All of Us program in the United States were not chosen because of any disease. Their DNA shows what ordinary variation looks like.

“Whole genome sequencing has become such an important tool in diagnosing genetic disease, and we’re increasingly moving towards genetic screening for predicting disease. Yet most people are unaware of just how much genetic variation is present in every genome. Actually, variation is the norm,” Wright said.

Scientists compare each person’s DNA with a reference genome, a standard copy of the 3.1 billion letters in human DNA.

A typical person differs from that standard at 4.3 million to 5.3 million spots, or roughly one letter in every 600 to 700.

People whose ancestry is genetically closest to African populations carry about a million more differences than everyone else.

The authors think that may be partly because the reference itself was built mostly from people of European ancestry, so it matches the DNA of people with African ancestry less well.

Most of those differences are single letters swapped, or a few letters added or dropped. The typical genome has 68 stretches longer than 10,000 letters that are either missing or present in extra copies.

Almost all of this variation is shared. In the typical genome, 98.4% of the variants are common, meaning they turn up in more than 1% of people from the same ancestry group.

Only about half a percent land in the parts of genes that spell out proteins.

Protein-coding variants can affect the proteins our bodies make.

A typical person has 21,000 to 26,000 of them, and the team predicts that about 48% change the protein in some way.

Even so, a computer score that flags protein changes likely to do harm picked out just 28 of the roughly 9,600 protein-altering variants in a typical genome.

Each person also carries about 229 variants predicted to break a gene outright, 165 of them with high confidence. That count is in line with earlier surveys of human variation, the authors wrote.

ClinVar, a public database at the U.S. National Institutes of Health, lists about 4 million variants, and around 300,000 of them are rated as causing or probably causing disease.

Eight to ten of those are in the average genome.

The team then narrowed the search to 4,262 genes with solid evidence of causing a single-gene disease and kept only rare variants. That leaves one to three disease-causing variants per person.

Most are in genes for recessive conditions, which need a broken copy from each parent before anyone gets sick.

One copy makes a carrier, and the average person may be a carrier for two to six such conditions.

Variants predicted to disrupt the gene for filaggrin, a skin protein linked to eczema, turn up in about 1 in 15 people of European ancestry in the study.

Not everyone who carries one gets eczema.

For genes associated with dominant conditions, in which one altered copy can cause disease, about 1 in 9 people carries a rare variant rated as disease-causing.

“Importantly, we found that everyone carries a small number of genetic variants linked to disease, although many of these will not actually cause disease in that individual,” Wright said.

“It is therefore crucial to consider context when interpreting findings from genetic testing, including symptoms or family history of disease as well as other clinical and environmental risk factors.”

Common diseases such as diabetes and heart disease usually involve many genetic variants alongside environmental and lifestyle factors.

Thousands of common variants each nudge the odds a little, and a polygenic risk score adds those nudges up to rank a person against everyone else.

Wright’s team used scores already calculated for 28 common diseases across UK Biobank. The average person ranked in the top 10% of risk for about three of them.

Among 450,209 participants of European ancestry, 102,831, or about 1 in 5 people, scored in the top 1% for at least one disease.

A high score for at least one condition is therefore relatively common. Participants of other ancestries landed in the top 1% even more often, about 1 in 3 people.

The authors read that as a flaw in the scores, which perform poorly outside the population they were built in, rather than as extra disease.

Run 100 such scores on one person, the authors calculate, and about 99% of people would land in the top 5% for at least one disease.

About 63% would be in the top 1%. Screening programs that run many scores at once, they wrote, carry significant potential for overdiagnosis.

Some variants come from neither parent. In 2,334 sets of two parents and an adult child, the child carried an average of 61 mutations found in neither parent, ranging from 30 to 113.

Typically only one of them fell inside a protein-coding stretch.

Three-quarters to four-fifths of those new mutations came from the father’s side.

Each year of a father’s age at the child’s birth added about 1.2 more of them, and each year of a mother’s age added about 0.4.

All three members of a trio had to be adults to join the studies, so the parents in this sample were young at the birth. That puts the average toward the low end of earlier estimates.

The volunteers came only from Britain and the United States, and 91.5% of the UK Biobank group was of European ancestry. So the figures say little about most of the world.

Sequencing read short fragments of DNA taken almost entirely from blood, which misses some kinds of variation and any change confined to other tissues.

Uncertainty is unevenly spread. People of European ancestry carried more variants with a known disease label, while everyone else carried more variants of unknown meaning.

The authors trace that gap partly to who has been sequenced so far, and it can affect who gets a diagnosis.

The largest open question is one the study did not try to answer.

The team did not assess whether participants had the diseases associated with their flagged variants, so it cannot say how often those variants were linked to illness.

Wright’s team is presenting the work at the American Society of Human Genetics annual meeting this week.

The authors call for genomes from more diverse populations, read with longer-range sequencing and from more than one tissue, and they urge caution as genetic screening of healthy people expands.

The full study was published in the journal Genome Medicine.

#6251. This magic mushroom can kill

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Hallucinogens and poisons have never been found in the same mushroom — until now

Meet the dark magic mushroom, Galerina indica. The tiny fungus makes both a hallucinogen and a deadly toxin.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

People who eat this tiny magic mushroom may hit a lethal low instead of getting high.

The fungus makes hallucinogenic psilocybin and deadly amatoxin, researchers report November 11 in Current Biology. Dubbed “dark magic mushrooms,” it is the first species of fungus discovered to make both types of compounds.

Chemist and fungal biologist Andrew Kunik found the dark magic mushroom in 2025 growing on a decaying moss-covered palm trunk in a central Florida wetland. Kunik, who was then doing post-baccalaureate research in the lab of fungal biologist Matthew Smith at the University of Florida in Gainesville, identified the mini mushroom as Galerina indica.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

That species had not been reported in Florida before, Kunik says. “It’s quite rare and unusual.” He also found two other new related species, tagged with the placeholder names Galerina species 1 and Galerina species 2.

Other researchers had previously described G. indica’s appearance and found DNA signatures that distinguish the fungus from related species. But no one had cataloged the mushroom’s complete chemical or genetic makeup.

Related Galerina species make amatoxins, deadly chemicals that can kill in even tiny amounts and are found in death cap mushrooms and other species. Kunik and colleagues looked for those toxins in G. indica and the two other new Galerina species. G. indica makes a previously undiscovered form of amatoxin the team is calling alpha-proamanitin, the chemical analysis revealed.

The small mushroom also had blue bruises, a clue that it might make psilocybin, a psychedelic chemical being tested as a treatment for mental health disorders. Fungi usually make either amatoxin or psilocybin. Not both. Galerina species 1 also makes psilocybin but doesn’t make amatoxin, and species 2 makes neither.

“This finding shows that there’s a lot more diversity in [fungal] chemistry and the ways that they’re combined than we had really thought about,” says Anne Pringle, a mycologist at the University of Wisconsin–Madison who was not involved in the work.

Discovering these dual compounds in one mushroom was both exciting and required further analysis to confirm, Kunik says. “Surprising discoveries require great depth of evidence,” he says.

A complete workup of the mushroom’s DNA revealed genes for producing both types of chemicals. Ancestors of these dark magic mushrooms probably picked up those genes by swapping DNA with other species. Such DNA swapping, called horizontal gene transfer, is one way that organisms can quickly evolve new traits, like when bacteria exchange antibiotic resistance genes with unrelated species.

Ancestors of G. indica and its relatives probably acquired amatoxin genes early on. Those toxins are made by many of G. indica’s cousins, which indicates that amatoxins are probably heirlooms passed down from common ancestors. Ancestors of species 1 and species 2 seem to have dropped the amatoxin genes at some point since they no longer make the compounds.

The two psilocybin-producing species may have independently obtained the psychedelic genes in separate DNA swap meets, or a common ancestor may have picked up the genes and then passed them down to G. indica and species 1. There’s not enough known about the fungi’s family tree to sort out which scenario is correct.

And there’s another unsolved evolutionary mystery, Pringle says. “We still don’t know why mushrooms are poisonous.” Many scientists think it is for defending against predators, but hard evidence is lacking, she says.

“Can I eat it?” is often the first question people ask when finding a new mushroom, Pringle says. “I’m always so uncomfortable with that question and that conversation. And this paper confirms that, in fact, you should be uncomfortable.” After all, eating these dark magic mushrooms could send people tripping into the grave.
