#6250. The 8 Best Space Heaters to Keep the Chill Out of Your Home and Office

We compared different models’ heating levels, timer functions, safety features, and more.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Take the edge off those chilly winter nights without ballooning your energy bill. Space heaters offer immediate warmth for cozy nights in the bedroom and for brisk days in a drafty office. The small radius of heat also makes them ideal for improving the temperature in your immediate surroundings without wasting energy turning up the thermostat and heating the entire house. Some even double as fans during the summer.

The top space heaters run quietly and efficiently, offer multiple heating levels, and come with safety features like automatic shut-off for accidental tipping. We researched and tested the most promising models from brands like Vornado, Lasko, and Dreo. Below, you’ll find our selections for the most efficient, durable, and safest space heaters out there.

We tested space heaters by first evaluating each model based on important factors like safety, setting variety, and size. We paid attention to how well the appliances were able to warm up a space by using them around our homes and offices. We also took note of the number of heat settings each unit had and the temperature range they offered.

To evaluate the unit’s heat capabilities, we took into account its temperature range and wattage, and prioritized heaters that offered a broad range with good control and output of at least 1,200 watts or more. We’ve made a point to include options that operate via remote-controlled desktops and smart picks that come with a companion app as well.

For heaters that we haven’t had the chance to try in person, we heavily vetted specs and assessed each space heater based on the same factors we used during testing.

Lasko calls the CW100 bladeless because it doesn’t technically have a fan, per se. Instead, it uses a multi-vane impeller. That design contributes to the appliance’s quiet operation because it pulls in air through its base and into the tower. It comes with a cleanable air filter, which is accessible via a tool-free hatch at the back of the heater—no tools required.

We appreciate the slick touchpad on the front for adjusting the wattage for the heating element, tower oscillation, and the eight-hour timer. The space heater only has two actual heat settings—high and low—but there is a manual thermostat for controlling temperatures, which helps make up for the lack of power options.

The wide window of airflow and consistent heat distribution helps bring a room up to temp faster than most space heaters on this list, and this unit covers up to 300 square feet. One gripe: The battery hatch cover on the remote is tricky to remove. There is a holster for that remote control, though, making for one tidy package.

Full Lasko Oscillating Bladeless Ceramic Tower Space Heater Review

For a low-cost option, the Vornado MVH Vortex Heater heats a surprisingly large area—up to 256 square feet—with minimal noise. This unit worked well in a bedroom that has exterior walls on five sides, even during cold overnight temperatures. We like how simple, compact, and lightweight this unit is, and the appliance case stays cool to the touch, so you can move it around safely without concern.

The unit’s controls are a miss for us, though. While we liked the simple on/off button and the three-position toggle for heat levels, the thermostat dial is vague. The numbers on this dial range from 1 to 7, which don’t really show how warm each setting is.

As a result, we had to experiment with different settings until we figured out what worked best for us (you’ll likely have to do the same). Despite this drawback, the thermostat feature is helpful for when temperatures dip or get too high, as it manages the unit’s auto shutoff/on feature.

Full Vornado MVH Vortex Space Heater Review

It’s rare to come across a space heater that oscillates both horizontally and vertically, and that’s the feature we liked the most while testing the Dreo Whole Room Heater. It rotates 60 degrees up and down and 90 degrees from side to side for noticeably more coverage. Better yet, you can use both oscillation modes at the same time.

This space heater also has three heat and fan settings, and we appreciated being able to control the fan speed separately, even if we were running on high heat. Temperatures range from 41 to 95 degrees Fahrenheit, so we were able to truly customize the output. We kept our space heater at 73°F a majority of the time, and we never felt overheated or chilly.

The space heater comes with a remote, but there’s also a control panel on the base of the unit. The main thing we don’t like is that the remote was a little confusing to navigate at first. You have to use one button to access the fan speeds, heat levels, and temperatures, so we found ourselves clicking through a few times to get to the setting we wanted.

If your office is generally cold, then a heater small enough to sit on your desk might be the perfect solution for dealing with the frigid temperatures of your building. At only 12 inches tall, the Ellipse ceramic heater from Lasko is truly a compact model— discreet enough to tuck into the corner or underneath a workspace.

The highest settings pump out powerful heat in seconds, but there are medium and low settings if you want toned-down warmth. Temperatures are adjustable through the touch panel on the space heater.

We appreciate that even though this is a smaller design, it comes with its own remote. You can make the space heater oscillate and conveniently set a timer with the press of a couple buttons, and everything is viewable from the LED panel on the front.

The only thing we didn’t particularly like is that the Ellipse turns on at the highest setting automatically, so you’ll have to make adjustments almost immediately to find the ideal temperature and power.

A tech-facing space heater certainly has its benefits. The Lasko Therma-Smart tower heater has WiFi connectivity and pairs with the Aria home app for a virtual remote.

Connecting the heater was fairly easy: simply hold the WiFi button on the space heater for five seconds so it enters “pairing mode,” and then connect the device to the app. You can see wattage use and heat levels, and there’s a temperature dial in the center of the page to adjust to your liking. The Therma-Smart heater also pairs with Google and Alexa if you prefer to use voice commands.

Otherwise, the space heater has similar settings to other Lasko models that we recommend, like touch-sense controls and a digital window for viewing purposes. There are low, medium, and high heat settings, a max heat output of 1,500 watts, and a 12-hour timer function for running most of the day. One thing we noticed is that the oscillating feature seems to move very slowly, so you still might get hit with targeted heat if you’re sitting directly in front of the heater before it starts the rotation again.

The Lasko 751320 Ceramic Tower Heater is a reliable, mid-range option for homes and offices. Tester and Popular Mechanics editor Tom Price loves this model for its versatility. “The tower design and mid-sized build mean you can comfortably place it on a coffee table in the living room without it taking over the space. At the same time, it isn’t so small that I don’t feel the heat in larger spaces.”

The space heater has programmable controls that will turn the unit off and on after a certain period of time (or once the room has reached the desired temperature). It’s also equipped with an oscillating mode and comes with a multi-functioning remote control, too.

Although the gate on the front of the heater is designed to be cool to the touch, one aspect to keep in mind is that this unit does not come with an auto shutoff feature in case it gets tipped over.

A cold bathroom early in the morning feels like punishment, but a space heater on the floor near a bathtub or shower isn’t exactly a safe alternative. This fixed, wall-mounted unit from Dreo is a more reliable alternative. It’s IP24 waterproof-rated, so it’s protected against splashes from every direction, and has the same kind of ALCI plug you typically find on hair tools.

The bathroom heater accommodates spaces up to 200 square feet. With smart functionality, the companion app allows you to schedule timers, adjust temperatures, and change heat levels remotely.

Though this model has a child lock and a cool-touch exterior, we recommend mounting it out of reach of littles because the exhaust vent gets pretty warm.

If noise is one of your biggest concerns while shopping for a space heater, then an oil-filled radiator heater might be the right option. The Pelonis heater doesn’t use an internal fan, and offers the quietest noise operation on our list, maxing out right around five decibels.

It offers just about the same features as the ceramic heaters we recommend, with three different heating modes, tip-over security, and overheat protection. The heater has 360-degree warmth circulation, so you’re covered from every angle.

The radiator sits on four casters so it easily moves from room to room. It has a carrying handle, but it’s relatively small compared to the overall size of the unit and may overheat, so we recommend moving to your desired space before turning it on.

Simple, affordable, and versatile, these use electrical resistance to warm your space. A ceramic block or element is electrically conductive and heats up, and that heat is transferred to the air with an internal fan. The majority of the heaters on our list fall into this category.

Ideal use: These are great for general household use, shared offices, or wherever quiet heat is needed. Their simplicity makes them quite rugged; they have fewer parts to wear out or break.

This style of space heater emits infrared radiation rays that heat objects and individuals rather than the air, and it’s one of the more straightforward designs. They provide warmth almost instantly and aren’t loud while running, but they do have limited range.

Ideal use: Spot heating or small areas that need to be warmed up in a short amount of time.

These appliances burn propane or kerosene to warm an infrared emitter that projects the energy to heat your space. They’re considered convection heaters because they transfer thermal energy through a fluid, either by gas or oil.

They elevate the temperature of the air in certain spaces and are most suitable for delivering warmth in an area where you might walk around, like the surroundings of your desk or workshop.

Ideal use: Construction sites, garages, or work areas are the best places to use these heaters, since you want to place one at a comfortable distance and keep the work area unobstructed. Gas or liquid-fuel heaters direct the heat wherever you’re working.

Most residential space heaters use about 1,500 watts of power. If you’re using one of these devices as a primary heat source, it’s recommended to choose a model that offers 10 watts of heat output per square foot of space. 150 square feet is the common standard for coverage. You may consider investing in more than one unit if you’re trying to warm a larger space, or finding a design that has the right power combined with a fan or oscillating mode to disperse heat more evenly.

If you have pets or young children, then choosing a space heater with safety features is especially important for avoiding accidental burns and fires. The majority of the heaters on our list come with an automatic shut-off feature if it tips over. A good portion of our recommended heaters also include a timer to prevent the device from running for the entire day if you forget to shut it off.

During our testing and research journey, we learned some other valuable safety tips along the way such as the “three feet rule” (keeping the space heater at a distance from anything flammable) and not using these appliances in moist areas. But most importantly, you should never plug a space heater into an extension cord, power cord, or power strip. They’re not equipped for the electrical load that these devices require, and can be a potential fire hazard.

The short answer is it depends. Whether it’s “a lot” depends mainly on how long you run the heater and your local electricity rate. In the U.S., residential electricity prices typically range from $0.12 to $0.20 per kWh, with the average being around $0.17 per kWh as of December 2025.

Because most space heaters operate at 1,500 watts, they can cost between $0.18 and $0.30 per hour at average electricity rates. To find a more accurate estimate, divide the heater’s wattage by 1,000 to convert to kilowatts, then multiply that number by the number of hours the heater is running, and multiply that result by your electricity rate per kilowatt-hour (kWh).

These appliances aren’t intended to replace your home’s central heating system, so it’s better to use them supplementally if you don’t want to pay more on your electric bill.

You should turn them off when sleeping or left unattended. Common overnight hazards like a unit tipping over, bedding sitting too close to the heater, or an outlet overheating pose significant risks that you might not notice until you wake up. While most space heaters have preventative safety features like automatic shutoff or built-in thermostats, and may even be rated for continuous use, it’s best to resist the temptation of 24-hour warmth for safer operation.

#6249. Water near the Great Pacific Garbage Patch is changing color, and plastic may be the reason

Water near the Great Pacific Garbage Patch brightened in blue and green over 20 years, and microplastics are the likely cause, a study finds.

Satellites cannot see tiny pieces of plastic in the ocean, but they can see the color of the water. Over the last 20 years, the ocean near the Great Pacific Garbage Patch has actually changed color.

New research suggests that microscopic plastics are to blame. If this is true, scientists might soon be able to track invisible plastic pollution from space just by looking at the color of the sea.

Shea Cheatham, Daniel Koestner, and Børge Hamre of the University of Bergen in Norway carried out the study. They didn’t collect water samples. Instead, they compared three satellite records with computer simulations of how light travels through seawater.

Between Hawaii and California, clockwise surface currents carry floating plastic into an area called the Great Pacific Garbage Patch.

In the summer of 2015, The Ocean Cleanup, a nonprofit group, ran a survey in which boats towed nets in and around the patch 652 times. The group then tallied the catch piece by piece.

Using that survey, the group’s researchers estimated the patch’s area at about 620,000 square miles (1.6 million square kilometers) in a 2018 study. The group describes that area as twice the size of Texas.

The researchers put the number of plastic pieces at 1.8 trillion. They estimated that larger objects made up 92% of the weight, while microplastics made up 94% of the pieces.

But the plastic in the new study is too small to be in that count. Its pieces are no bigger than about a hundredth of an inch (0.3 millimeters), roughly the thickness of three sheets of printer paper.

Plastics that small are the most likely to enter the ocean’s food chain at its lowest level, the authors wrote.

These plastics are also hard to measure at sea, and cleaning them up on a large scale would be difficult, if not impossible.

The color of the ocean depends on what’s in the water. Microscopic algae called phytoplankton absorb some colors of light far more than others.

Plastic behaves differently. In earlier lab work, Koestner and his colleagues measured how water with microplastics mixed in absorbs and scatters light.

The plastic absorbed light fairly evenly across colors. It also scattered a lot of light back the way it came.

In the team’s simulations, seawater with these particles in it looked brighter from above. Blue-green light increased the most.

When the amount of phytoplankton or other natural material changes, blue light tends to get brighter while green gets dimmer, or the other way around. Plastic should brighten both at once.

The team analyzed three records of ocean color. Each ran from August 2002 through September 2022.

One came from an instrument on NASA’s Aqua satellite. The other two, from the European Space Agency and the Copernicus Marine Service, combine readings from several satellite sensors.

Large parts of the ocean have changed color in recent decades, often because of shifts in ocean life. So the team compared the patch with the water around it.

In all three records, areas in and near the patch grew brighter in both blue and green light. Together, those colors make cyan.

The cyan areas were shifted west and north of the patch’s densest part. That may be because wind pushes large floating objects, while microplastics travel with the water, the authors wrote.

Elsewhere, the three records didn’t always match. Farther south, the NASA record showed much more brightening in red light than the other two.

Two likely causes, the authors wrote, are an aging NASA instrument and differences in how the records were processed.

The European Space Agency record showed the fewest areas of clear change. Even so, it showed cyan in and near the patch.

How much plastic would it take to change the ocean’s color enough for a satellite to detect? The team ran 1,100 simulations to find out.

By their calculation, it would take about 5 milligrams of small microplastics in a cube of seawater 3.3 feet (1 meter) on each side.

At that level, the plastic brightened the simulated water more than satellite readings normally vary from one pixel to the next.

Suppose plastic alone caused the change in the brightest area on the patch’s western edge. In that area, a cube of water that size would have gained 11 to 25 milligrams of plastic over 20 years, depending on the satellite record.

The authors called those amounts reasonable. Net surveys by The Ocean Cleanup suggest that larger microplastics may reach similar concentrations near the surface.

In 2018, the group’s researchers also reported that the amount of plastic in the patch appeared to be rising exponentially, and more quickly than in nearby waters.

A color that fits plastic isn’t proof of plastic, the authors wrote, so they tested what natural changes could do alone.

The team simulated 500 versions of the ocean in which only natural material varied: phytoplankton, other natural particles, and colored material dissolved in the water.

In 500 more versions, the amount of microplastics varied too.

Then they compared the versions two at a time and sorted every case of brightening by its color: blue, cyan, green, or red.

With only natural material varying, 3% of the brightening cases were cyan. With microplastics added, 13% were cyan.

In the simulations, adding plastic made a cyan change more than four times as likely.

Without plastic, cyan appeared only when phytoplankton shifted from mostly larger kinds to mostly smaller ones, usually with less living material overall. With plastic, much smaller natural changes were enough.

Blooms of plankton called coccolithophores can brighten seawater too. But these plankton haven’t historically been active here, and their blooms would likely turn the water greener than the satellites recorded.

Mineral dust can brighten the ocean as well. But a dust record at Station ALOHA, north of Hawaii, appears to show no significant change between 1980 and 2025.

The study can’t say for certain that plastic is the cause. The satellites recorded color, and more than one thing in seawater can change it.

In one plausible scenario, the authors wrote, moderate changes in ocean life and a buildup of microplastics are both adding to the brightening.

Plastic could also be acting indirectly, they wrote. Chemical pollutants that come with plastic could be disrupting ocean life, and that disruption could change the water’s color.

Scientists haven’t directly measured how much plastic this small is in the patch.

The team also built its simulated seawater to match a measurement from the South Pacific. No complete set of light measurements exists for the patch’s own region.

Researchers will need to measure light and particles directly, at different depths near the patch, to check the result.

If those measurements confirm the pattern, satellites that already record ocean color could help scientists monitor where small microplastics are building up.

The full study was published in the journal Communications Earth & Environment.

#6248. The Sky This Week from November 13 to 20: The Leonids peak

Friday, November 20The Moon reaches apogee, the farthest point from Earth in its orbit, at 12:50 P.M. EST. At that time, our satellite will be 252,040 miles (405,619 kilometers) from Earth.

Already 60° high in the east by 8 P.M. local time is M33, the Pinwheel Galaxy in Triangulum. This lovely spiral glows at 6th magnitude and is technically visible from a dark site with sharp eyes — just wait until after moonset if you want to give it a try. You’ll find it in far western Triangulum, about 4.3° west-northwest of 3rd-magnitude Alpha (α) Trianguli.

Any telescope will show M33, but larger ones are better because its considerable size — some 70’ across along its longer axis — spreads its light out and makes its surface brightness quite low. Instruments 10 inches or larger will show some detail along the spiral arms, including brighter knots of star formation.

Located some 2.7 million light-years away, M33 is the third-largest galaxy in our Local Group, after Andromeda and our own Milky Way. This cosmic neighbor is a classic spiral with no central bar and a round, bright nucleus wrapped by its dusty arms. Oriented more closely to face-on than Andromeda, M33 is a popular target for visual observers as well as astrophotographers.

Sunrise: 6:43 A.M. Sunset: 4:45 P.M. Moonrise: 10:54 A.M. Moonset: 7:55 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (21%) *Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Saturday, November 14Following inferior conjunction early this month, Mercury has reappeared in the morning sky. Now magnitude 0.3, you can find the small planet some 5° above the eastern horizon an hour before sunrise. It lies to the lower left of brighter Venus (magnitude –4.8), which sits alongside Virgo’s luminary Spica, about 12° to Mercury’s west.

This morning, Mercury is less than 1° south of 4th-magnitude Kappa (κ) Virginis, which should be visible until the sky brightens enough to wash out the star. You can capture both in the same field of view in either binoculars or a telescope. Mercury now appears as a 32%-lit disk that is 8” across. Compare that with Venus, which features a narrower phase just 13% lit but stretches 51” by comparison. The brighter planet lies just 1.4° northwest of Spica, the brightest star in Virgo.

Both Spica and Kappa can act as guideposts to help you spot Venus’ and Mercury’s motion, respectively, over the next few days. Mercury is moving east and will pull away from Kappa to the lower left. Venus, which just recently reached a stationary point, is also moving east, but will swing slightly northeast (to the upper left) of Spica for a few days before tracking more directly east.

Mars passes 1.2° north of Jupiter at 10 P.M. EST — we’ll focus on this pair in the early-morning sky tomorrow.

Sunrise: 6:44 A.M. Sunset: 4:44 P.M. Moonrise: 11:33 A.M. Moonset: 8:56 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (29%)

Sunday, November 15Jupiter and Mars are approaching opposition in February next year. They are now rising late in the evening and dominate the early-morning sky. By 3 A.M. local time, the two planets are 40° high in the east. Mars sits just to the upper left (north) of Jupiter, having passed 1.2° due north of the gas giant late last night, shortly before rising. Both planets sit to the upper right (west) of Regulus, the brightest star in Leo the Lion.

In addition to spotting the pair of planets together in a telescope, you’ll want to zoom in on Jupiter in particular, as its Galilean moons are showing off this morning. Around 3 A.M. EST, Callisto stands alone west of the planet, with Io (closest) and Ganymede to the east. Twenty-two minutes later (at 3:22 A.M. EST), Io’s shadow appears at the eastern limb and begins to transit. Just over an hour later, with Io closing in on the same limb, Europa pops into view as it reappears from an occultation at 4:27 A.M. EST. It is just south of Io, which passes due north of Europa at 4:34 A.M. EST. Io then begins a transit two minutes later, slowly following its shadow. Io’s shadow reaches the western limb and disappears at 5:38 A.M. EST, while the moon takes a little over an hour to reach the same point, ending its transit at 5:52 A.M. CST (now daylight in the Eastern time zone).

Sunrise: 6:45 A.M. Sunset: 4:43 P.M. Moonrise: 12:05 P.M. Moonset: 9:58 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (38%)

Monday, November 16It’s a great night to catch Saturn’s largest and brightest moon, Titan, as it skims south of the planet. Two hours after sunset, Saturn is roughly 40° high in the southeast, outshining all the other stars in this region of the sky. It lies to the lower left of the Circlet of Pisces and to the upper left of the bright star Fomalhaut in Piscis Austrinus.

Zoom in on Saturn with a telescope to first catch sight of its ring system, stretching 43” from end to end and tilted 8° to our line of sight. Currently we are seeing Saturn’s southern side, including the entirety of the planet’s southern hemisphere. The gas giant’s disk now measures 19” across.

Titan is difficult to miss, shining at mid-8th magnitude just south of the ringed planet. Don’t be fooled by a fainter 10th-magnitude field star, which lies just to Titan’s west. The three next-brightest moons, also 10th magnitude, are Tethys, Dione, and Rhea. They lie closer to the planet. Tethys sits about 40” west of Saturn’s center shortly before 8 P.M. EST, while Dione is just west of the limb and Rhea just east of the planet. Dione and Rhea are moving westward, and Rhea will skim just north of Saturn’s pole along the way, standing due north of the planet around 10:40 P.M. EST. Tethys is moving east, and will disappear behind the planet’s southwestern limb in an occultation around 2:35 A.M. EST on the 16th (still late on the 15th along the Pacific Coast).

Sunrise: 6:46 A.M. Sunset: 4:43 P.M. Moonrise: 12:32 P.M. Moonset: 11:00 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (47%)

Tuesday, November 17First Quarter Moon occurs at 6:48 A.M. EST, floating among the stars of Aquarius.

Early this evening brighter targets are best, as the Moon doesn’t set until late. Ready for viewing as the winter constellations start to dominate earlier each day is the Pleiades, an open cluster cataloged as M45.

Known since antiquity and readily visible to the naked eye, the Pleiades contains several bright stars arranged in a tiny dipperlike shape. Located in northwestern Taurus, the cluster is sometimes mistaken for the Little Dipper, although that asterism is much larger and lies in the northern sky, anchored at the end of its handle by Polaris, the North Star. The Pleiades shines with a collective magnitude of 1.6 and spans roughly 110’ — a huge swath of sky. It lies above the sideways V-shape of Taurus’ face as the Bull rises in the east this evening, and is already 30° high by 7:30 P.M. local time. How many stars can you make out with the naked eye? Most observers see six or seven.

Once you’ve taken in the cluster without any optical aid, zoom in with binoculars or a finder scope. (Any higher magnification and you won’t see most of the cluster at once, but instead be limited to a smaller portion.) Many more stars will now pop into your field of view. If you do opt for high magnification, look for a faint grayish haze around the stars — this is nearby dust reflecting the stars’ light, and requires clear, dark conditions to make out.

The Leonid meteor shower peaks tonight, with the best meteor viewing overnight into the early-morning hours of November 18, as the Moon sets around midnight and the radiant rises higher. Check out tomorrow’s entry for more detail.

Sunrise: 6:47 A.M. Sunset: 4:42 P.M. Moonrise: 12:56 P.M. Moonset: — Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (57%)

Wednesday, November 18The peak of the Leonid meteor shower, caused by the dusty debris of Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, is best seen early this morning after the Moon has set and the shower’s radiant rises high in the hours before dawn.

Two hours before sunrise, Leo is high in the southeast, with bright Jupiter and Mars joining the curved shape of the Sickle asterism. The Leonids’ radiant is located just inside the cuved blade’s inner edge, near 3rd-magnitude Zeta (ζ) Leonis to the upper left (north) of Mars and Jupiter. The two planets appear roughly side by side in the sky around this time, with ruddy Mars at left and more golden-yellow Jupiter at right. Regulus sits just to their lower left.

To catch the most meteors, you’ll actually want to look a little ways away from Leo, about 40° to 60° to the left or right of the constellation. This is where meteors with the longest trains will also occur. Although this shower isn’t particularly strong, you can expect to see roughly a half-dozen or more Leonid meteors per hour. The Leonid shower produces some of the fastest-moving meteors we experience all year, streaking through the sky at some 44 miles (70 kilometers) per hour.

Sunrise: 6:49 A.M. Sunset: 4:41 P.M. Moonrise: 1:19 P.M. Moonset: 12:03 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (67%)

Thursday, November 19The solar system is a dynamic place. Let’s return to the predawn sky today to check out the inner planets’ progress relative to the stars of Virgo. An hour before sunrise, both Mercury and Venus are again well above the eastern horizon, with the stars around them still visible before twilight brightens too much.

Compared with earlier in the week, Venus now sits to the upper left of Spica, rather than directly above it. Venus will pass 1.8° due north of Spica later today at 6 P.M. EST. Now moving steadily east, it will track along the ecliptic, slowly headed for Libra. Mercury has already reached the Balance, sitting within its domain and to the far lower left of Kappa (κ) Virginis, as opposed to the pair’s close proximity a few days ago.

Pull out your telescope to see how the planets’ appearances have changed, too. Mercury is now 55% lit and 7” across, while Venus is 18% lit and has shrunk more noticeably, now 47” across.

Sunrise: 6:50 A.M. Sunset: 4:40 P.M. Moonrise: 1:41 P.M. Moonset: 1:07 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (76%)

Friday, November 20The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M. EST; 12 hours later, our satellite passes 7° north of Saturn at 8 P.M. EST. The trio is visible in the southeastern sky two hours after sunset, forming a triangle with the Moon to the upper left of Saturn, and Neptune to Saturn’s right. Only the Moon and Saturn are visible to the naked eye, while Neptune will require optical aid.

From the gibbous Moon, drop down first to check out Saturn through a telescope, including its lovely ring system and brightest moon, Titan. Saturn is the brightest object in this part of the sky after the Moon, so you don’t have to worry about misidentifying it. After passing south of the ringed world earlier this week, Titan now sits about 3.2’ to Saturn’s west, in line with the rings. Fainter moons Tethys, Rhea, and Dione may be visible clustered closer to the planet, but the bright moonlight might also make them challenging for visual observation.

From Saturn, scan 6.6° west-southwest to land on Neptune. If you have a go-to scope, it may take you right to the outermost planet, which glows at magnitude 7.7 and offers up a tiny, 2”-wide disk. It may look like a “flat,” bluish-gray star, rather than a bright pinprick of white light. Look for a large parallelogram of 4th- and 5th-magnitude stars just over 9° to Saturn’s southwest if you need a closer stepping stone. The star at the northeastern point of that shape is 5th-magnitude 29 Piscium, and it lies about 2.6° southwest of Neptune.

Mercury reaches greatest western elongation (20°) at 7 P.M. EST. We’ll check out the planet in the predawn sky in next week’s column.

Sunrise: 6:51 A.M. Sunset: 4:40 P.M. Moonrise: 2:04 P.M. Moonset: 2:12 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (84%)

A mysterious bronze foot found in a bog was likely once part of a monumental statue of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius, who tried to conquer Scotland.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

All that remains of a larger-than-life statue of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius once erected in Scotland is a lower right leg. Experts have now reconstructed what the entire sculpture looked like but are still unsure why it was carefully dismantled over 1,800 years ago.

The gold-covered bronze foot and calf, also known as the Milsington leg, was discovered in a bog in 1820, according to a Nov. 12 statement from National Museums Scotland. It is the only example of a monumental Roman emperor statue ever found in Scotland and was likely made around A.D. 140.

Initially, experts thought the bronze statue had been looted from York, England, which was founded by the Romans in A.D. 71 as the town of Eboracum. But as research into the Roman frontier advanced over the years, it became clear that equestrian statues were often set up in forts along the border of the Roman Empire.

This lower leg, experts now believe, originally came from an equestrian statue of Emperor Antoninus Pius that was similar to the famous statue of Marcus Aurelius in Rome.

Antoninus Pius was Roman emperor from A.D. 138 to 161, succeeding Hadrian, who had built an enormous wall to defend the northernmost limit of the Roman Empire. To add to Rome's territory, Antoninus Pius directed the imperial governor of Roman Britain to move north, invade southern Scotland and build a second wall, called the Antonine Wall. But that wall was left undefended after Antoninus Pius died, and the Romans retreated from Scotland.

During that retreat, the Romans may have dismantled any valuable statues that they had set up, according to the statement. An examination of the Milsington leg ahead of a new exhibition showed that the bronze had no cut marks, suggesting it was removed carefully and not "brutally hacked off."

"This contrasts with examples of statues being deliberately destroyed after a battle, when an emperor's memory was condemned, or when they were chopped up for scrap," according to National Museums Scotland.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

With the Scottish provenance firmly established, National Museums Scotland curators were able to learn more about Antoninus Pius and his approach to imperial expansion.

"This really turns on its head our understanding of Rome's second attempt at conquering Scotland," Fraser Hunter, principal curator of prehistoric art and Roman archaeology at National Museums Scotland, said in the statement. "This was a big deal for the Emperor, something which was worth celebrating."

But while the boot-clad bronze leg provides a glimpse into the monuments that may have graced southern Scotland nearly two millennia ago, it raises an important question for Hunter: Where is the rest of the statue?

The Milsington leg, the Inveresk Mithras altars and other Roman-period finds are on display beginning Nov. 14 in the exhibit "Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire" at the National Museum of Scotland.

#6246. You Were More Conscious as a Child Than You Are Now, Neuroscientist Claims

What if growing up makes you more knowledgeable but less aware of reality?

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

When you were a child, did you ever wonder what happened to the sea at the horizon? Perhaps you imagined it stretching forever. Or perhaps, like me, you believed that where the blue ended, the water simply fell off the edge of the world, spilling over in some enormous, invisible waterfall. It made perfect sense at the time, and there was quite a lot of magic involved, too. Then came geography lessons, maps, explanations, terminology, and the gradual realization that the world did not end where your vision did—that it was, in fact, far vaster than anything the eye could take in. So why has it become so difficult to recapture the purity and intensity of that experience as an adult?

Could there be a chance, however counterintuitive it sounds, that you were actually more conscious back then?

It sounds counterintuitive, but Alysson Muotri, PhD, a professor of pediatrics and cellular and molecular medicine at the University of California, San Diego, has given this poetic—almost philosophical—idea scientific legs. To do so, he used one of the most futuristic tools that currently exists for investigating the human brain: brain organoids, tiny clusters of living neural tissue grown from stem cells in a laboratory. He wondered whether these tiny lumps of living human brain tissue could illuminate that elusive inner experience. What he found was that as we grow and learn about the world, this process might really be changing how we perceive reality.

But before you can explore consciousness in a lab, you need to build the organoids. The process begins with ordinary human cells, often collected from the skin. Scientists reprogram them into induced pluripotent stem cells, which regain the ability to develop into almost any cell type in the body. Researchers use chemical signals to turn these cells into neurons and other brain cells. The cells multiply, gathering into tiny clumps of tissue. Inside them, neurons begin making contact, and electrical signals pass between them. However, calling these organoids “brains in a dish” is rather generous, though tempting; they lack much of the anatomy of a developed human brain. Still, organoids allow scientists to watch human neural tissue take shape in ways that would be impossible to witness inside a living person’s skull.

Muotri’s team discovered in 2019 that maturing organoids produced electrical rhythms resembling certain features of brain activity recorded in premature infants. Here was human neural tissue, deprived of the sights and sounds accompanying a child’s development, nevertheless organizing itself into patterns observed in living brains. Four years later, researchers at Indiana University Bloomington incorporated brain organoids into an experimental computing system that used their electrical responses to help recognize spoken sounds and predict mathematical patterns. By 2025, other scientists had reported that repeated electrical stimulation could alter how individual neurons in organoids responded, with some changes lingering for hours after the stimulation came to a halt—evidence of cellular mechanisms associated with learning and memory.

Muotri, meanwhile, had begun wondering whether the electrical activity of his brain organoids could offer any clues to that elusive inner experience we call consciousness. Of course, even if we assume that consciousness arises entirely from the brain, there is something peculiar about trying to measure it. It’s not as though you can insert a thermometer into someone’s head and pinpoint the experience of being alive and aware—or the feeling of experiencing the world as a child.

Muotri decided to investigate by borrowing an approach from consciousness research called the perturbational complexity index (PCI). In humans, the method involves delivering a brief magnetic pulse to the brain and recording the resulting electrical activity through electrodes placed on the scalp. Earlier researchers have analyzed the responses and calculated a score that has helped distinguish wakefulness from deep sleep and general anesthesia; a higher score indicates greater conscious awareness. While PCI cannot measure consciousness directly, it offers clues about the brain’s capacity to sustain it.

In preliminary findings, Muotri measured the organoids’ electrical activity before exposing them to repeated stimulation, using an approach similar to PCI. To say that he found a startling degree of complexity in the way their neurons communicate with one another—with scores that exceeded those typically recorded in awake human brains—is an understatement. Because the organoid and human measurements use different methods, however, the scores cannot be compared directly. Still, he wasn’t expecting the organoids to have this PCI level, he says. “It’s very new, and I’m still thinking about what it means.”

Muotri also found something shocking about how the organoids behaved as they were stimulated repeatedly with light. Gradually, the cells began reacting differently to the stimulation, and some of those changes lingered after the light was switched off. “So there is some kind of a memory embedded in those networks,” he says. But even more astounding was that, as the organoids adapted to the stimulation, their complexity score actually fell, similar to the way human brains with lower PCI scores were less aware.

He thinks the reason is that a brain organoid increases its bias as it learns, just as we become more biased as we learn more over the years. By bias, Muotri means that experience makes certain neural responses, particularly those reinforced through repeated exposure, more likely than others. Learning, apparently, does more than give us knowledge. It may also condition us to overlook parts of the world we once experienced more freely.

“It’s almost like when you are born…as soon as your brain is naive and fresh, you’re more conscious than when you are an adult,” Muotri continues. By adulthood, however, experience has cramped your brain’s style. “Because you already experienced so many things, you’re already [so] attached to the physical environment, that you become less conscious than you were [as] a baby.”

The suggestion is extraordinary, especially coming from experiments involving tissue that has never seen a sunset, heard a lullaby, obeyed a teacher, or encountered anything resembling a childhood whatsoever.

Yet there is a recognizable human parallel. Developmental psychologist Alison Gopnik has compared adult attention to a spotlight, concentrated on what matters for an immediate goal, and children’s attention to a lantern, illuminating more of their surroundings. A toddler entering an unfamiliar room might become absorbed by a patch of sunlight that an adult barely notices. The adult knows more about the room, but familiarity helps determine what deserves attention. Noticing more of the world doesn’t necessarily mean being more conscious of it.

However, a baby’s brain, already shaped by months of development in the womb, is hardly comparable to an organoid that has never experienced the world outside a laboratory. That’s why Kenneth Kosik, MD, a neuroscience professor at the University of California, Santa Barbara, is skeptical. In a 2024 paper published in the journal Patterns, titled Why Brain Organoids Are Not Conscious Yet, he argued that organoids lack much of the organization and communication between brain regions that may be necessary for consciousness. And electrical activity, however complicated, is not enough to prove an inner life. Neurons firing independently can produce unpredictable signals that are difficult to reduce to a simpler description, even when there is no evidence that anything is being experienced. “So we still have a little bit of a jump there, yeah, to say that compressibility is related to consciousness,” Kosik says.

Muotri himself is cautious about what the numbers mean and says they are still preliminary data. Nor does he claim that his organoids actually experience anything. “I should not say they are conscious outright,” he says.

For now, Muotri’s experiments cannot definitively tell us whether we were more conscious as children than we are as adults, but they do open a window onto something just as intriguing: what happens to our experience of the world if learning itself changes how our brains encounter our environment? After all, the day I discovered that the sea did not plunge into an abyss, I gained precious knowledge that generations before me had strived to acquire. But have I ever again experienced the sea quite as fully as I did when I was a child, believing it could spill over the world’s edge? That is a whole different question, and we don’t have the answer yet.

Stav Dimitropoulos is a Gold and Community Anthem Award–winning journalist, and writes about consciousness, science, and culture for Popular Mechanics, Nature, and the BBC. Her work often explores mind-stretching angles where science meets philosophy. Her debut nonfiction book, Slow, Lazy, Gluttons (Greystone Books, 2026) asks: What if the traits society shames — laziness, darkness, nostalgia, and more — are actually survival superpowers?

#6245. Archaeologists found a rare gold bear hiding inside an ancient grave in Kazakhstan that was raided by robbers thousands of years ago

A small gold bear from the 4th-3rd century B.C. was found in a looted Saka mound in Almaty, with remains of perhaps seven people.

Earlier this year, staff of the Almaty Museums Association dug into a Saka burial mound at Karagaily, in the city’s Nauryzbay district. They found a small gold bear and a lot of human bones.

Somebody had been there first. Robbers in antiquity left a 10-foot (3 meter) pit in the mound.

On November 5 the Almaty city administration published the result and called the bear figurine unique for Kazakhstan. The date it gave is preliminary, and nobody yet knows how many people lay in the grave.

Karagaily is a cemetery of the Early Iron Age, and the mound dug this year was an emergency job done with the support of the city administration. It is 25 to 26 meters wide, or roughly 82 to 85 feet, and about 8 feet (2.5 meters) high.

Based on its knowledge of the cemetery, the team put the mound in the 4th or 3rd century B.C., the time of the Saka, nomadic peoples of the Central Asian steppe. Broken Saka pots came out of the dig too.

Meanwhile, Marat Nurpeisov, senior researcher at the association, said the work at Karagaily has not finished.

The statement calls the object “presumably” a small cast figurine of a bear. In the photos the city released, it stands on its hind legs on a scrap of thin gold sheet, and rows of short notches cover its back and flanks.

Because the sheet has holes in it, the excavators think somebody stitched it to a headdress. They point to two Kazakh parallels for animals worn on the head.

The first is the gold argali, a wild mountain sheep, that topped the hat of the Golden Man, the young man buried in a suit with more than 4,000 gold pieces and dug up near Almaty in 1969. Kok-Kainar cemetery gave the second in 2014, a small snow leopard that had also been part of a headdress.

Lyazzat Sagyndykova, who directs the association, was blunt about the bear. In the statement, translated here from Russian, she said the sculptural figurine of a bear “is unique for Kazakhstan.”

She also said the find lets researchers trace cultural parallels across Eurasia, from the Black Sea region to the Altai, though the statement names no objects from either end of that range.

Altogether, excavators think four adults and three children may have gone into this one mound. However, the administration is careful to say nobody has established the exact number.

Nurpeisov said mounds of comparable size were usually meant for one or two people, and that such burials are atypical for Kazakhstan.

Anthropologists will join the work, along with other tests, to find out how many bodies there were and how they came to be there.

Kinship is one thing those tests could look at, although the Almaty statement never mentions DNA. In a study of 85 people from 20 Scythian-era sites on the steppe, elite burials turned out about eleven times more likely to be relatives of each other than of lower-status people at the same sites.

Only in 2022 did the association get its special license to excavate, and it began work inside the city that same year.

In Alatau district it found an untouched burial of a Saka warrior, dated between the 5th and 2nd centuries B.C., with pieces of a sword inlaid with gold, animal-style gold ornaments and silver.

Another Alatau mound in 2024 gave up bits of human bone, bronze fasteners and nails. Italian and French specialists meanwhile ran geophysical surveys with the museum staff at the park called the Saka Mounds of Boralday. That site has 52 mounds over about 430 hectares (1,060 acres) northwest of Almaty.

Last year the team came across an old robbers’ tunnel in a further Early Iron Age mound and recorded how it was built and what the damage was.

Digs forced by development have paid off in other countries. Infrastructure work in southeastern Bulgaria led to a Thracian warrior buried beside his horse with a gilded silver wreath.

At Tepe Chalow in northeastern Iran a teenage girl’s Bronze Age tomb held 34 objects, gold rings and earrings among them.

Everything official so far comes from that one city statement, which is not a scientific paper. It gives no height or weight for the figure.

It does not say where in the mound the bear was lying or how the robbers came to miss it.

“Unique” is the association’s own word. The date, too, comes from the cemetery as a whole and not from a laboratory result on this mound.

Once the research is over, the association intends to put the best pieces on show at the Almaty Museum. Robbers left a 10-foot hole at Karagaily, and the bear is headed for a glass case.

The information was obtained from the Almaty city administration.

#6243. Students helped astronomers track a rare alien comet that contains strange chemicals

Students helped the Webb Telescope locate a rare interstellar comet, revealing record-high heavy hydrogen levels that prove it was born in an incredibly cold, unknown star system.

School groups in Upminster, Bridgend, Alcarràs and Zagreb were among the observers who sent in position measurements of an interstellar comet in the weeks before the Webb Telescope observed it on December 22, 2025.

Those positions helped astronomers refine the predicted location of 3I/ATLAS before beginning their study. Webb then discovered that the comet contained methane with a higher share of heavy hydrogen than had ever been measured in the solar system.

Nathan X. Roth and 17 co-authors put the ratio at 3.18 percent. They link it to a very cold birthplace, but the paper names no star system.

The paper credits Comet Chasers, a school outreach program led by Helen Usher, with supporting position measurements, and lists the schools among the observers. The program reaches telescopes in the Las Cumbres Observatory network.

The target had been known for less than six months. The ATLAS survey telescope in Río Hurtado, Chile, reported the object on July 1, 2025, according to NASA. It was the third known visitor from outside the solar system, and it passed closest to the sun around October 30.

Roth, of NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center and American University, did the spectral modeling and led the writing. Martin Cordiner, also at Goddard, calibrated the Webb data.

Webb observed the comet under General Observer program 5094 with its Near-Infrared Spectrograph. On December 22, the telescope took a single 642-second exposure starting at 03:36 Universal Time.

The key data came the next day. Five exposures of 700 seconds each began at 08:07 Universal Time and covered wavelengths where methane emits strongly.

The comet was then about 223 million miles (360 million kilometers) from the sun and 167 million miles (269 million kilometers) from Webb. Roth’s team extracted light from a small circle reaching about 610 miles (980 kilometers) from the nucleus.

Lines from ordinary methane were up to 100 times stronger than those from the heavy form. Methanol, formaldehyde and ethane also emit at nearby wavelengths.

The team used NASA’s Planetary Spectrum Generator to model those gases and subtract them from the spectrum.

They removed ordinary methane next, masked its line positions and fitted what remained. They fitted the spectral baseline together with the gas emission, using low-order polynomials.

Deuterium is a form of hydrogen with a neutron in its nucleus. In the molecule CH3D, one deuterium atom replaces one of the four hydrogen atoms in methane.

The measured ratio was 3.18 percent, with an uncertainty of 0.30 points. The authors wrote that it “exceeds any other value for methane measured in the Solar System,” a list that includes Venus, the giant planets, Titan and the dwarf planets Eris and Makemake.

Carbon monoxide was the most abundant molecule in the gas around the comet on December 23. Water usually leads closer to the sun. Methane escapes ice very easily, so the authors concluded that this shift should not have changed the ratio they derived.

A second Webb instrument looked at the comet that same month. The Mid-Infrared Instrument observed the comet on December 15 and 16 and again on December 27.

That’s when Webb directly detected methane gas on an interstellar visitor for the first time, according to NASA. Other Webb work on the same comet found water ice mixed with dust in very small grains.

Only one other comet has a secure detection of this molecule. The European Space Agency’s Rosetta spacecraft measured it directly at comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko, and the 3I/ATLAS ratio is about 13 times higher.

Telescope searches at a few bright comets produced only upper limits, between 0.5 and 1 percent. The Webb spectrum therefore counts as a rare remote detection of CH3D in any comet’s atmosphere.

Methane is not the only enriched gas in this object. The earlier analysis of the same Webb observations put the heavy hydrogen ratio in its water at 0.98 percent, according to a paper in Nature, and a separate team reported water far richer in deuterium than comets near the sun.

The methane ratio is roughly three times the water ratio. Comet 67P shows the same direction of difference, and regions where stars form show organic molecules more enriched than water by up to a factor of 10. Around the young star V883 Orionis, astronomers have also reported heavy water older than the sun.

Roth and his colleagues wrote that the result fits ices formed in a cold interstellar or protostellar setting with few heavy elements and strong cosmic ray exposure.

Low temperatures keep deuterium attached to reactive ions, and a shortage of carbon monoxide leaves those ions alive for longer.

Cosmic rays add more of the ions that start this chemistry. Models of planet-forming disks that include X-rays give methane ratios of only about 0.2 to 0.6 percent, so the team argued that the ices were inherited from an earlier stage.

Cordiner’s team had estimated that the comet could have formed as long as 10 to 12 billion years ago, according to ESA/Webb.

“This was a unique opportunity to study an ancient object from the distant Galaxy,” Cordiner said in that release. Webb’s carbon and deuterium readings hint at a distant origin for the object.

Few published models list a heavy methane ratio at all, and none of those predicts more than 1 percent. The authors noted that astrochemical models have not yet tested deuterium chemistry with low heavy element levels and strong cosmic rays together.

The comparison also rests on two comets. Methane’s ratio is still unconstrained in sources outside the solar system, so the team estimated it from a small ring-shaped hydrocarbon called cyclopropenylidene. Those indirect values may reach at least 4 to 7 percent and offer tentative support only.

Two of the five background exposures failed because of background star problems, and the team worked without subtracting background light.

This article uses the journal figures. A preprint of the study lists 3.33 percent and a factor of 14, while the journal version gives 3.18 percent and a factor of 13.

The paper does not name a home star for 3I/ATLAS. It does name the schools in Upminster, Bridgend, Alcarràs and Zagreb.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Astronomy.

The paper’s acknowledgments thank optical observers whose position measurements helped refine the comet’s ephemeris, the table of its predicted positions.

They then name the schools, which include Coopers’ Company and Coborn School in Upminster, St Mary’s Catholic Primary School in Bridgend, Institut d’Alcarràs in Catalonia and Jelkovec High School in Zagreb.

J. M. Perez Redondo and students A. Matea, L. Guillamet, A. Montoy and A. Martin took part from the Catalan school.

#6242. GLP-1s Extend Life Span, New Research Suggests. Could They Be Key to Human Longevity?

This may mean the drug also has benefits outside of diabetes management.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

Roughly 11 percent of American adults are on a GLP-1 for weight loss, according to a 2026 Gallup survey; so chances are, you likely know someone who is using one for diabetes management, obesity treatment, or heart health—but the benefits might not stop there. Now, semaglutide, the popular GLP-1 medication found in Ozempic and Wegovy, is drawing serious attention from longevity experts.

A recent study published in Nature found that semaglutide administered to female mice late in life significantly extended their life span. The results pose a legitimate question: Could GLP-1 drugs lengthen human lives as well?

To understand whether GLP-1s have anti-aging benefits, researchers put mice that were 20 months old—or roughly 60 human years—on a semaglutide regimen for the rest of their lives. There was also a control group of female mice the same age that received saline injections instead of the semaglutide. The team targeted older, non-obese, non-diabetic female mice to minimize the effects of male aggression and injury, consistent with previous long-term aging research, according to study author Danica Chen, PhD, professor of metabolic biology and nutrition at the University of California, Berkeley.The results? The median life span of the mice that received the GLP-1 drug increased from 742 days to 834 days, roughly a 12 percent extension. The researchers also saw reduced inflammation and preserved cognitive and muscle function in the GLP-1 group.

But there’s a rub here: This study was done in mice, which are a far cry from human adults, meaning we don’t yet know the effects of GLP-1s on people—at least not yet. However, there has been research that suggests lower-calorie diets lead to longer life spans in humans. “The general cause of aging is accumulation of cellular damage,” Chen says. She explains that calorie restriction can reduce cell damage and improve the function of tissues (a group of similar cells working together to perform a specific task), both of which contribute to a longer life span.

Michael Corley, PhD, associate professor of medicine at the University of California San Diego, thinks the Nature study is “important and exciting” because it looks beyond the established metabolic benefits of GLP-1 drugs and tests whether they can influence the biological aging process. (Biological age denotes how well the body is functioning on cellular and molecular levels, while chronological age refers to the number of years a person has been alive.)

“The finding that semaglutide extended life span by approximately 12 percent in older female mice, while improving several measures of physical and cognitive function, adds important evidence to the emerging field of GLP-1 therapies as potential gerotherapeutics,” or treatments that target the root of aging, Corley says. In fact, Corley was involved in a separate study, published earlier this year in Nature Communications, that found that 32 weeks of semaglutide treatment improved multiple epigenetic aging clocks, including measures of biological age and the pace of aging.

Findings presented at the 2026 Aging Research and Drug Discovery Meeting have also strengthened this emerging picture, Corley explains. Novo Nordisk, a Danish pharmaceutical company with locations around the world, reported that semaglutide improved measures of biological aging across multiple organ systems, including the heart and kidneys.

Likewise, Eli Lilly, an American pharmaceutical company headquartered in Indiana, presented findings that tirzepatide—another GLP-1 medication, which is found in prescriptions like Mounjaro and Zepbound—positively influenced several epigenetic aging clocks, including organ-specific markers that measure the biological age of the heart, kidney, liver, and immune system.

“Together, these independent observations suggest that GLP-1-based therapies may affect biological aging through multiple molecular pathways,” Corley says. “The new mouse study is particularly interesting because it extends these molecular observations to actual life span, while also demonstrating improvements in several hallmarks of aging.”

So, could GLP-1 drugs actually extend the life span of humans? Corley thinks the more compelling opportunity isn’t necessarily extending life span, but extending health span—or the number of years people live in good health, free from chronic disease and disability.

“Human life span has biological constraints, and it is unlikely that GLP-1 drugs alone will dramatically extend the maximum limits of human longevity,” he says. “However, by reducing the burden of cardiovascular disease, metabolic dysfunction, and other age-related conditions, these medications could help more people remain healthy and independent for longer, potentially increasing average life span without fundamentally changing the upper limits of human longevity.”

However, improvements in biological aging don’t necessarily translate into longer lives, Corley cautions.

“The critical next step is determining whether these molecular changes predict meaningful improvements in physical function, cognition, and resilience,” Corley says. “I think the greatest potential of GLP-1 therapies is not to push humans beyond the limits of longevity, but to help more people reach older ages while maintaining their health, function, and independence.”

To find out whether or not GLP-1 drugs can eventually be used as a legitimate longevity tactic in humans, Chen says clinical trials in humans are an important next step. For now, GLP-1s remain a titan of diabetes and weight management—but their role in human longevity remains to be seen.

#6241. Stone Age children left fingerprints on ancient art projects

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Clay figurines hint at hands-on learning in the Levant

Stone Age hunter-gatherer children from the Levant may have helped make small clay sculptures of birds, gazelle, humans and more (some shown).

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Children have been making art with help from grown-ups for millennia.

Fragmented clay figurines dating as far back as 15,000 years ago, discovered in what is now Israel, preserve the fingerprints of both adults and young children. The finding suggests the grown-ups taught the kids how to shape and decorate clay, researchers report November 11 in PLOS One.

Children’s contributions to prehistoric art and culture aren’t well understood. Concrete evidence of their involvement has been hard to find, says archaeologist Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

In recent decades, researchers have found a handful of objects made by children — including 200,000-year-old rock art bearing child-sized handprints in Tibet and 30,000-year-old clay sculptures pockmarked with child-sized fingerprints in Czech Republic.

Davin and colleagues hadn’t set out to find Stone Age children’s artwork. They were investigating whether the Natufian culture — a group of hunter-gatherers who formed some of the first permanent settlements in the Levant about 14,000 years ago — made clay art before the advent of agriculture in the region.

The archaeologists came across the first set of fingerprints while sorting through 40 kilograms of clay collected at three Natufian sites, which range in age from 15,000 to 11,600 years old. Among tens of thousands of clay lumps, the team found some 150 fragments of sculptures, including 15 recognizable bird, gazelle and human figures. Around 60 of these pieces preserved fingerprints from where people had pinched or prodded the clay.

The distances between the fingerprints’ ridges, which are influenced by age and sex, suggest that most of the figurines were made by women and children — some younger than 10. Only a few sets of fingerprints belonged to men. And the torso of one tiny human statue had both adult and child fingerprints, hinting that an elder and child had passed it back and forth. Davin suspects that the adult actively taught a child how to work the clay.

This evidence of intergenerational learning so far back in time is fascinating, says archaeologist Steven Dorland of Grand Valley State University in Allendale, Mich. It demonstrates how much researchers can learn from broadening their focus beyond adult males, he says. Dorland has used pottery to understand social learning in Indigenous societies of the Great Lakes region. He has even studied children’s fingerprints on some of those artifacts.

The purpose of the Natufian figurines is unclear. Most of the statues are less than 2 centimeters long and don’t display signs of intense use, the team found, suggesting they weren’t treated as precious heirlooms.

Davin suspects the figurines may have represented stories, like how kids draw Disney characters today, he says. “Maybe the idea is that the role of children here is not necessarily to learn to make figurines, but more to learn the story behind them.”

#6240. The Sky Today on Friday, November 13: Spot Mirach’s Ghost

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Celebrate Friday the 13th with something spooky: a ghost in the constellation Andromeda. This evening, point your telescope toward 2nd-magnitude Mirach (Beta [β] Andromedae), already nearly 60° high in the east by 7 P.M. local time. One of the Princess’ brightest stars, Mirach is a cool, reddish M-type giant. It lies some 200 light-years away and shines nearly 2,000 times as brightly as our Sun.

But Mirach is not quite our target — we’re looking for its so-called ghost, just 6.8’ northwest of the star. You’ll need a big scope to see it, but look carefully: Can you spot a faint smudge of light, about 4’ across, close to the star? This is the Ghost of Mirach, a far more distant elliptical galaxy glowing at 10th magnitude and cataloged as NGC 404. It lies some 8 million to 10 million light-years away, just beyond the gravitational bounds of our Local Group of galaxies. It’s called a ghost because it appears almost like a ghostly image of the bright star Mirach, which dominates the view.

#6239. Scientists learned how to control physical movements by turning on just 20 individual cells inside the brain

Scientists found that turning on only 20 tiny brain cells is enough to trigger learned movements. This breakthrough could eventually help treat stroke and paralysis patients.

Learning a tennis serve or a piano scale leaves a mark in the brain. It’s a pattern of activity that plays out across the motor cortex every time the movement runs.

Does that pattern produce the movement, or just echo orders issued somewhere else? Scientists have argued over this for years.

Neurobiologists at the University of California San Diego have now switched on about 20 of a mouse’s motor cortex neurons with light.

The full learned pattern spread through the surrounding cells, and in many trials the mouse made the move it had been trained to make.

“We found that briefly activating only about 20 carefully selected neurons in the motor cortex could trigger the larger pattern of brain activity associated with a learned movement,” said Professor Takaki Komiyama, the senior author. In many cases, this also produced the learned movement itself.

Prof. Komiyama runs a lab in the University’s School of Biological Sciences and its medical school. “Considering that the mouse brain contains approximately 70 million neurons, it is surprising that such a small-scale stimulation can drive specific large-scale brain activity and behavior,” he added.

Graduate student Qiyu Chen led the work. It builds on experiments by An Wu, a scientist in the lab who died in a fire in Montreal, three years ago.

Each mouse learned to grab a small lever and, when a sound played, push it and hold it for one second to earn a drop of water.

After two weeks of daily practice the animals were experts, winning the reward on most tries and pressing the same way each time. The team then recorded the brains of 14 of them as they worked.

A virus had equipped the neurons in the outer layer of the motor cortex with two tools at once. One was a dye that glows when a cell fires. The other was a light-sensitive protein that makes the cell fire on command.

A two-photon microscope read the glow from about 550 neurons per session, across three depths. A second laser, shaped by a holographic projector, could then hit any chosen handful of those cells, one cell at a time.

Across 27 sessions and 14,779 neurons, about 30 percent of the cells ramped up during a press and about 16 percent went quiet.

A smaller group, roughly 13 percent of neurons in a session, switched on just before the lever started moving, and the team called them early-onset neurons.

The test was simple. In 30 percent of trials, chosen at random, the sound didn’t play. Instead a 3-millisecond flash of light hit about 20 early-onset neurons at once, and no water was offered whether or not the mouse pressed.

Mice pressed anyway, and far more often than in trials with neither sound nor light. About half of the light-triggered presses closely matched the trained movement, scored as a correlation above 0.5 with the mouse’s own practiced press.

Voluntary presses matched better, with a median of 0.785 against 0.455, so the flash was a strong but imperfect trigger. The part that mattered most was happening in the cells the laser didn’t touch.

Neurons that normally rose or fell during a voluntary press rose or fell the same way after the flash. Twenty synchronized cells, with no timing pattern of their own, had set off a network that filled in the rest, the way a few notes call up a tune.

Any jolt might do that, so the team ran the same experiment on late-onset neurons, about 14 percent of cells, whose activity begins after a press is under way.

Twenty of those, flashed the same way, produced presses in far fewer trials. The presses that did occur looked less like the trained one, and the flash recruited a smaller share of the surrounding neurons.

Both kinds of light-triggered presses started faster than voluntary ones. That fits the idea that the laser skipped the usual chain from sound to decision to movement.

Presses from the late-onset flash started fastest of all, hinting that the early-onset version was doing some extra computing before the lever moved.

Why did the same flash work on some trials and fail on others? The answer was in the half second before the light.

When the cortex’s activity just before the flash already resembled its state before a good voluntary press, the flash was more likely to produce a faithful one. The same held in voluntary trials, where the state before the cue predicted the quality of the movement.

A decoder, trained on 80 percent of voluntary trials, could read the lever’s path from the population’s activity on held-out trials, and it did even better on the light-triggered ones.

In the authors’ description, a learned movement needs two things. The motor cortex has to be in the right state, and the right small set of cells has to get the first push.

When both are present, the cortex generates the pattern that drives the movement.

All of this is in mice, in one layer of one brain region, during the first few weeks of expertise. Other parts of the nervous system, the spinal cord included, play their own parts in a practiced move.

Earlier work from the same lab found that months of extra practice can make a skill independent of the motor cortex. So the result describes a stage of learning, not a permanent arrangement.

The team also wrote that its data can’t rule out the pattern being completed through loops to deeper structures such as the thalamus. And the flash produced faithful presses only about half the time.

The next project in the lab is to map how the early-onset cells connect to the neurons they recruit.

The longer-term interest is in brain-computer interfaces for people with paralysis or stroke. There, knowing which few cells to address, and when, would matter most.

For now the demonstration is 20 cells, one lever, and a mouse that remembered how to press it.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

Jeremy Bentham, the "godless" philosopher who founded modern utilitarianism, had severe dental and jaw problems, a CT scan of his skull reveals.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The great and "godless" English philosopher Jeremy Bentham, whose remains have been on display at a U.K. university for over 150 years, suffered from severe dental problems, according to X-ray scans of his skull.

The scans were conducted with CT (computed tomography) scanning equipment to create a digital 3D model of his head and highlight Bentham's lengthy "presence" at University College London (UCL) as it celebrates its 200th anniversary.

The scans revealed that Bentham was missing many teeth and had advanced arthritis in his lower jaw when he died of natural causes at the age of 84. During the scanning process, project leader Tannis Davidson, curator of UCL's Grant Museum of Zoology, saw how thin the jawbone had become. "He must have been in excruciating pain," she told Live Science.

Bentham's utilitarian philosophy inspired UCL's founders; it was only the third university in England, after Oxford and Cambridge, which was founded as London University in 1826 and opened to students in 1828.

As a young man, Bentham had declared that he would donate his body to science after his death. This was a radical idea at the time; in the U.K., dissection after death was looked down upon, even if it was for scientific purposes, and it was reserved for the worst criminals. After Bentham died in 1832, his remains were fashioned into an auto-icon — a supposed replica of himself — to memorialize him in the way a tombstone might, Davidson said.

Except for brief visits across Europe and to the Met Breuer in New York City, this auto-icon has been in a display case at UCL since the 1850s, where it can be seen by students as they pass by.

To make the auto-icon (which is not a mummy), Bentham's body was dissected and studied. Then, his skeleton was dressed in his clothes, which were padded with straw. His severed head was badly disfigured during an attempt to preserve it with sulfuric acid, so a wax reconstruction based on paintings and death masks was attached to the body.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Bentham's real head was displayed at the feet of the clothed skeleton that had a lifelike wax head; the real head's eyes were replaced with highly detailed glass eyes, which can be seen in the scans. According to UCL lore, the real head was stolen in 1975 and held ransom for a few days by rivals from King's College London, after which it was locked away.

Davidson explained that Bentham had coined the term "auto-icon" to mean "self-representation" and was setting an example for others. "He imagined a future where people were making auto-icons to keep their dead relatives around," she said.

The CT scans of the real head show that Bentham had dental damage and jaw arthritis, and that his brain had been removed before it was preserved—although some of his dura mater, a layer of connective tissue that covers the brain and spinal cord, was preserved. Davidson said the brain extraction was done to keep with Bentham's instructions that his head be mummified in the same way as Māori heads, which had their brains removed. The scanning process is shown in a short film called "Bentham Revealed."

Jeremy Bentham's "auto-icon" on display at University College London in 2008.

Bentham wrote about his dental problems several times, Davidson said, but it is not clear if he understood that he also had severe arthritis in his lower jaw, which must have made the problems with his teeth much more painful. In addition, modern ideas about cleaning teeth had not been established by Bentham's time. "Dentistry 200 years ago was a very different kettle of fish than it is today," Davidson said.

Bentham was a polymath who hoped to improve the lives of ordinary people through social reform. He wrote extensively about subjects as varied as law, economics, education and animal rights, and he believed that society could be engineered to produce better outcomes through legislation and the objective measurement of "utility."

His most famous idea was the panopticon in 1791, a ring-shaped prison with one warden to watch all of the prisoners, which he proposed as a humane alternative to Australia's penal colonies. Today, however, it is a symbol of state control and surveillance. Bentham also invented a "felicific calculus" to numerically assess the benefits and drawbacks of any given action, based on variables like its intensity, duration, certainty, purity and extent.

Bentham's philosophy put him at odds with the established Church of England; he called himself an "unbeliever," while critics called him "godless."

This rift with the church may have played a part in Bentham's wishes for his remains. Davidson suggested that the auto-icon may have been a means for Bentham to avoid being buried with traditional Anglican rites. "Maybe this was a way he could 'stick it to them' a little bit," she said.

Tom writes mainly about science, space, archaeology, the Earth and the oceans. He has also written for the BBC, NBC News, National Geographic, Scientific American, Air & Space, and many others.
