#6237. A Dutch grandfather paid a few guilders for old prints a century ago, and 35 of them turned out to be Rembrandt etchings

A Dutch woman discovered 35 authentic Rembrandt etchings in her grandfather's collection, hidden away for a century and exhibited in 2026.

Charlotte Meyer of Zutphen, in the eastern Netherlands, inherited an art collection from her grandfather. He had assembled it early in the 20th century, and it included genuine etchings by Rembrandt van Rijn.

Meyer has said her grandfather paid only a few guilders for 35 different prints between 1900 and 1920. Her find became public in February 2026.

From March 21 to June 14, 2026, the Stedelijk Museum Zutphen showed the etchings in an exhibition titled “Rembrandt, From Darkness to Light.” The museum said the prints were seeing daylight for the first time in a hundred years.

The grandfather, a devoted admirer of Rembrandt, kept his art and coin collection in a vault in Amsterdam. The collection remained undisturbed until Meyer rediscovered it in 2020.

Meyer found the etchings there in 2020, according to the Zutphen exhibition listing. She then asked the Rembrandt House Museum in Amsterdam to examine them.

The museum occupies the house on the Jodenbreestraat where Rembrandt lived and worked from 1639 to 1658.

Its specialists confirmed that the prints were authentic. Epco Runia, head of the museum’s collection, has described such a large group of genuine etchings turning up together as very unusual.

Runia put the value of each print at thousands of euros and said the museum already knew these impressions.

Meyer chose the Stedelijk Museum Zutphen as the first museum in the Netherlands to open the etchings to the public. Works from its own collection and from Museum Henriette Polak completed the display.

The Rembrandt House Museum owns 260 of his etchings, a nearly complete overview of his work as a printmaker. It is one of the largest collections of Rembrandt’s graphic work in the world.

Its collection of etchings and drawings also includes four of his original copper plates. Because a plate prints in mirror image, Rembrandt usually placed his signature and date on it in reverse.

After Meyer’s find was announced, more collectors than usual contacted the museum about their own prints. Those checked turned out to be fakes.

The Rembrandt House Museum has not published a detailed account of how it examined Meyer’s etchings.

Meyer has since expanded her collection to more than 70 Rembrandt etchings. She also collects prints by artists who inspired him, by his contemporaries and by his followers.

An etching starts with a metal plate coated in a waxy layer called the etching ground. That acid-resistant mix of beeswax, resin and asphalt protects the metal, and Rembrandt worked on red copper.

The artist scratches a drawing through the ground with a needle. In an acid bath, the exposed lines are then eaten into the metal.

Ink rubbed into those grooves is transferred to damp paper under heavy pressure. Rembrandt used a wooden plate press.

He also scratched lines straight into the copper with a drypoint needle, skipping the acid bath. The ridge of metal raised beside each line prints a deep, velvety black but flattens after about 15 printings.

He often reworked a plate between printings, producing versions called states. Some of his plates went through as many as ten states.

Catalogs label each impression by state. A print marked “state V (8),” for example, shows the fifth of eight states.

Copper had been the main metal for etching plates since about 1520, long before Rembrandt took up the technique.

Rembrandt mostly printed on rag paper made in Germany and France. He also liked fine, yellowish Japanese paper, newly imported into the Netherlands, and now and then used costly parchment.

His etchings were already circulating across Europe during his lifetime. They were cheaper than paintings and easier to trade.

The late art historian Ernst van de Wetering, of the Rembrandt Research Project, observed that Rembrandt’s true genius shows most clearly in his etchings.

There is no single confirmed count of those prints. The Rembrandt House teaching guide on his etchings puts the total at about 290.

Meyer’s prints on view included Self-portrait in a Fur Cap, from 1630, and The Pancake Woman, from 1635. The second shows an elderly woman among a crowd of adults and children, on a plate about 4.4 by 3.1 inches (11.3 by 7.9 centimeters).

The exhibition followed key periods of Rembrandt’s life, from his early years and his years of success to his time of mourning and his years of poverty. While still young, he lost his wife, Saskia, and three of their children.

Interactive displays showed visitors how etching works. A limited-edition catalog, with contributions by Paulo Martina, Ghizlaine Jahidi and Meyer, was published in May 2026.

In 1656, Rembrandt narrowly avoided bankruptcy, and nearly everything he owned was sold at auction. Born in Leiden in 1606, he died in Amsterdam on October 4, 1669, and was buried anonymously.

The information was obtained from the Stedelijk Museum Zutphen.

#6236. 2026 Full Moon calendar: When to see the Full Moon and phases

The phenomenon of a Full Moon arises when our planet, Earth, is precisely sandwiched between the Sun and the Moon. This alignment ensures the entire side of the Moon that faces us gleams under sunlight. Thanks to the Moon’s orbit around Earth, the angle of sunlight hitting the lunar surface and being reflected back to our planet changes. That creates different lunar phases.

The next Full Moon will be the November Beaver Moon, which occurs at 9:54 a.m. EST on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. It will also be a Super Moon.

We’ll update this article multiple times each week with the latest moonrise, moonset, Full Moon schedule, and some of what you can see in the sky each week.

Here’s the complete list of Full Moons this year and their traditional names.

(All times Eastern; * denotes a Super Moon.)

The images below show the day-by-day phases of the Moon in November. The Full Moon this month will be on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026.

The times below for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location. All other times are Eastern unless otherwise specified. For more details on upcoming sky events, check out our full Sky This Week column.

Friday, November 13The Moon reaches apogee, the farthest point from Earth in its orbit, at 12:50 P.M. EST. At that time, our satellite will be 252,040 miles (405,619 kilometers) from Earth.

The phases of the Moon are: New Moon, waxing crescent, First Quarter, waxing gibbous, Full Moon, waning gibbous, Last Quarter, and waning crescent. A cycle starting from one Full Moon to its next counterpart, termed the synodic month or lunar month, lasts about 29.5 days.

Though a Full Moon only occurs during the exact moment when Earth, Moon, and Sun form a perfect alignment, to our eyes, the Moon seems Full for around three days.

There are a wide variety of specialized names used to identify distinct types or timings of Full Moons. These names primarily trace back to a blend of cultural, agricultural, and natural observations about the Moon, aimed at allowing humans to not only predict seasonal changes, but also track the passage of time.

For instance, almost every month’s Full Moon boasts a name sourced from Native American, Colonial American, or other North American traditions, with their titles mirroring seasonal shifts and nature’s events.

Wolf Moon (January): Inspired by the cries of hungry wolves.

Snow Moon (February): A nod to the month’s often heavy snowfall.

Worm Moon (March): Named after the earthworms that signal thawing grounds.

Pink Moon (April): In honor of the blossoming pink wildflowers.

Flower Moon (May): Celebrating the bloom of flowers.

Strawberry Moon (June): Marks the prime strawberry harvest season.

Buck Moon (July): Recognizing the new antlers on bucks.

Sturgeon Moon (August): Named after the abundant sturgeon fish.

Corn Moon (September): Signifying the corn harvesting period.

Hunter’s Moon (October): Commemorating the hunting season preceding winter.

Beaver Moon (November): Reflects the time when beavers are busy building their winter dams.

Cold Moon (December): Evocative of winter’s chill.

In addition, there are a few additional names for Full Moons that commonly make their way into public conversations and news.

Super Moon: This term is reserved for a Full Moon that aligns with the lunar perigee, which is the Moon’s nearest point to Earth in its orbit. This proximity renders the Full Moon unusually large and luminous. For a Full Moon to earn the Super Moon tag, it should be within approximately 90 percent of its closest distance to Earth.

Blue Moon: A Blue Moon is the second Full Moon in a month that experiences two Full Moons. This phenomenon graces our skies roughly every 2.7 years. Though the term suggests a color, Blue Moons aren’t truly blue. Very occasionally, atmospheric conditions such as recent volcanic eruptions might lend the Moon a slightly blueish tint, but this hue isn’t tied to the term.

Black Moon: A Black Moon is a recent, unofficial term that can describe one of two situations. Either the third of four New Moons in a single astronomical season or the second of two New Moons in a month is a Black Moon. As its name suggests, the Black Moon is completely dark, as it is a New Moon that occurs when the Moon is between the Sun and Earth. The New Moon cannot be observed except during a total solar eclipse.

Harvest Moon: Occurring closest to the autumnal equinox, typically in September, the Harvest Moon is often renowned for a distinct orange tint it might display. This Full Moon rises close to sunset and sets near sunrise, providing extended hours of bright moonlight. Historically, this was invaluable to farmers gathering their produce.

What is the difference between a Full Moon and a New Moon? A Full Moon is witnessed when Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, making the entire Moon’s face visible. Conversely, during a New Moon, the Moon lies between Earth and the Sun, shrouding its Earth-facing side in darkness.

How does the Full Moon influence tides? The Moon’s gravitational tug causes Earth’s waters to bulge, birthing tides. During both Full and New Moons, the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in alignment, generating “spring tides.” These tides can swing exceptionally high or low due to the combined gravitational influences of the Sun and Moon.

#6235. Anker’s New Power Station Is the Most Efficient I’ve Tested, Capable of Running My Fridge for 2 Days

My capacity test showed the Solix S5000 is nearly 97 percent efficient.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

How long a power station lasts has the most impact on your experience when using one, whether you’re experiencing a blackout or enjoying a weekend off the grid. This year, Anker has upped its game with the S-series stations. Advanced algorithms have improved how its inverters deliver power and extend battery life. Not long ago, I reviewed this technology in the small but powerful S2000 and was impressed. Now, I’ve put the newer and larger S5000 power station through its paces, and it didn’t disappoint.

For context, I also compared the S5000 to Anker's other large power station, the F3800 Plus (now only available as a bundle with other home power accessories), which has been on our list of the best portable power stations. Each model offers both 120- and 240-volt output, but the S5000 has a much larger battery capacity of 5,024 watt-hours (compared with 3,840 watt-hours with the F3800 Plus), and the S5000 is much smaller in size. While it offers less total power output (4,500 watts versus 6,000 watts for the F3800 Plus), I think the S5000 represents an overall improvement for those looking to buy a home backup station that’s more powerful than a typical portable power station.

This is what I cared about the most because better inverter efficiency is the primary feature Anker touts with the S5000. To evaluate its efficiency, I ran two tests. The first was to turn on the AC output and let it run overnight with nothing plugged into it, making sure to deactivate any auto-off features. I did this because, even when idling, most power station batteries lose some stored energy. But after 18 hours, the S5000’s battery capacity was still at 100 percent—that’s impressive. To make a comparison for context, I ran the F3800 alongside it for the same amount of time, and its battery capacity dipped to 81 percent.

For the second test, I plugged a watt meter into the station and plugged a space heater into the meter. I then ran the heater at full power, drawing around 1,500 watts, until it drained the battery fully. Using a resistive load like this (a device that turns energy to heat) can drain a battery pretty quickly, but this also gives you a good read on a power station's performance. It lasted just over three hours, and my meter measured just under 4,900 watt-hours. Compared with its official spec of 5,024 watt-hours of capacity, I determined that this station is around 97 percent efficient. Many stations hover around 89 percent on average, so this was a big win for the S5000.

The technology behind this ability enables the inverter to throttle itself up and down to meet the demands of the devices plugged into it. This is especially significant for lower-powered devices and cyclical appliances with fluctuating power needs, like refrigerators, because the inverter maintains its efficiency, regardless of what’s plugged into it. That means longer run times across the board. This station could easily power my full-size refrigerator for more than 48 hours.

The size of this station in relation to the battery capacity is its second most striking feature. It’s two-thirds smaller than the F3800 but offers 1,184 more watt-hours. At 99 pounds, I wouldn’t call it light, but with two wheels and a telescoping handle, it’s easy enough to roll around, and it’s not too hard to lift in and out of a vehicle. It would be easy to transport this to and from a second home or a job site.

There are a few other enhancements, as well. The 30-amp, 240-volt connection (great for powering an electric dryer or other 240-volt appliance) has its own on/off button, so it won’t create any unwanted drain when all you need is 120-volt AC power. It also accepts both low- and high-powered DC input, which means you get up to 3,000 watts of solar power if you have enough panels to achieve that.

There’s also a port connection for adding up to five expansion batteries, potentially increasing the total battery capacity to as much as 30,000 watt-hours. That same port can be used to connect to Anker’s Solix 5000 Smart Tri-Fuel Generator for direct DC recharging, which is three times faster than standard AC charging. I had this very generator on hand and was able to test this out. I observed around 4,000 watts of input while the generator was running on gasoline. In an emergency where the power has gone out for several days, you could use this method to fully recharge the S5000 in less than two hours.

The only downside is the maximum total output of 4,500 watts. While that’s perfectly fine for very basic home backup and RV use, it’s not going to power a heating/ventilation/air-conditioning system, let alone a full bank of circuits on a manual transfer switch, no matter how many expansion batteries are attached (they only add capacity, not output). True whole-home backup would require a larger station.

Sometimes, newer power station models are just more of the same, with only minor tweaks to power output, capacity, or outlet configuration. But the Anker S5000’s inverter efficiency technology is a notable upgrade that delivers on its promise of longer runtime than comparable models with the same capacity.

It’s not a contender for true whole-home backup (Anker’s E-10 system is a better option for that) and doesn’t have as much output power as the F3800, but it can bring substantial power during an emergency to several appliances or a couple of critical circuits, and it’s much more portable. And if you’re an RV owner looking for a compact yet powerful station, this should definitely be on your list for consideration.

#6234. Europe’s Hera mission is ready to double down on asteroid science

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Asteroid defense is the mission’s top priority, but there’s also fascinating science to be done.

The Hera spacecraft’s Asteroid Framing Camera captured this black-and-white image of Didymos and Dimorphos from about 60 kilometers away. The photo shows the far side of Didymos compared to the DART impact.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft is about to start a twofold mission to a twofold asteroid.

On November 4, after more than two years trekking through space, the spacecraft finally came within 30 kilometers of space rocks named Didymos and Dimorphos. The encounter marks the first time scientists will explore a pair of asteroids navigating the solar system together. To date, spacecraft have stopped to investigate just seven other asteroids, every one of them a lonely speck in outer space.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Hera will spend the coming weeks approaching Didymos and Dimorphos and will release two small companion spacecraft in January for an even closer look.

Didymos, a mass of rocks about twice as wide as the Empire State Building is tall, and its small moonlet Dimorphos have had a rough time lately. In 2022, NASA slammed its Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft into Dimorphos, sending a plume of debris into space and shortening its orbit around Didymos by more than half an hour.

The cosmic realignment wasn’t a mere lark. Such an impact is one of the few ways scientists can practice planetary defense, the field dedicated to searching for dangerous asteroids and developing ways to deal with them lest humans go the way of the dinosaurs. DART and Hera are a carefully coordinated pair, with Hera’s top priority being to investigate the aftermath of DART’s crash and inform future planetary defense efforts.

That process will also yield a treasure trove of observations asteroid scientists are determined to exploit.

“Planetary defense and science are sort of two sides of the same coin,” says planetary scientist Jessica Sunshine of the University of Maryland, who was on the DART team but is not involved in the Hera mission. On the science side, she says, “we’re trying to figure out not so much how did we break the thing, but how was it put together in the first place.”

DART purposefully targeted a binary system instead of a solo asteroid to make measuring the change in orbit it accomplished easier: Any difference would be much more obvious against the 12-hour baseline orbit of Dimorphos around Didymos than against the months- or yearslong orbit of an asteroid circling the sun. (Despite the difficulty, scientists were able to calculate that DART shortened the more-than-two-year orbit of the Didymos system around the sun by a fraction of a second.)

Hera’s observations will provide a crucial glimpse at binary asteroids generally, which astronomers believe account for some 15 percent of all asteroids. Scientists expect that most binary asteroids in the inner solar system, including the Didymos system, probably formed their moonlets from debris that sloughed off the larger object then clumped together in orbit.

Didymos spins so quickly that its gravity may not be strong enough to hold all its rock together. As the asteroid spins, it may send boulders into space, where they could end up landing on Dimorphos, continuing that material transfer today. Scientists will comb through Hera’s imagery for signs of rocks moving across each object’s surface, as well as between the two objects.

Scientists expect that Dimorphos is a rubble pile composed of boulders and rocky debris. It’s similar in structure to other recent spacecraft targets Ryugu and Bennu, although those are both significantly larger. The boulder-strewn landscape DART saw as it sped toward Dimorphos aligns with this theory, but how deep the rubbly structure extends is a mystery. “We’ve never seen the interior of an asteroid before,” says planetary scientist Angela Stickle of the Johns Hopkins University’s Applied Physics Laboratory.

Juventas, Hera’s companion cubesat about the size of a breadbox, will change that. It carries a first-of-its-kind radar instrument to investigate Dimorphos’ internal structure.

Juventas will also attempt to land on Dimorphos, allowing scientists to directly interact with the surface. That’s a particularly tantalizing endeavor given one of the biggest surprises of NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission. When that spacecraft grabbed a sample of Bennu, it accidentally sank some half a meter into the rubble as the asteroid unexpectedly gave way beneath it, even though the surface had looked perfectly sturdy.

“Even though we had amazing images, the reaction was not what we expected,” says planetary scientist Patrick Michel of the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) of that experience. “There is still sort of a mismatch between what we see and what we feel.” He hopes that the Juventas landing will help scientists better connect appearance and reality on this front.

Although scientists will need to pick out the ways DART made Didymos and Dimorphos different from other binary asteroids, observations with Hera will offer new avenues for investigating more general questions in asteroid science.

For example, scientists know that before DART’s impact, Dimorphos always showed the same face to Didymos, just like our moon does to Earth. The collision probably changed that, sending Dimorphos tumbling — but there’s no way to know what state it’s in now because scientists have never seen this resetting process unfold. “Eventually, the system might stabilize, but we don’t know how long it takes,” says planetary scientist Eva Lilly of the Planetary Science Institute, who is not involved in either mission.

Similarly, scientists know that the rain of charged particles onto an asteroid’s surface darkens a thin layer of rock at the surface, but without the detailed understanding they’d like. At Dimorphos, they’ll be able to observe fresh rock uncovered by a known event, potentially offering clearer insight into the universal process.

Cosmic crash scene or not, asteroid scientists are never going to miss out on up-close views of two different space rocks.

#6233. Scientists used a special CT scanner to crack the secret code that opened a brass lock from a 1583 shipwreck

A brass combination lock from a ship wrecked in Wales in 1583 has given up its four-letter code after a micro-CT scan at Cardiff University.

On the evening of December 28, 1583 (Julian calendar), a storm drove the merchant ship Ann Francis onto Margam Beach near Port Talbot, Wales. Somewhere onboard was a brass combination lock.

Peter Hughes, a metal detectorist, found the lock centuries later among the wreck’s scattered coins. It had stayed locked ever since, and nobody knew the code.

Now Amgueddfa Cymru – Museum Wales says a micro-CT scan at Cardiff University has revealed the code as ANCE. What the four letters meant to the owner, and what the lock protected, remain unknown.

The Ann Francis belonged to Francis Shaxton, a merchant from King’s Lynn in Norfolk. Shaxton’s family ran eight merchant ships by 1582, and the museum’s curator describes father and son as notorious smugglers.

Shaxton claimed the ship had sailed to Hartlepool. According to a Museum Wales account by curator Alastair Willis, it actually left for the Iberian Peninsula in October with a cargo of wheat.

Spain paid for imported grain with gold and silver bullion. The ship was carrying that payment home when it entered the Bristol Channel instead of the English Channel, possibly through a navigation error or strong southerly winds.

The parish register at Wells-next-the-Sea lists 14 sailors lost on the west coast that December, from Richard Waller to Richard Dye.

The register blamed their deaths on a King’s Lynn woman it called Mother Gabley, accused of witchcraft with eggs in a pail of cold water.

Accounts from the Star Chamber court record what happened next. There, the local lord Sir Edward Mansell accused George Williams, Steward of Afan, and 100 others of arming themselves and plundering the wreck.

Williams said the wreckage lay on land belonging to the Earl of Pembroke. Authorities arrested six people with loot, and Williams and Pembroke won the case.

Mansell’s inventory of impounded goods listed cannon, anchors, the ship’s boat, cloves, marmalade, a whistle and 12 pounds 6 shillings of Spanish silver. It also listed three chests with their locks broken.

By March 1584 Shaxton had claimed the wreck, and Mansell agreed to return two anchors, two cables, six cannon and half the money taken from the six looters.

An earlier museum note from 2007 says the silver coins were obsolete types, effectively bullion meant for recoining at the London Mint.

Objects from the wreck began turning up on the beach in the 1970s, including navigational compasses, coins and a bosun’s whistle. Local historians, archaeologists and curators linked them to the Ann Francis between the 1970s and the 1990s.

Hughes found most of the hoard over 21 years, from 1996 to 2017, after dredging and storms stripped sand from the beach.

The museum recently acquired about 870 gold and silver coins from his finds, along with personal belongings, ship’s equipment and kitchenware.

Over 120 Mexican silver coins have been found on the beach. Most of the silver carries the names of Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain, and German talers, Portuguese gold and an Elizabeth I sixpence dated 1580 turned up too.

The lock lay among a scatter of silver coins. Hughes, the finder, recalled moving its rings for the first time. They “turned with ease after over 400 years beneath the sands,” he said in the museum’s statement.

In the Conwy Valley of North Wales, a CT scan of the Caerhun coin pot showed coins tied up in leather bags before anyone opened it.

Dr. David Williams, a research associate at the Musculoskeletal Biomechanics Research Facility in Cardiff University’s School of Engineering, ran the scan. He built a detailed 3D image of the mechanism and studied how the notches lined up with the letters on each ring.

Williams got the combination that way and did no damage to the brass. Back at the facility the usual subjects are bones, so he said the 400-year-old padlock was “certainly a first for us.”

He had to wait until later that evening for the museum team to try the letters on the lock. The message that it opened was “incredibly satisfying,” Williams said.

At the far older Antikythera wreck in Greece, X-ray tomography of the Antikythera mechanism exposed inscriptions hidden inside the fragments.

Willis, Senior Curator for Numismatics and the Welsh Economy at Amgueddfa Cymru, said Elizabethan combination locks are known in Britain. This one is in exceptionally good condition and is associated with a dated wreck.

The museum offers no reading of the word ANCE. Willis said the team is “left wondering if the code meant something to its owner.”

The museum has published no paper on the scan, and its statement gives no scan settings or date beyond the year 2026. It also does not say which year of the 21-year search produced the lock.

The chest that the lock belonged to has not been identified. The press statement says it may have held valuable items that have not survived, such as documents or textiles. Willis wrote that it was perhaps one of the coffers on Mansell’s inventory.

The lock is on show in Tides of Treasure, a free display running until June 2027 at the National Waterfront Museum in Swansea. Gold coins from the reign of Ferdinand and Isabella and a boatswain’s whistle from the wreck sit in the same display.

The Welsh Government backed the purchase. Wales scheduled the wreck site under the Historic Environment (Wales) Act 2023, and Willis wrote that metal detecting there now needs consent from Cadw.

In March 2025 the French Navy found a likely 16th-century merchant ship off Ramatuelle, at more than 8,421 feet (about 2,500 meters).

The ring dials Hughes moved after more than 400 years are now on display in Swansea, and the museum still cannot say why anyone chose ANCE.

The information was obtained from Amgueddfa Cymru – Museum Wales.

A genetic analysis has identified two previously unrecognized species of howler monkey that change these primates' evolutionary tree.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have identified two newfound species of howler monkey in the Amazon rainforest. The discoveries could redraw branches of these primates' evolutionary tree, a new study shows.

The new species were named Alouatta iroi and Alouatta matogrossensis. The adorable creatures have bushy beards, winsome expressions and bright red fur. Their identification raises the number of known howler monkey species to 16, researchers said in a statement.

"Our study shows that the Amazon still holds remarkable biological secrets, even among well-known animals such as howler monkeys," study first author Romina Batista, a biodiversity scientist at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden and the University of Salford in the U.K., said in the statement.

One of the newfound species, A. matogrossensis, is probably on the brink of extinction. The other newfound species faces threats from a planned dam on the Rio Branco River, according to the study.

In addition to identifying the new species, the study, published Oct. 30 in the journal Communications Biology, used genetic evidence to understand when howler monkeys spread out and diversified. The researchers analyzed the genomes of 11 howler monkey species living in South and Central America, combining existing DNA datasets with new genomic information from specimens in Brazilian zoological collections.

The newfound howler monkey species Alouatta iroi, photographed in Guiana.

Overall, the genetic data confirmed that howler monkeys diverged from close relatives between 19 million and 13.5 million years ago. But the analysis changed the picture of more recent evolution.

For instance, the team argued that the Tapajós red-handed howler (A. tapajozensis) and the Amazonian black howler (A. nigerrima) are not as closely related as scientists previously thought. The researchers also said that the Trinidad howler (A. insulanus), whose status has been unclear, should be confirmed as a separate species.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"This discovery comes at a critical time, as increasing deforestation, climate change and habitat loss threaten many Amazonian species before they are fully understood or even discovered by science," study co-author Jean Boubli, a professor and chair of primate ecology and evolution at the University of Salford in the U.K., said in the statement.

The scientists found that natural barriers such as the Amazon River, the Xingu River and the Branco River drove many howler monkeys to develop separately. Researchers believe that howler monkeys can swim across small waterways, but big rivers block groups from mixing, which led to different traits and species evolving over time. Natural barriers are a common reason why species emerge in the Amazon, the researchers noted in the study.

#6231. Nov. 13, 1971: Mariner 9 orbits Mars

On May 30, 1971, Mariner 9 launched, setting off on its mission to Mars. On Nov. 13, 167 days later, it entered orbit around Mars, making it the first spacecraft to orbit another planet.

With Mariner 8, Mariner 9 was one half of the Mars 71 mission. But when Mariner 8 launched on May 9, it failed to achieve orbit and tumbled out of the sky after five minutes, crashing into the Atlantic Ocean. As a result, Mariner 9 inherited all of 8’s goals in addition to its own, giving it an extensive list of objectives: surface mapping, atmospheric monitoring and analysis, surface data collection, and returning around 3,000 photographs.

When Mariner 9 arrived at Mars, it encountered a global dust storm. Because it had been designed for longevity, the orbiter was able to wait out the storm and begin its mission afterwards. (Soviet spacecraft Mars 2 and Mars 3 did not fare as well.) Over the course of about a year, Mariner 9 returned 7,329 photos and mapped 85% of the martian surface. It also revealed a dynamic and active world – including shield volcanoes, dry river valleys, ice at the martian poles – and gave researchers close-up views of the surfaces of Phobos and Deimos.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

#6230. Venus flytraps have no muscles, yet their ‘mouths’ snap shut on their prey in less than a second

Researchers solved how Venus flytraps catch bugs without muscles. The plant actually softens its outer cell walls in seconds to release stored energy and snap shut.

Even without a single muscle, the popular Venus flytrap (Dionaea muscipula) can snap its jaws shut on an insect in a split second.

For decades, researchers thought the plant pulled off this quick trick simply by rushing water from one side of its leaf to the other.

In France, a team of scientists wanted to settle this debate once and for all. They tested living traps and found that water moves far too slowly to close a trap that fast.

Instead, the team found the cause in the trap’s cell walls. Every plant cell is wrapped in a stiff wall. When an insect sets off the trap, the walls on its outer surface soften within seconds.

The softening releases energy stored in the leaf.

So the plant moves by changing how stiff its own tissue is. The study’s authors wrote that this way of moving had not been recognized in plants before.

Jeongeun Ryu, Yoël Forterre, and three colleagues at Aix-Marseille University and CNRS, France’s national research organization, ran the experiments. The team doesn’t yet know what makes the walls soften so quickly.

Each trap is a leaf with two lobes joined along a central rib. The trap closes when an insect touches its sensitive hairs twice within a short time, and each touch sends an electrical signal across the leaf.

Open lobes curve outward, and closed lobes curve inward. The switch is sudden, the way an umbrella flips inside out in a gust.

Forterre co-authored a 2005 study that found the flip releases energy stored in the curved leaf.

But something has to bend the lobes far enough to start the flip. The cause of that first bend had been unknown since Charles Darwin’s time.

To watch the bend without the flip, the team sliced the lobes of 11 traps into thin strips, which can bend but can’t snap.

The sliced traps took about 3 seconds to close. In an uncut trap, the flip itself takes about a fifth of a second.

In 10 uncut traps clamped open against a force sensor, the push from the triggered lobes built up over about 4 seconds.

So the plant’s own bending is the slow part. The lobes only have to bend partway before the stored energy snaps the leaf shut.

Under the old explanation, the plant moves water across the leaf once the trap is triggered. The outer side swells, and the lobes bend inward.

Direct evidence for that water movement had been hard to find, so the team timed it. They measured the pressure inside 14 leaf cells and found that water needs about 3.7 seconds to move through one cell.

The leaf is only about 0.02 inches (0.5 millimeters) thick, roughly five sheets of printer paper. But water has to cross 5 to 10 layers of cells, and by the team’s calculation that would take 30 to 150 seconds.

In a second test, the team moved strips of trap tissue from a concentrated solution into a weaker one, and the strips absorbed water. The team timed how fast the strips swelled and bent.

Using 48 strips from six traps, they calculated that water needs 38 seconds on average to cross the leaf.

Yet the lobes bend in 3 to 4 seconds. In both tests, water needed about 10 times that long, or longer, to cross the leaf.

And the flytrap’s cells aren’t unusually watertight. Their membranes let water through nearly as fast as any plant cell on record.

For decades, a second explanation held that the trap closes because its cell walls loosen or soften. It lacked direct evidence too.

Each lobe is covered on both sides by a thick, stiff layer of cells.

The team held traps open with silicone paste and pressed a fine probe into single cells on both layers, measuring each cell’s stiffness before and after triggering.

On the inner layer, almost nothing changed. On the outer layer, the cells lost nearly a third of their stiffness and stayed softer for at least an hour.

The team pressed the probe about 300 times per layer, across 10 traps. After a single touch, which doesn’t close the trap, the cells didn’t soften.

But the readings were taken several minutes after triggering, too late to tell whether the softening came before the bend.

So Forterre tracked stiffness as each trap was triggered. Each trap was held so still that it could move only about a ten-thousandth of an inch (a few microns).

In five traps, the outer cells softened within seconds of triggering, about as fast as the lobes bend.

The close match suggests the softening causes the bend, the authors wrote. They called the softening “likely the fastest mechanical shift reported to date in plant cell walls.”

A cell can lose stiffness in two ways. The water pressure inside it can fall, or the wall around it can soften.

The probe alone can’t easily tell the two apart. But a cell that loses pressure bulges less, and a cell whose wall softens bulges more.

So the team made molds of the outer surface of five traps, before and after triggering, and scanned the molds. After triggering, the cells bulged about 8% more.

The extra bulge was only a few millionths of an inch (several tens of nanometers). The team took it as direct evidence that the softening came from the walls, not from lost pressure.

Using computer simulations of a single cell, the team estimated that the wall lost roughly 30% to 40% of its stiffness.

While the trap is open, the team explained, cells inside the lobe are swollen with water, and their pressure stretches both surface layers.

When the outer layer softens, it stretches more than the inner layer, and the lobe bends inward.

No water has to cross the leaf, at least at first. The amount of bend the team calculated from that softening agreed with the bend measured in the sliced traps.

In a commentary published with the study, Jacques Dumais of Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez in Chile described the softening as a kind of fast growth. Dumais did not take part in the experiments but co-authored the 2005 paper with Forterre.

Plants grow by letting their cell walls relax, Dumais wrote. The flytrap does the same thing, only far faster than a plant normally grows.

Dumais also compared the flytrap with related plants. Sundews take 60 seconds or more to bend their sticky hairs over a trapped insect.

The hairs are thin enough, and the movement slow enough, for ordinary growth to explain it.

Waterwheel plants, the flytrap’s closest relatives, close much smaller traps in 0.02 to 0.05 seconds. The part of a waterwheel trap that bends is only three cells thick, and that thinness lets the trap close so fast.

The commentary also raised a question about evolution: how could a trap this fast arise through trial and error?

“After all, a slow flytrap is not a trap,” Dumais wrote.

Ryu’s team, Dumais added, has filled a large gap in scientists’ understanding of how such a trap could evolve one step at a time.

The experiments show that the outer wall softens. They don’t show what happens inside the wall to soften it.

Calcium is one possible cause. It’s released inside cells when the trap is touched, and it’s known to affect wall stiffness.

But a single touch also sends a wave of calcium across the whole trap, and a single touch didn’t soften the walls. So calcium’s role may be indirect, the authors wrote.

The probe has a limit, too. It mainly detects elastic changes, the kind a wall can spring back from. A slower, lasting loosening of the wall could go undetected.

Water isn’t fully ruled out, either. The measurements show that water crossing the whole leaf can’t be the main driver, Dumais wrote, but water could still move over shorter distances.

The authors suggested engineers could copy the approach in soft robots, with parts that change stiffness to release stored energy. The team didn’t build or test any device.

Researchers still need to find what changes inside the wall as it softens. Future research could use newly developed, genetically altered flytraps to trace the signals that lead to the softening.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

#6229. The 7 Best Electric Stoves to Upgrade Your Kitchen

These expert-picked models cook cleaner than gas, and offer features like convection and air fry.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Electric stoves burn cleaner and more efficiently than gas—in fact, per the Department of Energy, they’re about three times more energy-efficient than their gas counterparts. They’re also more straightforward to install—no gas line needed—and often feature flat, easy-to-clean, glass-ceramic cooktops. Plus, their ovens preheat quickly and provide even and consistent heat, which is ideal for anyone who loves to bake. No wonder electric stoves have become the go-to for the majority of households in the U.S.

Electric stoves and ranges come in a wide range of sizes and styles, and many models even have high-tech features such as convection baking, air frying with more room for food than countertop models, and Wi-Fi connectivity. These stoves make a great addition to any kitchen as they’re versatile, reliable, and often quite affordable, too. Plus, some even qualify for a tax rebate.

We rounded up the best of the best, so when you're ready to replace your existing electric stove—or switch from gas—you’ll know just what you need.

Frigidaire makes several lines of well-regarded electric stoves. This 30-inch freestanding model strikes a balance between affordability and modern features like air fry, standard convection, and a user-friendly mix of four stove-top control knobs and an oven touch screen. It’s also available as a slide-in version.

The spacious oven ensures even baking and roasting, with ample room between pans. It also lets you switch between standard baking and convection, making it ideal for those new to convection cooking. The built-in air fry function delivers crisp results without excess oil, and many customers report the fan is surprisingly quiet.

There are a few minor drawbacks: While the storage drawer is roomier than some, it feels quite flimsy. And you’ll need to purchase the air fry tray separately. Still, for the price, it’s hard to beat. For a step up, the brand’s Gallery range has a fifth knob, synchronized burner, and European convection at a slightly higher price point.

Outfit your kitchen on a budget with this freestanding electric range from GE. The no-frills 30-inch model has coil burners and limited features, but it still performs reliably, earning high praise from reviewers.

The stove delivers the power you want and offers decent oven capacity with 5 cubic feet of space. Dual bake elements in the oven provide more-even cooking. There’s also a full-width storage drawer at the bottom. If you just need your electric stove to handle the essentials at a low price point, look no further. It's also available in a white finish.

This LG range is a smart, energy-efficient pick that pairs a two-speed fan with a powerful rear heating element to preheat faster and bake more evenly across multiple racks. A built-in air fry feature can crisp up wings, fries, and veggies with no preheating, and the roomy 6.3-cubic-foot oven can easily accommodate large dishes, including a 20-pound turkey and the sides.

The five-burner cooktop has a 3,200-watt element that take dishes from a rapid boil to a simmer, with flexible 2-in-1 elements to fit everything from a small saucepan to your largest sauté pan. Wi-Fi and the LG ThinQ app let you preheat, adjust, and monitor the oven from your phone, or run it hands-free though Alexa or Google. For instance, you can turn a burner off from the other side of your house. It’s also Energy Star-certified, while cleanup is simple thanks to a 10-minute EasyClean cycle and a coating that helps repel spills and stains.

There is no steam-clean option, and the cooktop lacks a control lockout, so it’s not completely kid-proof. Otherwise, LG’s electric range is a solid smart option that makes cooking (and cleaning) easier.

This GE profile range is a top choice for tech-savvy home cooks looking for a sleek, high-performance stove with cutting-edge features. The slide-in model includes no-preheat air-fry mode and built-in Wi-Fi that lets you control oven functions remotely via the SmartHQ app, compatible with Alexa, Google Assistant, iOS, and Android.

The five-burner cooktop offers versatile heating, and includes a 12-inch/9-inch/6-inch power boil element for rapid heating, plus synchronized burners for large cookware and griddles. Inside, European convection ensures even baking and roasting. The fingerprint-resistant stainless-steel finish keeps it looking pristine outside; a 30-minute steam-clean cycle handles messes inside.

All of these bells and whistles make it a pricier option. And, its glide touch controls, which contribute to the stove’s ultra-modern aesthetic, means that every function is operated via touch—much like swiping on an iPad. If you prefer to use physical knobs, this will not be the best fit.

Built for speed and convenience, this freestanding double oven is a great choice for busy kitchens and home chefs who need flexibility, extra cooking space, and power.

Its five burners include a triple-radiant element that adapts to different cookware sizes while the extra-large European convection double oven—at 6.3 cubic feet, one of the largest in this size—ensures faster, even cooking.

A no-preheat setting lets you cook frozen favorites like pizza and lasagna straight from the freezer, saving time on weeknight meals, and a 50-minute steam-cleaning cycle tackles grime. The only downsides? No Wi-Fi or app support, and surprisingly, no air fry.

While most electric stoves on the market span 30 inches, this sleek freestanding GE model maxes out at just 24 inches across—making it a perfect fit for smaller kitchens. Despite its compact size, it doesn’t skimp on functionality: The front controls are easy to reach, the smooth ceramic glass cooktop wipes clean in seconds, and, thanks to its modular backguard, you can choose to install it with a traditional backguard or flip it down to create a slide-in look.

While there are only four burners, no timer, and a smallish standard (not convection) oven, it’s a stylish, efficient choice for studio apartments, small homes, or anyone cooking for one. It also has a 30-minute steam-clean cycle and a built-in storage drawer that’s deeper than many other stoves on the market. (And if your kitchen can handle a standard-sized stove, GE’s 30-inch free-standing range is a solid, very affordable, choice.)

If you need a stove that’s even more compact than the 24-inch GE, the freestanding 19.5-inch Avanti stove offers serious space efficiency and decent functionality at a very low price. Available in stainless or white, it easily tucks into small kitchens, RVs, and tiny homes. Plus, its retro aesthetic adds a vintage touch.

The four old-school coil burners—three 6-inch and one 8-inch—feature chrome reflector bowls and temperature safety sensors for efficient cooking. While they lack the modern sleekness of a glass cooktop, users report they heat up fast. Inside, the 2.1 cubic feet of oven capacity is roomy enough for one-pan baking and roasting and comes with a broiling pan.

That said, this stove is as basic as it gets. It’s perfect for simple fry-ups and one-pan roasts, but serious home cooks will definitely want more precision and features. If size is your limiting factor, Avanti also makes a more-expensive 19.5-inch glass-top electric stove, which some users say is worth the extra cost, as it provides more even contact with cookware for better heat distribution.

Size can be a significant limiting factor, so measure your stove space first. The standard width for ranges is 30 inches, but if you’re outfitting an apartment kitchen, tiny home, or RV, you’ll want to focus on the few narrower models available.

Next, choose your style: Freestanding stoves have finished sides and back guards, allowing them to stand alone. Slide-in models are designed to sit between cabinets for a seamless look; their stovetops typically sit flush to the back wall, which may require a backsplash update. Drop-in ranges need a custom cabinet base for installation.

Most electric cooktops feature smooth surfaces with heating elements housed beneath tempered glass or ceramic, though traditional coil-style options still exist and tend to be much cheaper. Smooth-top stoves are easier to clean, while coil burners are simpler to replace if one fails.

Standard electric ranges typically come with five burners (four on narrower models). One is often a warming burner, useful for timing multiple dishes. Some models also offer bridge elements—also referred to as "synchronized burners"—which link two burners, handy for griddles or oversized pots. If you frequently boil water, look for one with an express boil burner, designed to heat up faster.

Conventional ovens rely on stationary heating elements—one at the bottom for baking, one at the top for broiling—leading to natural heat rise and possible temperature variations. Standard convection improves on this by adding a fan to circulate hot air for more even cooking. European convection (also called “true” convection) goes a step further, with a third heating element behind the fan for uniform heat distribution across multiple racks.

For everyday cooking, conventional or standard convection works fine. But if you want more precise, even baking and roasting, true convection is worth considering. Be prepared for a slight learning curve if switching to convection, as most recipes are designed for conventional ovens. A good rule of thumb: reduce the temperature by 25°F (e.g., 450°F to 425°F, or 375°F to 350°F), or keep the same temperature but cut the cooking time by about 25 percent. Either way, start checking for doneness earlier than the recipe suggests. A meat thermometer can also help ensure accuracy.

Control panel placement affects both aesthetics and functionality. Backguard controls, found on most freestanding stoves, keep buttons and knobs safely out of reach of children but may be less visually streamlined. Front-control stoves, common in slide-in models, offer a sleek, built-in look and easier access to settings but can be a hazard if you have small kids or frequently lean against the stove while cooking. Many models now include touchscreen controls, which allow for precise adjustments and smart features but may require more care to keep clean.

Many newer electric stoves come with high-tech features designed to make cooking more efficient and hands-free. Wi-Fi-enabled models let you monitor and control your oven remotely via an app—preheating, adjusting temperatures, and setting timers from anywhere. Some even integrate with voice assistants like Alexa or Google Assistant for hands-free commands.

Touchscreen controls and digital displays offer a sleek, modern look, but keep in mind that they can be more finicky than traditional knobs, especially when wet or smudged. If you prefer a more tactile experience, look for models with physical dials or a hybrid control panel.

Some ovens now include built-in air fry functions, which circulate superheated air for crispy, fried-like results without the oil. It’s a great feature for quickly roasting veggies, crisping up frozen snacks, or making healthier versions of fried favorites—no extra countertop appliance needed.

Beyond the sticker price, you’ll want to factor in some extra costs. For one, power cords aren’t usually included in the price, and you can’t reuse your old one. Lowe’s, for example, charges $39.98 to install—which includes a new power cord. Some retailers also charge a separate delivery fee. And, if you’re replacing an existing stove, you should expect to pay around $50 to have your old one hauled away and disposed of. Finally, while most stoves come with a one-year limited warranty (which typically covers manufacturing defects and basic repairs), some retailers offer extended protection plans (for an additional fee) at checkout.

When the glass top of my ancient JennAir electric stove cracked—thanks to a DIY mishap (we stood on it to paint a high part of the kitchen; lesson learned)—I had to find an unplanned replacement. Fortunately, the stovetop still worked, giving me time to explore my options. I visited my local Lowe’s and other reputable retailers to assess everything in person and quickly noticed a difference in selection. Suburban stores only carried standard 30-inch ranges, while city retailers stocked a wider variety, including smaller 24-inch models—something to keep in mind if you’re shopping for a compact space.

I assessed everything: control placement (knobs vs. touchscreen and ease of use), oven heating methods, aesthetics, and extra features like voice control (we’re a household that regularly asks Alexa for help in the kitchen). The models I selected come from trusted brands like GE, Samsung, and Frigidaire, with thousands of positive reviews attesting to their reliability and efficiency. Many are top-sellers across multiple retailers, and some incorporate the latest technology to make cooking faster and more enjoyable. I also chose options across various sizes and price points to fit different spaces and budgets—and included a few solid upgrade picks from the same brands for a slight price increase.

Arabella Bowen is a seasoned product tester who specializes in travel, design, tech, home improvement, and outdoor essentials. She’s reviewed everything from roller bags and cameras to hiking equipment and home decor for outlets such as The Montreal Gazette, Fodor's, AFAR, and US Park Pass. Arabella can often be found immersed in DIY projects at her mid-century modern house in upstate New York—a hands-on pursuit that inspires many trips to Lowe’s.

#6228. Four French teenagers climbed down a hole and found cave paintings that are 17,000 years old

Discovered by four teenagers in 1940, France's Lascaux Cave holds hundreds of prehistoric Ice Age paintings.

On September 12, 1940, four teenagers slid down a narrow shaft on a hill above Montignac, in southwestern France. At the bottom, they found the painted cave of Lascaux.

The cave contains hundreds of prehistoric animal paintings and engravings. Radiocarbon results on charcoal from the cave first came out at about 15,500 to 17,200 years, though the art is now thought to be older.

Lascaux closed to visitors in April 1963, after crowds of tourists began to damage its fragile painted walls.

The opening was a foxes’ den halfway up the hill. A local legend said it led to an underground passage to the Lascaux manor.

Marcel Ravidat, a young apprentice mechanic, made the first attempt to explore it, as the French Ministry of Culture recounts in its history of the discovery. He had to put it off for lack of the right tools.

Four days after his first attempt, Ravidat returned with the necessary tools. The group enlarged the opening, allowing him to slip down a small vertical shaft.

He landed on a cone of rubble and slid to the bottom, and his three friends followed. By the light of a hastily made lamp, they walked along a gallery about 100 feet (30 meters) long.

As the passage narrowed, they spotted the first paintings, in what is now called the Axial Gallery.

The next day, the boys brought a rope, and Ravidat lowered himself down a shaft about 26 feet (8 meters) deep. There he found a scene of a man facing a bison.

All four discoverers were teenagers. Ravidat, from Montignac, was 17, and Jacques Marsal, also from Montignac, was 15.

Simon Coencas, 15, had taken refuge in the town. Georges Agniel, 16, was from Nogent-sur-Seine and was on vacation at his grandmother’s house.

The boys told their teacher, Léon Laval, who went into the cave on September 18. Prehistorian Henri Breuil, who had taken refuge in the region, visited soon after to authenticate the figures.

Photographer Fernand Windels began documenting the cave the following month, under Breuil’s direction.

Ravidat and Marsal guarded the entrance during the winter of 1940 to 1941. Both later became guides at the cave.

The four friends were not reunited until November 1986, 46 years after their discovery.

All of the accessible parts of Lascaux add up to no more than about 770 feet (235 meters). The cave is traditionally divided into seven sectors, including the Hall of the Bulls, the Nave and the Shaft.

Horses are by far the most common animals on the walls, followed by equal numbers of stags and aurochs, then ibexes and bison.

The few carnivores, such as bears and felines, appear in the farthest corners of the cave. The only human-like figure is in the Shaft scene.

Lascaux also holds many Ice Age engravings, which the prehistorian Father André Glory studied from 1952 to 1963. He identified 286 figures in the Passageway, most of which he recorded, and 87 in the Chamber of the Felines.

Deciphering and recording the roughly 600 figures of the Apse required prolonged visits.

In 1951, charcoal from the Shaft gave a radiocarbon result of 15,516 ± 900 years, equated with about 19,000 years before present.

Glory’s charcoal later returned 17,190 ± 140 and 16,000 ± 500 years, or between 21,000 and 18,000 years before present, according to the ministry’s review of the dates.

In 1998 and 2002, dates on reindeer antler from earlier excavations pushed the estimate back to between 23,500 and 22,000 years before present.

A newer radiocarbon program on reindeer bone places the occupation of the cave slightly later, between 21,500 and 21,000 years ago.

The results remain puzzling: some artifacts have Magdalenian characteristics, while the painting style looks Solutrean. Both are cultures of the late Ice Age.

Work to open the cave to the public was completed in 1948. Before its closure, Lascaux received up to 1,800 visitors a day, according to the regional cultural affairs office.

The ever-increasing numbers of tourists were raising carbon dioxide levels inside. Ravidat and Marsal pointed out the appearance of green algae in 1958 and 1959.

Max Sarradet, the cave’s curator, alerted Culture Minister André Malraux to the danger from 1960. On Sarradet’s advice, Malraux closed the cave on April 20, 1963, and Marsal became its guardian.

Lascaux II, a replica of the Hall of the Bulls and the Axial Gallery, opened in 1983 and has since drawn ten million visitors. Another replica, Lascaux IV, has welcomed visitors since 2016.

As of 2020, research and monitoring inside the original cave were limited to fewer than 200 hours a year. The Apse remained the most sensitive area.

The information was obtained from the French Ministry of Culture.

#6227. REVIEW: Spectrum Optics SkyPilot 127

The smart telescope revolution has grown rapidly over the past few years. Most of these scopes focus primarily on electronic imaging, though, and while amateur astronomers may marvel at the images, they also still enjoy the simple pleasure of looking directly through a telescope.

That’s where the SkyPilot 127 from Spectrum Optics ($999) takes a different approach. Rather than replacing direct observing with a screen-based experience, the SP127 combines a traditional 5-inch (127 millimeters) f/15 Maksutov-Cassegrain telescope with a smart guidance and imaging system.

At first glance, the SP127 looks like a conventional catadioptric with a standard finder on a motorized alt-azimuth mount. But looks can be deceiving.

The secret lies in that “finder.” On closer inspection, it is not a finder at all, but a 2.1-inch (53 mm) f/4 ED refractor outfitted with a digital camera. This second optical tube is the heart of the SP127’s electronically assisted system, serving as both guide scope and imager. The guide scope determines the telescope’s position through plate solving, slews to selected targets, maintains tracking, and captures images. Spectrum Optics also includes the same intelligent camera and 53 mm refractor in its separately sold SPi53 Smart Telescope system.

The camera is built around a Sony IMX662 CMOS color sensor with 2.9-micrometer pixels and a resolution of 1920×1080 pixels. It includes 64 gigabytes of onboard storage.

The MirroSky app, available for iOS and Android, is central to the SP127’s operation. It controls target selection, image capture, live stacking, and display, while the guide scope and camera work together to find objects and produce live-stacked images.

Meanwhile, the Maksutov is dedicated primarily to visual observing. The optical tube weighs approximately 6.5 pounds (2.95 kilograms) and measures 14.6 inches (370 mm) long. A Vixen-style dovetail makes it easy to remove the optical tube from the mount. Total weight for the assembled SP127 is about 26 pounds (11.8 kg).

In addition to the guide scope/imager, the SP127 comes with a 25 mm Plössl eyepiece, a 90° 1¼” star diagonal, a screw-on visual back, an adjustable tripod with steel legs 1.5 inches (3.8 centimeters) in diameter, cables, an AC adapter, and a Bahtinov focusing mask for the guide scope. The camera’s nosepiece is also internally threaded to accept standard 1¼” filters.

In its standard configuration, the included camera photographs through the 53 mm refractor rather than the Maksutov. Although the camera is removable, Spectrum Optics recommends a separate camera for imaging through the Maksutov because its long focal length and narrow field are not well-suited to the included camera’s plate-solving system. That doesn’t mean you have to invest in more equipment, though; I took some very nice shots of the Moon simply by holding my iPhone to the Mak’s 25 mm eyepiece.

The SP127’s hybrid arrangement works well in practice. After the user selects a target in the app, the guide scope directs the mount to the correct location, then tracks the sky. The observer can view the target visually through the Maksutov while the guide scope stacks and displays images via the app. A word of caution, however: Be careful not to shake the instrument when looking through the eyepiece. Even a slight motion will blur the image being photographed.

Like most Maksutov-Cassegrain systems, the SP127 excels at medium and high magnifications. Its 1,900 mm focal length is especially well-suited for observing the Moon, planets, planetary nebulae, and double stars.

Spectrum Optics MirroSky SkyPilot SP127 Primary Optical Tube: 5-inch 127mm Maksutov-Cassegrain Focal Length: 1900mm Length: 14.6 inches (370 mm) Focal Ratio: f/15 Guide Scope Optical Tube: 53mm ED refractor with Sony IMX662 CMOS camera Focal Length: 200mm Focal Ratio: f/4 Assembled Weight: 26 lbs. (11.8 kg) Mount Payload: 9 lbs. (4 kg) Connectivity: built-in Wi-Fi, 2.4 and 5 GHz Camera Storage: 64GB onboard storage Tripod: Full-size adjustable steel-leg tripod Eyepiece: 25mm Plössl Price: $999.99 Contact: Spectrum Optics 2175 S Grand Ave Santa Ana, CA 92705 1-888-879-5143 spectrumoi.com

For this review, I arranged to receive a sample SP127 directly from Spectrum Optics. It arrived securely packed and in perfect condition.

Setup was easy, thanks to the well-illustrated paper manual that came with the scope. After I aligned the guide scope with the Maksutov during the day, as the instructions suggested, the scope was ready to go. I had everything together in under half an hour.

Control is handled entirely through the MirroSky app. To initialize the scope to the sky, the system uses onboard sensors combined with date, time, and location information supplied by the connected smart device. The camera includes dual-band Wi‑Fi capability supporting both 2.4 and 5 gigahertz connections. During use, the app’s interface was straightforward and easy to navigate. Target acquisition was quick and accurate. Chosen objects were always centered in the field of view. The app also provides guided tours and a database containing more than 100,000 stars, solar system members, and deep-sky sights.

Tracking performance was accurate for visual observations and short-exposure imaging. Since the SP127 uses an alt-azimuth mount, field rotation may become evident around the edges with longer exposures.

The SP127 can be powered by eight user-supplied AA batteries in the mount, a suitable external 12-volt power source, or the included AC adapter.

I found that the Maksutov performed very well. Lunar views were well-defined, with crater walls, rilles, and other surface features standing out crisply. I was especially impressed when, in moments of steady seeing, the SP127 detected a few of the craterlets on the floor of Plato. It passed another tough test by resolving Schröter’s Valley, a sinuous rille near craters Aristarchus and Herodotus.

Planetary performance also proved impressive. Multiple cloud bands as well as the Great Red Spot were clearly visible on Jupiter, and shadows cast by Galilean moons could also be seen on the planet’s cloud tops.

Double stars were another strong point, thanks to the long focal length. The Trapezium in the Orion Nebula, for instance, was striking. The included eyepiece did well, but the view really sparkled when I swapped in my own eyepieces with shorter focal lengths.

Throughout it all, I was very impressed with the crispness of the images, showing the high quality of the Maksutov’s optics. Like most catadioptric telescopes, the SP127 focuses by moving the primary mirror. This takes tight manufacturing tolerances to maintain a precise focus without tilting the mirror. I found that alignment stayed spot-on after swapping eyepieces and refocusing the view.

I was equally impressed with the imaging results using the 53 mm guide scope. The app allows you to customize settings, including gain, exposure length, number of frames to capture, and dark frames. After I experimented with the settings, the Orion Nebula appeared in vivid color after only two minutes of exposure, even as it was setting in my light-polluted sky. The Pleiades also recorded beautifully, although not all members squeezed into the guide scope’s approximately 1.6° by 0.9° field. The Horsehead Nebula, the Whirlpool Galaxy, the Great Globular Cluster in Hercules, and more displayed details exceeding what you might expect from such a small aperture, especially after post-processing using apps like PixInsight, GIMP, and Photoshop.

The SkyPilot 127 is one of the most original entries in today’s smart telescope market. For observers who still enjoy looking through an eyepiece but appreciate the convenience of app-driven targeting and imaging, the SP127 offers something genuinely special. In a small but growing group of smart telescopes that combine traditional eyepiece observing with integrated electronic imaging, the SP127’s hybrid design makes it an appealing bridge between conventional astronomy and the smart telescope revolution.

Contributing Editor Phil Harrington received the Walter Scott Houston Award in 2018 for his lifelong work in astronomy.

#6225. A trapped drop of water might be the secret to how brain diseases spread from cell to cell

Scientists found that a tiny pocket of water acts as a hotspot, causing healthy brain proteins to misfold.

Water fills gaps in the brain between molecules, playing an important role by keeping them wet. Yet in the tau protein tangles of Alzheimer’s disease, water marks the exact spot where one damaged tau grabs the next. Letting go of that water is what pulls the two tau molecules together.

Researchers at Northwestern University and the University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB) found this in a short, lab-made piece of tau, not in a brain.

In a test tube, the fragment latched onto a growing tau fiber at one spot first. A chemical cap placed on that one spot left the fibers barely growing.

“We might have found a shortcut for the pharmacist or biochemist because instead of searching for everything, we can say, ‘Look for that hotspot. That’s the spot that matters,'” said Songi Han, the study’s senior author, who runs a chemistry lab at Northwestern.

Healthy tau is a floppy protein with no fixed shape that helps keep the tiny support tubes inside a neuron stable. In Alzheimer’s disease and related conditions, tau folds wrongly and stacks into long fibers.

Those fibers pile up inside neurons as the tau tangles that a brain scan may spot before symptoms appear, and a blood test may flag years earlier.

When a neuron dies, the fibers spill out. A fiber’s loose end can then grab healthy tau nearby and bend it into the same wrong shape. That is how the damage spreads from cell to cell, though some neurons resist it.

Copying a shape that precisely was the puzzle. A floppy molecule has no obvious way to land in the same alignment thousands of times over.

Full-length tau is too unruly to watch, piece by piece, so Han’s team used a slice of it. The slice is 19 amino acids – the building blocks of a protein – long, and it comes from the region where tau fibers form their core.

One block, at position 301, is changed in a way known to speed up clumping, and in earlier work fibers made from the slice recruited full-length tau.

The team mixed fresh fragments with fibers made in advance. Clumping began the moment the two met and leveled off after about two hours. Fragments with no fibers to join didn’t clump at all in the same period.

To see which part of the fragments grabbed the fiber first, the team tagged seven of its 19 positions with heavy forms of carbon and nitrogen.

A magnetic resonance machine, a cousin of a hospital MRI scanner, then took a picture of those seven positions about every 15 minutes for 12 hours. A free position shows up in the picture, and one locked into a fiber goes dark.

Position 300 went dark first, and fastest. Positions 301 and 306, its neighbors at the bottom of the fragment’s U-shaped fold, followed. The three positions at the open ends of the U, 308, 309 and 313, lagged well behind.

So the fragment doesn’t fall onto the fiber all at once. It attaches at one spot, and the rest of the chain folds into place afterward.

The team got the same answer with a tiny magnetic tag attached to position 300, 306 or 314 on separate batches of the fragment. As each batch joined fibers, the tag at position 300 slowed down soonest.

Parts of a protein’s surface mix with water easily. Other patches repel it, the way oil does. The water next to those patches arranges itself into a loose, ice-like cap that still keeps moving.

In the team’s computer simulations of a fiber’s end, position 300 showed the largest change in the water around it between the free fragment and the tau fiber.

A second measurement reads how fast water moves next to a magnetic tag. It showed the most slow-moving, ordered water at position 300 as well, with less at positions 306 and 314.

“You have a certain site, and water cannot quite coat it because it doesn’t like water. But that part still needs to be protected, because if you don’t, then the protein crashes out and is no longer available,” Han explained.

“What water tends to do is build a stabilizing cap around it and basically these water caps attract each other.”

When two capped spots meet, the ordered water is set free. Freeing that water releases energy, and that energy is what holds the two tau molecules together, lined up the same way every time.

If position 300 is where joining begins, blocking it should hurt the fiber most.

The team’s magnetic tags doubled as caps, because a tagged fragment that joins a fiber leaves its tag on the fiber’s new end.

After 12 hours, fibers grown from fragments tagged at position 300 looked almost like the starting fibers, in both length and number, under an electron microscope. Fibers tagged at positions 306 or 314 had stretched out well beyond them.

A tag at position 300 still let the next fragment dock, but it stalled the locking step that extends the fiber.

Everything here happened in a tube, to a 19-piece fragment carrying one mutation. Full-length tau in a living neuron can carry chemical add-ons, including phosphate groups, that the fragment lacked.

The team expects the first-contact spot to move as those add-ons and other mutations change the protein’s surface. The point, they wrote, is not position 300 itself but that a growing tau fiber has a dominant first-contact spot at all.

Whether the matching spot on full-length tau can be blocked inside a living neuron, and whether that slows the spread of tangles, are open questions.

The team hopes others can now design molecules that cover the hotspot and stop fibers from growing.

Han also said a disease has to be recreated before it can be cured, and lab-made tau fibers that copy each disease are still hard to make.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#6224. The brain’s fear center moonlights as the save button for memories

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Amygdala neurons activated when people viewed images they later remembered

The amygdala, highlighted in orange, is responsible for regulating emotions like fear and aggression. A new study also reveals its role sorting memories for longer term storage.

KATERYNA KON/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The walnut-sized fear center of the brain also distinguishes the memorable from the mundane.

Neurons in the amygdala act like a save button for memories, scientists report October 27 in Nature Neuroscience. Though the study doesn’t nail down the exact mechanism for memory formation, it points to a broader role for the amygdala within the memory-sorting apparatus.

The study probes an enduring quandary about the mind, says neuroscientist Jiayang Xiao of Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University in Los Angeles. “We forget much of what we experience … only a fraction of the information we encounter becomes a lasting memory,” she says.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Although a role for the amygdala in memory has been suggested before, previous studies that used electrodes reading brain activity through the scalp, or at the scale of thousands rather than individual neurons, captured a blurrier picture. It’s akin to a microphone recording from outside of a stadium, says cognitive neuroscientist Cory Inman at the University of Utah in Salt Lake City, who was not involved in the study.

“You might be able to tell that there’s a game happening. You might be able to tell when somebody scores a touchdown. You might even be able to tell that one side of the stadium is cheering for one team and another side of the stadium is cheering for another team,” but that’s about it, Inman says. The new study is more like a lapel mic pinned on a single fan in terms of scale and what the researchers were able to capture, adding clarity.

The amygdala, which is typically associated with regulating emotions like fear and aggression, has neurons that are challenging to reach, residing in two clusters deep within the brain. Xiao and her colleagues leveraged electrodes previously surgically implanted in more than 90 people with drug-resistant epilepsy to identify where seizures originate. In their new role, the electrodes singled out neurons involved in saving memories.

Patients were shown images of everyday objects belonging to five categories such as food and animals. About 10 to 30 minutes later, they attempted to recall which images were already shown. Xiao and her colleagues found that activity in certain amygdala neurons corresponded with an image being remembered. The image had been earmarked for longer term storage, Xiao says.

Although participants had to recall something from half an hour ago at most and the exact mechanism for saving memories is still unclear, the researchers think there are two main steps of the process. The team showed that individual neurons have a preference for one of the five categories of images. First the image is categorized by the amygdala. Then, the strength of the category neuron response the first time the image is shown dictates whether the image is later recalled.

A better understanding of this mechanism may pave the way for more effective treatments of memory disorders, Xiao says, a medical conundrum for which there are currently no broadly effective treatments.

The hippocampus is typically more directly linked to memory, so “it surprised me that we observe such a clear relationship between memory formation and activity in the amygdala,” Xiao says. By contrast, the correlation between hippocampus neuron activity and image recall was weaker and slightly delayed.

Future work like observing the impacts of stimulating amygdala neurons on memory will help researchers discern if this region can be targeted to improve memory, Xiao says.

For now, the secret to memory’s hidden machinations remains in the shadows.
