#6157. America’s Most Famous Ocean Liner Is Sent to a Watery Grave—and a New Life

In a secluded corner of Mobile, Alabama, past train tracks, deserted lots, and a county jail, sits a treasure of American history: the SS United States. The country’s flagship ocean liner, once proudly painted red, white, and blue, is now faded and marred by rust. Today, rather than sailing the silver swell of Atlantic waves, it sits in the flotsam-filled murk of the Mobile River. Yet even in the ship’s diminished state, I was awestruck by the sheer force of her towering presence when I paid her a visit on a sticky August afternoon. I wondered: What life remained in the SS United States yet?

A view of the SS United States from above

At nearly 1,000 feet long, the SS United States has always occupied a world of superlatives. When she was built in the early 1950s, she was the largest ocean liner ever constructed entirely in the United States, measuring a cool 100 feet longer than the RMS Titanic and boasting five more decks than the doomed British passenger liner. To this day, SS United States still holds the record for the fastest transatlantic crossing by an ocean liner, made on her maiden voyage in July 1952 when she tore from New York City to the United Kingdom in just 3 days, 10 hours, and 40 minutes. She regularly hosted the biggest names of the time, from artistic celebrities like Marilyn Monroe, Salvador Dalí, and Marlon Brando, to former presidents and first ladies like Harry Truman, Dwight Eisenhower, and Eleanor Roosevelt.

Passengers on the maiden voyage included Margaret Truman and Commodore Harry Manning Bridge.

Those glory days did not last. In November 1969, the crew had just disembarked from the ship’s 400th voyage when they were abruptly informed that it had been their last. A perfect storm of affordable passenger jet travel, rising oil and labor costs, and the withdrawal of government subsidies had put the SS United States out of business after only 17 years of passenger travel. She has since spent nearly six decades bouncing from buyer to buyer, searching for a purpose.

Now, the storied liner at last has a new home and calling: She’s becoming the world’s largest artificial reef.

On November 12, the SS United States will be sunk off the coast of Destin, Florida, where she will shelter dozens of species of fish and other marine life, and become a major destination for recreational divers and fishers. I had come to her current home in Alabama for a behind-the-scenes tour of her labyrinthine corridors and expansive decks—one of the last ever above water.

Alex Fogg, the natural resources chief for Destin-Fort Walton Beach tourism, and the mastermind behind the project, was my guide for the day. Despite the blanket-like heat, we both wore long pants, closed-toe shoes, and white safety helmets. “We are going to be on a ship that has holes that have been cut in the floor, and there’s things above your head,” Fogg warned me. “So just be aware of where you’re stepping.”

With that, we walked up a narrow plank leading to a small, rusted steel door on the ship’s towering port side. The light inside was dim, and came only from the gaps where glass windows and portholes once stood. We marched up a narrow spiral staircase to a deck two floors above, where the first-class cabins once were. The doors and walls had long since been removed, but outlines of the floor plans still remained etched into the metal, as did shower and toilet drains, giving an idea of how the poshest passengers lived on board.

We climbed the remnants of a grand staircase, and reached a long indoor promenade deck that was once lined with floor-to-ceiling windows, but is was now exposedopen to the elements. The tour continued past empty lounges where copious martinis were no doubt served, and I imagined the ghosts of jazz bands past playing on now-hollowed-out stages. We passed the captain’s dining room, where the most elite guests took their meals, but now spiders were the only diners. On the bow, I took a photo for scale with the ship’s anchor—the largest I’d ever seen, resembling an ancient vertebra from some prehistoric leviathan. The tour wrapped up with a visit to the engine room, a jumble of pipes, catwalks and rails that were like a steampunk rendition of Chutes and Ladders.

It was surreal to imagine all of this, the entirety of the SS United States, soon underwater, given over to the crustaceans and fishes and sea turtles. Marine life will likely arrive within hours of the ship sinking, Fogg says, but it will probably take at least a year for the ecosystem to fully blossom.

Unlike other parts of Florida, the aquamarine waters off Destin-Fort Walton Beach lack an abundance of reef and other habitat that encourage a greater diversity and population of marine species. But artificial reefs can provide a substitute for these natural features. Thanks in part to Fogg’s leadership, more than 600 artificial reefs, ranging from small blocks of concrete to entire sunken ships, have already been installed in Destin-Fort Walton Beach since 2017, greatly boosting diving and fishing opportunities.

Fogg had been looking for an iconic vessel to become the crown jewel of this program when he received a message from a contractor about the SS United States needing a new home. After Googling the ship, he realized it more than fit the bill. “I was like, ‘Man, I really want that,’” he told me. Despite the suitability of the ship for his needs, he had little idea of how complicated it would be to turn his vision into a reality.

At the time, the ship was in Philadelphia, owned and cared for by a nonprofit organization called the SS United States Conservancy. Some conservancy officers and board members had family ties or personal histories with their group’s namesake vessel, however, and sinking it was, according to Fogg, “not their number one choice.”

Board member Warren Jones, for example, was a passenger in 1961 and 1962. “It was just so unforgettable, sailing past the Statue of Liberty and just thinking, ‘Wow, we are going out to sea!’” Jones told me. He was just eight years old at the time of his sailings, but he still vividly remembers his time on board, including running through the black-and-silver first-class ballroom with his sister, watching Disney movies in the theater, and almost getting blown overboard by the North Atlantic wind.

Jones, like others at the conservancy, originally hoped to find a developer who would refurbish the ship. But after various deals fell through—including one to turn her into a recreational destination at Pier 76 in Manhattan—their choices began to narrow. Fogg and his colleagues’ solution was much better than the alternatives, Jones admitted: “She’s not being scrapped, and she’s not just deteriorating at some pier somewhere.” Still, he said, “bittersweet is the best way to describe my feelings.”

Purchasing the ship from the conservancy was only the first step. Getting her out of Philadelphia was another major feat, requiring a detailed survey and much negotiation with the Coast Guard. After finally arriving in Mobile in March 2025, the ship began an extensive environmental remediation process. The asbestos walls that once made up the cabins had already been removed years before, but a specialized team still had to spend the better part of a year cleaning out around 120 fuel tanks, scraping off loose paint, carting away debris, ripping out the old ventilation system, and responsibly disposing of toxic materials.

The ship’s dozen elevators were also removed, in part because they were covered in grease, but also to aid in sinking the ship efficiently, by opening up a path for the air to escape. “When you deploy a vessel, you want the air to get out very quickly and the water to get in very quickly,” Fogg said. “If not, it’ll weeble-wobble and could potentially end up on its side.”

The sinking will be carried out not with explosives, as was the past norm, but by opening valves connected to huge, disconnected boiler pipes to allow water to flood in. A naval architect on the project calculated that the ship will be fully submerged within 45 minutes after these valves are opened. Fogg and a few others will dive the wreck that very day to survey how she settled and remove mounted IMAX cameras that will capture video of the sinking. By the next day, according to Fogg, eager recreational divers will arrive.

Above the waterline, visitor center exhibits and a land-based museum will also soon keep the ship’s legacy alive, filled with artifacts and stories that the conservancy has carefully preserved. Jones said he takes comfort in the truth that, once again, the SS United States will be a source of wonder and delight for the public. Of his time on board, he said, “It was a real feeling of joy. People were just so happy to be there.”

#6156. Schumer's leadership rival reveals major Senate rule change he'd pursue if elected

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., tells Fox News Digital at What's Next conference that he’s running to lead Senate Democrats because voters called for change.

DENVER — A mile above much of the country, and leagues away from Washington, D.C., Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., is facing a progressive rebellion that threatens his grip on power.

The challenge is being led by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who has served under Schumer since 2017. And he is willing to go further than Schumer ever has on one issue: terminating the filibuster.

Years ago, Schumer tried and failed to narrowly change the Senate’s rule to pass a sweeping voting rights package. Republicans have toyed with it over the last two years, but never pulled the trigger.

SCHUMER'S FORMER ALLY MOUNTS LEADERSHIP CHALLENGE AS DEMOCRATS FACE RARE INTERNAL POWER STRUGGLE

Van Hollen said, "We need democracy in the United States Senate, and that means allowing, ultimately, a majority of senators to answer the call of the American people.

"So, that means 51 votes. So, my personal view has been all along that the filibuster is an anti-democratic … provision. It's not in our Constitution," Van Hollen added.

"It was put in there by senators to enhance their power over the power of the people."

Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., who has led Senate Democrats since 2017, says he has the votes to remain leader and guide the party’s incoming majority. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Van Hollen announced his challenge against Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats for nearly a decade, Thursday night after a listening campaign with Senate Democrats. It presents a rare opportunity for Senate Democrats since there hasn’t been a contested Democratic leadership election since 1994.

Just a week earlier, Van Hollen was mulling higher office, but now he’s giving up a potential bid for the White House in 2028 to do one thing: beat Schumer and grapple with President Donald Trump.

"I’m no longer pursuing that," Van Hollen told reporters at the What’s Next conference in Denver, where Democratic leaders, strategists and activists gathered to debate the party’s direction after its midterm wins.

Van Hollen framed his challenge to Schumer as a response to voters’ calls for change after Democrats’ sweeping wins and President Donald Trump’s policies.

"I did discuss this with Senator Schumer," Van Hollen told Fox News Digital. "We understand that this will be a competition. I think it’s important to give Senate Democrats a choice."

DEMS ADMIT UNCOMFORTABLE ELECTION SWEEP TRUTH AS PARTY DESCEND ON DENVER TO SHAPE 2028 WITHOUT A FRONTRUNNER

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., speaks to reporters at the What’s Next conference in Denver Nov. 13, 2026, as he campaigns to lead Senate Democrats. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News Digital)

Voters "chose change," he said, adding that the Democratic caucus needs "new ideas" and "a different way of governing."

Van Hollen has also criticized Schumer for limiting votes on legislation popular with Democrats, including a bill to boost unions. He said the incoming majority should pass the bills candidates campaigned on and challenge Trump to respond.

"We shouldn’t wait to hear what President Trump may or may not do," Van Hollen said. "We should answer the call of the American people."

Toppling Schumer will be an uphill climb. As the incumbent leader, he has an established network of support and can offer colleagues leadership posts.

Either candidate will need 28 votes in the secret ballot contest expected in early December or 29 if Democrats win Alaska, where ballots are still being counted in the Senate race between Democratic nominee Mary Peltola and incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.

THE MISTAKE NEWLY ELECTED DEMS ADMIT THEY CAN’T AFFORD TO MAKE WITH TRUMP AFTER SWEEPING 2026 WINS

A protest sign calling for Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y. to step aside as Democrats debate who should lead the party. (Amanda Macias/Fox News Digital)

Some What’s Next attendees said Van Hollen could deliver the Senate leadership shake-up they want.

"We definitely want change. We don’t want to go back to the way things have been. This is a turning point for our country," Jenny, a Denver resident, said, adding it was time for Schumer to go.

"This is the time for us to really, really go after what is right for everyone, not the status quo."

Ara, also of Denver, was optimistic about Van Hollen’s chances, saying she believes he already has significant support.

"I think there’s a really good chance," Ara told Fox News Digital. "I think there were a lot of people that were already willing to support him. So I feel very good about this," she added.

Zoe said Van Hollen’s willingness to stand up for his constituents is the kind of fight young people want from their representatives.

"He goes out there, and he puts his body on the line for his constituents. And I think that’s what we’re looking for, the kind of fight we’re looking for from our representatives as young people," Zoe told Fox News Digital.

#6155. United Airlines Passenger Accused Of Storming Cockpit Had Been Deported Twice And Granted Asylum, DHS Says

A passenger accused of claiming to have a bomb and trying to enter the cockpit of a United Airlines flight had previously been deported twice, then received asylum, according to the Department of Homeland Security. The newly disclosed immigration history adds another troubling layer to an incident that thankfully ended with the aircraft landing safely and the suspect in custody.

Rony Alexander Gomez-Alberto, 34, was arrested after United Airlines flight 2174 from Newark (EWR) to New Orleans (MSY) landed on November 9, 2026.

According the Jefferson Parish Sheriff’s Office, Gomez-Alberto allegedly told cabin crew there was a bomb onboard. DHS separately alleges an attempt to enter the cockpit. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said:

“This criminal illegal alien attempted to storm the cockpit, hijack a plane and claimed he had a bomb. Thanks to law enforcement, he is now behind bars. This twice-deported criminal illegal alien was allowed into our country because of a weak asylum system that allowed him to game the system.”

He went on to claim Gomez-Alberto was a “fraudster” trying to scam his way into the USA, but President Trump is cracking down.

The Boeing 737 MAX 9 carried 46 passengers and six crew members. Deputies arrested Gomez-Alberto after arrival, with local booking charges including communicating false information of planned arson and terrorizing. The FAA confirms that the flight landed safely around 11:10 pm following a passenger disturbance and says it will investigate.

The immigration history has attracted considerable attention, and understandably so.

According to DHS, Gomez-Alberto was apprehended after entering the United States illegally in 2011 and again in 2014, and removed following both encounters. A third encounter with Border Patrol occurred near San Ysidro, California, in 2019.

An immigration judge ordered release from custody pending removal proceedings in January 2020. DHS now says an immigration judge subsequently granted asylum. The asylum claim cited fear of persecution for being transgender.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement has lodged a detainer with the local sheriff’s office, which is a a legal notice or hold placed on an individual or property to prevent their release or transfer.

Two deportations followed by another entry and an eventual asylum grant certainly warrant a closer look at the record. What information did the government have? What did the judge consider? Were there warning signs relevant to public safety? Was there anything more than this?

But the reported asylum grant is also an important part of that record. Describing the earlier illegal entries does not, by itself, establish the person’s immigration status at the time of this flight, not that I am trying to defend him here.

DHS has accused Gomez-Alberto of exploiting the asylum system. That may well be the case, but the subsequent alleged conduct aboard an airplane does not establish that the original persecution claim was fabricated…we have not seen the full immigration decision or the evidence considered.

Thus, we need those answers before declaring exactly where the system failed.

Meanwhile, imagine being aboard that flight. A claimed bomb and an alleged attempt to reach the pilots are about as frightening as an onboard disturbance gets.

I am thankful this flight reached New Orleans safely and that law enforcement took the suspect into custody. Whatever the eventual criminal findings or immigration consequences, the allegations concern conduct that could have endangered everyone onboard.

There is no basis here to conclude that United should have refused transportation simply because of his asylum history. If authorities had information that should have prevented boarding, that would be a separate and very important question…

I expect this to be counterproductively politicized, but I also think this person is very sick to engage in such an act.

A United Airlines passenger faces criminal charges following an alleged bomb threat and attempted cockpit intrusion. DHS now says the suspect had been deported twice before receiving asylum based on a claim of feared persecution for being transgender.

That history deserves scrutiny, including a clear account of what officials knew and when. But at least he is in custody and I am grateful the aircraft landed safely and this frightening incident ended without a successful cockpit breach.

The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card

Earn up to $4,300 in travel value when you spend $120,000 in your first 4 months as a cardholder

As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

The  is one of the most recognizable premium travel rewards cards on the market, offering everything from airport lounge access and hotel elite status to a long list of travel and lifestyle statement credits.

But with an $895 annual fee (see rates and fees), it's also a significant investment.

The Amex Platinum offers plenty of opportunities to offset that cost, especially if you travel frequently and can take advantage of its statement credits. However, many of its benefits come with restrictions, and getting the full value requires some effort.

So, who can actually get enough value from the Amex Platinum to justify its annual fee? Let's take a closer look at who should — and shouldn't — consider adding this card to their wallet.

For frequent travelers, airport lounge access is one of the biggest reasons to consider the .

The card offers access to one of the most extensive airport lounge networks available through a credit card, making it especially valuable if you spend a lot of time in airports.

Cardmembers can access American Express Centurion Lounges, receive a Priority Pass Select membership (enrollment required) and visit Delta Sky Clubs when flying on eligible same-day Delta flights. Delta Sky Club access is limited to 10 visits per year unless you spend $75,000 on eligible purchases in a calendar year to unlock unlimited visits. Access is subject to eligibility requirements.

Amex also operates Centurion Lounges at more than 20 airports, so the benefit can be particularly valuable if you live near or frequently connect through an airport with one.

If you travel frequently and would otherwise pay for lounge access, the Platinum could help you save money while making your time at the airport more comfortable. And when combined with the card's other travel benefits and statement credits, lounge access can help make the $895 annual fee easier to justify.

While the is best known for its premium travel benefits, it also offers a growing list of lifestyle statement credits that can help offset its $895 annual fee.

For example, cardmembers can receive up to $400 in Resy statement credits each calendar year (distributed as up to $100 per quarter) at eligible U.S. Resy restaurants* and up to $300 in Lululemon statement credits* (up to $75 quarterly) at U.S. stores (excluding outlets) and online.

The card also offers up to $300 annually in digital entertainment statement credits* (up to $25 monthly) for eligible subscriptions, along with up to $120 annually toward an Uber One membership to fully cover an auto-renewing $96 annual or $9.99 monthly membership*.

If you're already spending money on dining, shopping and entertainment in these categories, the credits can provide meaningful value without requiring you to change your spending habits.

However, many of these benefits are divided into monthly or quarterly credits, so you'll need to keep track of when to use them. The Platinum is a particularly good fit for someone who doesn't mind managing these benefits and can consistently take advantage of them year-round.

Related: How to maximize benefits with the American Express Platinum

The Amex Platinum can also be a valuable addition to your wallet if you regularly stay at Hilton, Marriott or luxury hotels.

Cardmembers receive complimentary Hilton Honors Gold and Marriott Bonvoy Gold Elite status, which can provide benefits such as bonus points on stays and potential room upgrades. You'll also receive Leaders Club Sterling status with The Leading Hotels of the World, a collection of independent luxury hotels. Enrollment is required for select benefits.

Beyond elite status, one of the Platinum's most valuable hotel-related perks is its up to $600 annual lodging statement credit (up to $300 semiannually).

Cardmembers can receive up to $300 in statement credits every six months on eligible prepaid bookings through American Express Travel®, including stays at Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection properties, as well as select Airbnb Luxe stays.

The Hotel Collection and Airbnb Luxe require a minimum two-night stay, and beginning Jan. 1, 2027, Fine Hotels + Resorts bookings will also require at least two nights to qualify for the lodging credit.

Fine Hotels + Resorts bookings also come with valuable benefits, including daily breakfast for two, guaranteed 4 p.m. late checkout, room upgrades when available and a property credit valued at $100.

If you regularly book these types of stays, the lodging credit and additional perks can go a long way toward offsetting the card's annual fee. Just be sure to compare prices with booking directly, since rates through Amex Travel aren't always the lowest.

Related: How to maximize the Amex Platinum hotel statement credit

Chase's unofficial 5/24 rule generally makes applicants ineligible for many Chase cards if they've opened five or more personal credit cards across issuers within the past 24 months.

Travelers who are still eligible for Chase cards may want to prioritize products such as the (see rates and fees) or (see rates and fees) before exceeding that threshold.

If you've already built a collection of Chase rewards cards, the Amex Platinum could be worth considering as your next premium travel card.

The card also earns Membership Rewards points, giving you access to a separate collection of airline and hotel transfer partners that can complement an existing Chase Ultimate Rewards strategy.

Many people just starting in the points world underestimate the stringency of Chase’s 5/24 rule. If you're just getting started with travel rewards and remain under Chase's 5/24 threshold, you may want to think carefully before applying for the Amex Platinum.

Opening the card could count toward your 5/24 total and potentially limit your eligibility for Chase cards in the future. That could mean missing out on valuable welcome offers or benefits from cards you planned to open later.

However, once you get over 5/24, it may be hard to get back under, and there’s a massive opportunity cost in doing so. Having a plan and sticking to it will serve you well in the long term.

Of course, that doesn't mean everyone under 5/24 should avoid the Platinum. If its benefits are a particularly good fit for your travel habits, it may still make sense.

The provides 5 Membership Rewards points per dollar spent on flights booked directly with airlines or with American Express Travel (on up to $500,000 of spending each calendar year, then 1 point per dollar spent).

A card like the or (see rates and fees) may be a better fit because their broader travel earning categories can include eligible third-party airfare bookings.

The offers a long list of statement credits, but that doesn't necessarily mean every cardholder will get enough value from them to justify the $895 annual fee.

Following the card's 2025 refresh, several of its benefits are geared toward specific lifestyle purchases, including dining at Resy restaurants, shopping at Lululemon and purchasing an Oura Ring. (Cardmembers receive up to a $200 Oura Ring statement credit each calendar year. This statement credit applies to ring purchases only and doesn't cover subscriptions. Enrollment is required.)

Many of these credits also come with restrictions. For example, the Resy and Lululemon credits are distributed quarterly, meaning you'll need to use them throughout the year rather than all at once.

If you don't already spend money with these merchants, or you don't want to keep track of multiple credits and enrollment requirements, the Platinum may not be the best fit.

Before applying, carefully consider just how much these credits are worth to you; if they provide little to no value, another Amex card might be a better fit.

Related: 4 different flavors of Amex Platinum — which one is right for you?

Business owners with substantial expenses may find that is a better fit than the personal Platinum.

Although both cards carry an $895 annual fee (see rates and fees), their earning rates and statement credits differ in ways that could make one more valuable than the other.

For example, the Business Platinum earns 2 points per dollar spent on eligible purchases in select business categories and on purchases of $5,000 or more, on up to $2 million in combined eligible purchases per calendar year, then 1 point per dollar.

The Business Platinum also provides up to $1,150 in statement credits per calendar year for U.S. Dell purchases: up to $150 each calendar year and an additional $1,000 statement credit after spending $5,000 on Dell purchases with the same card each calendar year (enrollment required).

You can also access the Pay with Points redemption option on the Business Platinum card, which gets you a 35% bonus for eligible flights with your selected airline using your Amex points (up to 1 million points back per calendar year). This is notably not available on the personal Amex Platinum.

These business-focused benefits may be more useful for someone with significant company expenses, while the personal Platinum may be a better fit for travelers who can maximize its lifestyle credits.

New cardmembers can find out their offer and may be eligible for as high as 175,000 bonus points after spending $12,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, that bonus could be worth up to $3,500, which is nearly four times the card's $895 annual fee.

While this is the card's standard welcome offer, now could still be a good time to apply if you're eligible for an offer you're happy with and can comfortably meet the spending requirement without making unnecessary purchases.

Just make sure you'll also get enough value from the card's ongoing benefits to justify its annual fee beyond the first year.

Related: The best time to apply for Amex cards based on offer history

The offers an impressive lineup of premium travel benefits and statement credits, but its $895 annual fee means it won't make sense for everyone.

For frequent travelers who value airport lounge access and luxury hotel perks, and can consistently use the card's lifestyle credits, there's plenty of potential to get more value than the annual fee.

On the other hand, travelers who prefer straightforward rewards or don't regularly use the card's benefits may find better value with a lower-annual-fee option.

Ultimately, the Platinum is worth considering if its benefits fit your existing spending and travel habits — not because of the total advertised value of its credits.

#6153. A Flight Only Bookable With Points Offers Amazing Winter Sun

I often tell people that the best unkept secret with Avios is, in fact, the Avios app. Separate to the British Airways app, the Avios app allows users to set flight alerts and goals, but also gives a heads up about opportunities before they appear anywhere else.

Case in point: before a press release had even hit my inbox, the Avios app alerted me that an ‘Avios only’ flight had just launched. This isn’t the first time Avios has launched a flight only bookable with points, but it is the first time they’ve done one to CAPE TOWN, during peak winter break time.

British Airways and Avios have collaborated on a flight only bookable with Avios, where every seat on the plane is available for sale with points. First, business, premium and economy, all available using Avios. The flights depart as follows…

As noted, these flights are now bookable and if history repeats itself, they won’t be available for long. This plane only has 8 seats in first, so get in quick! One amazing thing about Avios is that they aren’t just the currency of one airline, but a whopping seven. If you have any points with Finnair, Iberia, Qatar, Aer Lingus, Logainair, Vueling or British Airways you can pool points together to book these flights.

Avios is also a transfer partner of Amex, Bilt, Capital One, Chase and plenty of other global financial institutions, so there should be ample opportunity to convert bank points into Avios and get these booked. Hot tip though, ensure there are seats available before you make your transfer, since this will be a hot commodity.

I love any airline rewarding members with flights entirely bookable with points. What makes this one different is that it’s not some off peak, off season destination. It’s Cape Town, easily one of the toughest tickets with any currency, during peak time, perfect for people looking to ditch the weather for the holidays and catch NYE in one of the best cities on earth.

Yes, Cape Town is by far one of my favorites and for any oenophiles, a trip to nearby Stellenbosch or Franschoek is a must. Standard luggage limits apply, so definitely bring enough suitcases to haul back wine. Fin. Head to British Airways website to book.

#6152. 15 Hotels With Actually Luxurious Indoor Pools

It’s hard to nail an indoor pool—they can very easily veer into athletic club territory, where the smell of chlorine is inescapable, and every splash seems to elicit an unwanted echo. Outdoor pools, with their trompe l’oeil effects and decadent sun loungers, often get most of the credit, but some of their indoor counterparts can pull off even better architectural shows. From thermal baths powered by hot springs to top-level tanks with skyline views, the indoor pools on this list are nothing short of spectacular—not to mention, they can be enjoyed year-round, so you won’t miss out when it rains in New York or Paris. Far from your YMCA, these pools have design details you’ll swoon over: skylights, floor-to-ceiling windows, vaulted ceilings, mosaic tiling, and more. Yes, these hotels are worth booking for the awe-inspiring swims alone. Read on for the best indoor pools at hotels around the world, spanning Mexico to Vietnam.

Location: Lake Louise, CanadaThe pool: A heated pool with an adjacent steam room, featuring views of Lake Louise

Nestled in Alberta’s Banff National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, the Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise is surrounded by the best of nature. Clear blue skies, mountain peaks, the Victoria Glacier, and the emerald-colored Lake Louise create a storybook backdrop that’s worth traveling for. One of the newest and most exciting additions to the Fairmont is the 2025 opening of Basin Glacial Waters, an all-sensory thermal bathing facility that fuses nature and science to offer its guests the ultimate indoor-outdoor wellness experience. From cold plunges and steam rooms to indoor-outdoor thermal pools with some of the best views that Lake Louise has to offer, there are restorative options for every individual’s needs. White-glove service, a cutting-edge wellness space, and once-in-a-lifetime vistas await. —Meaghan Kenny

Location: New York City, New YorkThe pool: A 65-foot, heated, Japanese-inspired sanctuary

In the four decades since Aman was founded and its first property opened its doors in Phuket, the brand has come to represent a certain kind of experience for a certain kind of traveler: discreet, expansive, and intimate, with a full-bodied approach to wellness (one of the best spas in New York) and an almost chameleon-like ability to adapt to the surrounding landscape. Aman New York is the brand’s very first urban outpost in the United States and only its second urban property in the world after Aman Tokyo. The Beaux Arts landmark was carefully renovated by Belgian designer Jean-Michel Gathy of Denniston Architects; the space dazzles with a 7,000-square-foot outdoor terrace, a spa and wellness center spread over three floors, and serene guest suites (each with its own fireplace). You can swim laps in the magnificent 65-foot pool, or post up on one of the poolside chaises, which are interspersed with fireplaces. —Betsy Blumenthal

Location: Chicago, IllinoisThe pool: A heated pool with floor-to-ceiling windows offering views of Lake Michigan and the Chicago River

When the undulating tower that is the St. Regis opened in 2020, it became the tallest building in the world by a female architect (Jeanne Gang)—a title it still holds. And the wait was worth it: Glorious city, lake, and river views; a stellar hotel gym; two restaurants; and a world-class spa with an indoor pool and outdoor terrace bring a new dimension to urban luxury. Though the tower sits right above the Chicago River, the space between its circular driveway and Lake Michigan is a very posh (and quiet) residential area called Lakeshore East. The wellness floor includes a 12,000-square-foot spa and boasts an athletic club with a full fleet of state-of-the-art equipment, daily and group fitness classes, plus a dedicated Pilates reformer studio. —Heidi Mitchell

Location: Mexico City, MexicoThe pool: A heated saltwater pool on the 38th floor, adjacent to the Cityzen Rooftop Bar

The Sofitel Mexico City Reforma is a contemporary oasis to both imbibe and reset along Mexico City’s most enigmatic avenue. The property features 275 guest rooms, of which 56 are suites—for something truly special, book the Imperial Suite, which features floor-to-ceiling windows that look out onto the iconic Angel of Independence monument. The expansive urban spa (probably the best in the entire city) has hot and cold dipping tubs, both a steam and sauna room, and—best of all—a heated indoor pool, set one floor below the spa on the 38th level, where you can relax post-treatment with an unmatched view of Mexico City. But the real star of the property is Cityzen, a rooftop restaurant and cocktail bar that offers the perfect perch to view the city from above. —Michaela Trimble

Location: Torres del Paine National Park, ChileThe pool: A glass-fronted, heated indoor infinity pool located within the Uma Spa

Tinged red at dawn, the granite towers of Torres del Paine are a blazing centerpiece in Chile’s premier national park. But no view compares to the scene that greets guests from their bed at this exquisitely crafted lodge. Barely visible along the skyline, the lakeside building sinks comfortably into the landscape, giving all rooms a view onto the soaring peaks. Light pours through glass walls to illuminate a panoramic restaurant and spa with a heated indoor infinity pool, complete with a hydro-massage and water jets—watch the natural towers play hide-and-seek as clouds breeze by, and keep an eye out for guanacos and rheas, which come close to the lodge. Far from the crowd-clogged trails, this coolly unassuming property invites endless possibilities at the bottom of the world. —Sarah Marshall

Location: Cadenabbia, ItalyThe pool: Part of the Longevity Spa, an indoor vitality pool featuring floor-to-ceiling views of Lake Como

The Lake Como Edition merges palatial grandeur with the Edition group’s signature cutting-edge design. In a destination saturated with old-school addresses, this hotel might be exactly what Italy’s grandest lake needs to inject a dose of contemporary cool. Located just over an hour’s drive from Milan airport, the Lake Como Edition is housed within a restored 19th-century palazzo, and sits on the lake’s western shore in the small but charming village of Cadenabbia, just steps from the water’s edge. Across the glassy expanse, postcard-perfect Bellagio stretches into view, as ferries glide hypnotically back and forth between the shores. A standout feature of the hotel is the Longevity Spa: Facilities include an indoor pool, steam room, herbal sauna, and plunge pools, all set within a deeply tranquil space. Following a meticulous four-year renovation that was completed in 2026, creative directors Kirstin Bailey and Paul Haslhofer have carefully preserved the building’s historic bones while introducing a more contemporary aesthetic.—Lucy Bruton

Location: Bad Ragaz, SwitzerlandThe pool: A 19th-century thermal pool fed by the Tamina Gorge waters

In 1242, a bird hunter in the Tamina Gorge discovered a pure hot spring with healing minerals and a consistently toasty temperature of 97 degrees. Visitors have been traveling here to take advantage of the thermal water’s healing properties ever since. Today, that “blue gold” is one of many draws of Grand Resort Bad Ragaz in eastern Switzerland, about an hour’s drive from Zurich. Comprising four interconnected hotels, the resort offers guests two thermal spas, saunas, steam rooms, and hammams, as well as its signature NewYou Method: A holistic, evidence-based approach that uses the latest findings in medicine and wellness to help each individual. For dining options, you’ll find at least six Michelin stars among the seven restaurants, including the three-Michelin-starred Sven Wassmer Memories. There, Chef Wassmer uses the Alpine region as his seasonal pantry. —Caitlin Gunther

Location: Berlin, GermanyThe pool: A 65-foot-long indoor pool, part of a 19th-century bathhouse

Hotel Oderberger's setting is one of the most splendid in Berlin: It's inside Prenzlauer Berg's landmarked 19th-century Stadtbad Oderberger, a public bathhouse designed by architect Ludwig Hoffmann, who also created the city’s iconic Pergamon Museum. The conversion to a boutique hotel preserved many of the grand building’s original details, most notably the 65-foot-long indoor pool, set beneath a magnificent vaulted stone ceiling and surrounded by massive arched columns and huge, church-like windows. It's the first thing you see when you enter the lobby, and it definitely impresses. The 72 rooms are all unique in layout, and the modern design incorporates historic details in a clever way: Original numbered wood doors from the bathing cabins, now glassed in, live on as bathroom doors. Go for the cool historical details and great location in the heart of buzzy Prenzlauer Berg. —Jennifer Ceaser

Location: Furnas, PortugalThe pool: A thermal spring pool fed by heated volcanic waters

Octant Furnas offers a calming, restorative escape from the already serene São Miguel, the largest island of the Azores archipelago. You’ll feel taken care of at every moment, and the scenery is some of the most beautiful you’ll ever lay eyes on. It occupies the structure that was once the old Furnas Thermal Center, and while the Furnas volcano last erupted in 1630, the geothermal activity remains around both the hotel and the entire town of Furnas. That means the indoor pool is filled with naturally heated thermal water, and yes, one dip will melt all your troubles away. The hotel boasts 54 rooms of various sizes with something for parties of every size; every room is spacious, incorporating small details like Marshall speakers, and comes with robes, slippers, and sun hats for enjoying the pools. The central meeting place of the hotel is the signature restaurant À Terra, with its beautiful outdoor seating area, glass roof, and hanging plants. —Kate Kassin

Location: Cádiz, SpainThe pool: Part of the on-site spa, a light-filled indoor pool overlooking the gardens of La Alcaidesa

Oku Andalusia brings the wabi-sabi cool of its Ibiza and Kos siblings to a sprawling beachfront resort on Cádiz’s quieter stretch of the Costa del Sol. Its 255 rooms and suites pair earthy minimalism with thoughtful design details; families and groups will particularly appreciate the impressive 72 suites, private-pool options, and four-bedroom villa. Not to mention there’s a world-class kids club and extensive activity programming for toddlers to teens. Yet adults aren’t forgotten: Two child-free pools, DJs, and wellness experiences create a grown-up counterpoint. Even if you’re not booked in for a treatment, make time for the spa’s indoor pool. It is an arch-filled architectural delight, and offers a serene contrast to the cool Balearic-house soundtrack of the main pools. Oku is that rare, family-friendly resort where couples and child-free guests can still enjoy a more grown-up experience. —Bridget Mills-Powell

Location: Paris, FranceThe pool: Paris’s longest indoor pool, featuring handcrafted mosaics and digital depictions of the city skyline

Skip the sleepy districts that house so many of Paris’s plush hotels, and book a private perch with a bird’s-eye view of the river and La Samaritaine as your fashion-forward neighbor. From a sophisticated suburban crowd to the “bobos” (bourgeois-bohème) of the right bank, every type of Parisian rubs shoulders with jet-setting guests in the convivial seventh-floor Art Deco brasserie-meets-cocktail bar, Le Tout-Paris. It’s the place to be seen before you escape to the subterranean spa or your room with a view. More than half of the 72 elegant rooms, 46 of which are suites, overlook the Seine. Tucked away below ground, the brightly lit spa, designed like a modern living room, is helmed by another member of the LVMH équipe and star of both Parisian couture and beauty: Christian Dior. The nearly 100‑foot pool is said to be the city’s (and continent's) longest hotel pool; it’s designed by architect Peter Marino, situated under a mirrored ceiling, and surrounded by handcrafted mosaics by Michael Mayer and large-scale digital screens that create the effect of looking out at the Seine and Paris’s skyline. —Madison Flager

Location: Oyama, JapanThe pool: A 59-foot-long, groundwater-fed pool with a view of Mount Fuji

Practically every window, every sliding door, and every gap between the trees at Gora Kadan Fuji frames Japan’s most iconic peak, Mount Fuji. The mountain may be the star of the show here, but there’s a lot more to love when it’s shrouded in clouds. Gora Kadan Fuji’s 39 suites and three villas feature tatami, granite, paper, and cypress in a flawless blend of traditional Japanese design and contemporary comfort. Service, delivered by attentive staff in exquisite kimonos, is calm and caring. Breakfast is a succession of delicate, locally sourced morsels presented in pretty little dishes. Convivial dinners take place at the seven-seater counter of Kappo and at equally bijou Sushi Fuji Takumi, where seafood from nearby waters is transformed into seasonal nigiri. Guests soak neck-deep in communal and private onsen baths, filled from underground springs and snowmelt groundwater. The spa also has a 59-foot indoor pool with Fuji views and a small outdoor infinity pool, as well as a 24-hour gym. Gora Kadan Fuji is a place to return to in every season. —Nicola Chilton

Location: Hanoi, VietnamThe pool: One of the largest pools you'll find at any hotel in Hanoi, with views of the skyline

The brainchild of architect Carlos Zapata, whose striking design draws inspiration from Vietnam's coastline and is meant to look like a dragon rising beside the water, the 450-room JW Marriott Hotel Hanoi has become one of the capital's defining business hotels. Its generous rooms and warm, intuitive service make it a rewarding retreat from the city's frenetic center, while standout dining—from the upscale French Grill to one of Hanoi's most expansive breakfast buffets—ensures there's plenty of reason to stay in. Suspended on the eighth floor beneath soaring floor-to-ceiling windows, the enormous indoor lap pool has the scale to make swimming a proper part of your stay rather than an afterthought. The surrounding wellness complex includes a well-equipped fitness center, sauna and steam rooms, and the Spa by JW. For travelers who value space, comfort, and a quieter setting, it's an easy recommendation. —Dan Q. Dao

Location: Rabat, MoroccoThe pool: A year-round saltwater pool located within the spa

A shiny, super-sized proposition from Four Seasons, this palatial hotel successfully incorporates beautiful Moroccan touches in the shared areas and sleek luxuries in the private spaces. This would be an ideal three- or four-night stop for a bit of sightseeing and a lot of pampering as part of a wider Moroccan tour, with Rabat being a serene introduction to what is a very colorful and frenetic country. The true headliner here is the spa, which has thorough and high-end treatments for every mood, with the opportunity to relax by the magnificent indoor pool afterwards (here, you can either get your laps in, or recline in a hot tub or steam room with bottled water or even Moroccan mint tea brought to your lounge chair). There’s an effortless blending of old and new, and a devotion to looking after the guest. —Matt Charlton

Location: Melbourne, AustraliaThe pool: Located on the 64th floor, a heated infinity pool offering views of Melbourne’s skyline

When booking a stay down under, why not go to the very top? The Ritz-Carlton, Melbourne is Australia’s tallest hotel, housed in the top 17 floors of an 80-story building. The hotel’s unprecedented vantage point envelops guests in panoramic views of the city and the ocean lapping at Port Phillip Bay. If you find the views hard to pull away from, the in-house restaurant Atria, helmed by chef David Green, serves a seasonal five-course tasting menu for dinner, showcasing modern Australian cuisine at its freshest, with seats right at the window. With door-to-door valets and a Ritz Kids program where story time brings local Australian culture to life, the standard of service is as sky-high as the rooms. The chic, modern pool sits on the 64th floor, offering 24/7 access to water with an excellent view over the city.

Every hotel review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6151. American Airlines Confirms First Class “Mini-Meals” On Shorter Flights, Reveals Menu

UPDATE: American Airlines has now officially confirmed the return of first class “light bites,” beginning this month between Chicago and New York. We also have the menus, and I like what I see.

Following the report below, American has announced that first class passengers traveling between Chicago O’Hare (ORD) and New York Kennedy (JFK) or LaGuardia (LGA) will receive more substantial food starting in November 2026.

Passengers will have a choice of two light bites, with menus rotating throughout the year. These will be available exclusively onboard, with no preorder option.

To be clear, these are examples from the rotating menus, rather than a list of everything available on each flight.

This is exactly what I hoped American would offer. Smoked salmon in the morning or a shrimp salad in the afternoon sounds far more appealing than another packaged snack, particularly when traveling around a meal time. A fresh plate of food makes first class feel more like first class, and these menus suggest American is putting some thought into the offering. I would happily order several of these dishes.

The announcement also clarifies the initial scope. American has confirmed service between ORD and JFK or LGA. It has not announced a broader rollout across all flights of 700–899 miles, though I hope that will follow.

That includes my recent Boston–Chicago flight, where a light meal would have been very welcome. Hopefully, that comes next.

I remain enthusiastic about this change. Now I want to try the food and see whether the presentation and portions live up to the promise. Credit to American for investing in something passengers can actually enjoy onboard.

My original report, published November 11, 2026, follows.

American Airlines reportedly plans to bring back “light bites” in first class on flights of 700–899 miles, beginning on flights between New York and Chicago. I love this concept. A shorter flight does not require an elaborate meal, but something fresh would be a welcome improvement over another trip through the snack basket.

JonNYC reports that American will restore its light-bites concept on shorter domestic first class flights, starting with New York–Chicago service.

AA:"Light bites”/mini-meals coming back to short haul domestic first class flights 700-899 milesStarting on NYC/ORD.

We do not yet have a firm launch date, menus, or a detailed rollout schedule.  American’s published dining page still lists a snack basket on flights of 500–899 miles during meal times, with meal service on longer flights. The proposed change would give passengers at the upper end of that snack-basket range something more substantial.

A full meal is not necessary on every flight, but there is a lot of room between a hot entrée with multiple accompaniments and a bag of pretzels. A ramekin of warmed mixed nuts followed by a small fresh plate would be a very fitting compromise.

Think small dishes like a bowl of fruit in the morning or hummus with vegetables in the afternoon. The point is that a modest offering can still feel thoughtful and satisfy a bit of hunger…it also adds a premium touch that would nicely distinguish American from Delta and United (Alaska Airlines, to its credit, already serves meals on shorter flights).

A recent example: I flew from Boston to Chicago on AA, a flight of 867 miles and blocked at over 2.5 hours. No real food in first class, just a snack basket. A light meal would have been very appreciated and I was hungry.

There is something frustrating about boarding a first class flight around meal times and discovering that the route falls just short of the meal threshold…so-called “exception markets” used to exist, but have been cut on AA (oddly, except for Chicago – Denver).

My hope is that American focuses on quality, though I already give AA credit for better food than on Delta and United.

I am certainly quick to criticize American when the experience falls short, but I have also enjoyed some very good meals onboard. That is worth applauding, as is this change. A larger seat remains the primary reason many people buy domestic first class. Still, when airlines ask passengers to pay a premium, the experience should reflect some care beyond the dimensions of the seat, especially when AA will be charging a lot more than Frontier.

American Airlines reportedly plans to restore light bites in first class on flights of 700–899 miles, beginning on New York / Chicago routes. The timing and actual food remain to be seen, but I am enthusiastic about the direction. This is a sensible and competitive improvement, and I hope American gets it right and expands it.
